title: Hitachi Digital, Physical AI and Manufacturing
content:
Hitachi Digital, Physical AI and Manufacturing
Prioritise Us
on Google
Hitachi Digital will combine GlobalLogic and Hitachi Digital Services under one brand from April 2027,
Hitachi Digital CEO Anand Birje outlines cloud, data and physical AI for supply chain and other complex industries
Hitachi is launching Hitachi Digital, a global digital services company designed to help manufacturing and other asset-intensive industries connect cloud, data and artificial intelligence with measurable operational outcomes.
Scheduled to begin legal operations on 1 April 2027, Hitachi Digital will combine GlobalLogic and Hitachi Digital Services under one brand. The new company will bring together software engineering, enterprise systems, operational technology (OT), cloud, data and AI capabilities for complex industries including energy, mobility and manufacturing and their respective supply chains.
Hitachi Digital targets industrial transformation
Hitachi Digital will have approximately 35,000 professionals, operations in 27 countries and more than 880 active clients.
The business will support organisations across the digital and physical layers of operations, including: cloud transformation, data and intelligence, digital operations and and physical AI.
Other enterprise services include software and product engineering, site reliability engineering (SRE), enterprise systems integration, AI development and deployment and operational technology modernisation.
The company will be headquartered in Santa Clara, California, and led by Anand Birje, Chief Executive Officer and Chairman.
The executive’s original launch statement said Hitachi Digital would combine digital engineering and operations at global scale, supported by Hitachi’s industrial experience in mission-critical infrastructure.
Anand Birje, CEO and Chairman, Hitachi Digital
Physical AI connects data to supply chain operations
Physical AI refers to artificial intelligence operating in or interacting with the physical world. In the supply chain sphere, applications may include autonomous and semi-autonomous supply chains, robotics, autonomous vehicles and AI-supported safety systems.
Hitachi Digital will focus on physical AI alongside:
Enterprise AI
Industrial data platforms
Cloud architecture
Digital twins
Robotics
Edge intelligence
Connected products
Asset performance
Operational resilience
The company said its physical AI strategy will be supported by Hitachi’s long-standing OT and industry knowledge. Target sectors include manufacturing, mobility and energy, with supply chain positioned within the wider industrial and mission-critical market opportunity.
For supply chain operators, the value proposition is the connection between digital systems and physical operations. Rather than treating AI as a standalone software layer, Hitachi Digital aims to deploy it within environments such as manufacturing plants, fulfilment sites, depots and logistics networks.
Penske Truck Leasing and Hitachi Digital have a productive partnership. Credit: Hitachi Digital
Forward-Deployed Engineers work at the operational edge
A central element of Hitachi Digital’s model is its use of Forward-Deployed Engineers (FDEs).
FDE teams, including AI specialists, data scientists and engineers, work alongside customers and technology partners in operational environments. Their role is to apply digital capabilities to real business processes rather than develop systems in isolation.
In addition to industry specific workflows in manufacturing and supply chain, FDEs could support digital control rooms, operational data capture, AI governance, safety and reliability workflows and wider integration between
enterprise
and OT systems.
Hitachi said the teams will help capture operational rules, technical know-how and tacit knowledge from frontline environments. That information can then support HMAX, Hitachi’s AI suite for social infrastructure.
HMAX grounds AI in industrial context
HMAX by Hitachi is described as a next-generation suite that brings AI capabilities to social infrastructure.
The platform is intended to help translate operational knowledge into AI-enabled systems. For individual manufacturing sectors, this could be important because industrial AI must account for site conditions, equipment constraints, production targets, safety requirements and regulatory obligations.
Hitachi’s model is based on a feedback loop in which FDEs work alongside operational teams. After the engineer teams capture rules and frontline knowledge, the resultant data and context are incorporated into AI systems.
The insight generated by AI-backed tools is then used to support operational decisions and workflows. Each deployment generates further knowledge for future use. This iterative approach is designed to make AI more context-aware and reliable in complex physical environments.
Hitachi becomes customer zero
Hitachi Digital will serve external customers while also supporting Hitachi’s own transformation programme.
The company will work with Hitachi business units including Energy, Mobility and Connective Industries. FDEs are expected to operate alongside teams at locations such as depots, substations and plants.
Hitachi’s internal businesses therefore become a customer zero: a live environment in which digital and physical AI solutions can be tested, refined and scaled before being applied more broadly.
The company said synergy revenue with the Hitachi Group grew 46% year on year in the first half.
Cloud, data and AI enter a convergence zone
Hitachi Digital’s launch is based on the view that cloud, data and
are no longer separate technology programmes.
Hitachi Digital describes a convergence period between 2025 and 2027, as organisations increasingly seek one partner capable of delivering all three capabilities together.
For manufacturing companies and their supply chain divisions, Hitachi expects this convergence to support:
Cloud-based operational platforms
Real-time data from manufacturing, distribution and fulfilment sites
Integrated enterprise and OT systems
Secure AI deployment
Scalable digital products
The strategic challenge is not only implementing an AI model. It is connecting that model to the data, infrastructure, workflows and physical assets needed to create measurable value.
Penske Truck Leasing has achieved substantial cost savings and improved operational reliability via its partnership with Hitachi Digital. (Credit: Getty)
Digital engineering and enterprise operations unite
GlobalLogic contributes digital engineering, product development and software capabilities. Hitachi Digital Services contributes enterprise systems, cloud, infrastructure and operational expertise.
Under Hitachi Digital, the combined organisation will operate as a single global company using the Hitachi brand.
Hitachi Digital will also support adoption of Lumada 3.0, Hitachi’s digital solutions and co-creation platform. Lumada is positioned as a mechanism for working with customers to develop digital solutions for industrial and social infrastructure challenges. The company said its engineering and operational expertise will continue to support intellectual property development, including HMAX and Lumada 3.0.
The new structure will include Hitachi Digital Inc. as the operating company serving clients.
Industry sectors and supply chain relevance
Hitachi Digital will target a range of vertical markets, including:
Automotive and mobility
Banking, financial services and insurance
Healthcare and life sciences
High technology and semiconductors
Industrial and manufacturing
Logistics
Energy and utilities
Media and entertainment
Retail and consumer packaged goods
Telecommunications and networking
Supply chain sits within the wider industrial, energy, mobility and logistics ecosystem. Its relevance to Hitachi Digital’s strategy comes from the sector’s need to integrate physical assets, operational technology, enterprise systems, data platforms and AI.
Key Partners
Headquarters: Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo
CEO: Toshiaki Tokunaga
Hitachi is the parent company behind Hitachi Digital and provides more than a century of experience in mission-critical infrastructure. Its industrial footprint spans energy, mobility, digital systems and social infrastructure. Hitachi will act both as the new company’s owner and as a customer zero, using Hitachi Digital to support internal transformation across operational businesses.
Penske Truck Leasing
Headquarters: Reading, Pennsylvania
President: Art Vallely
Penske is a partner that uses Hitachi Digital's services to address complex operational challenges and maintain fleet uptime. The company has achieved US$18 million in savings through proactive diagnostics work, demonstrating how connected data and predictive insight can support asset reliability and measurable operational value.

title: Webasto poised to sell its battery systems business - electrive.com
content:
According to media reports, Webasto is seeking to divest its battery systems division. CEO Jörg Buchheim stated that the company is in advanced negotiations with two strategic investors. A deal could be finalised later this year. The proceeds would provide financial relief to the struggling supplier.
Production lines at Webasto's Korea plant.
Image: Webasto
This is according to consistent reports from
Handelsblatt
Automobilwoche
, citing statements by high-ranking company representatives on the sidelines of Webasto’s 125th anniversary celebration. The Stockdorf-based group intends to use the impending sale of its battery division to stabilise its financial position. Webasto had originally explored all options, including cooperation or a partial sale, it is said. However, the two interested parties with whom Webasto is currently in advanced negotiations are “both interested in a complete takeover,” Buchheim is quoted as saying.
As a reminder: nearly ten years ago, Webasto invested significant capital in
future markets for battery systems and charging solutions
. The supplier
launched production of battery packs in Germany in 2019
– specifically at a plant in Schierling. Following this model, Webasto opened another battery assembly facility in Dangjin, South Korea, about three years later, and
expanded it further in 2024
. This was driven by ongoing orders from Hyundai-Kia for the supply of battery systems for several high-volume all-electric passenger car models. To this day, the Hyundai-Kia Group remains Webasto’s anchor customer in the battery business. In 2025, this division generated approx. €300 million in revenue.
In this context, Buchheim emphasises that while the battery business is attractive, it also requires significant investment. According to the company, the division grows by an average of 25 per cent annually, and current demand exceeds available capacities.
Automobilwoche
adds: “However, Webasto itself lacks the funds to finance this growth alone. New production capacities can […] require investments of up to €100 million.”
The sale now explicitly concerns the global high-voltage battery business.
Automobilwoche
quotes Buchheim as stating that both interested parties bring not only sufficient equity but also industrialisation expertise and access to additional applications beyond the automotive sector. The division is currently operating at a loss, but the business plan forecasts a turnaround in 2027. While the supplier would lose a lucrative growth field through a potential sale, it could avoid future financing requirements for the division and use the proceeds to pay down pressing debts. However, no information has been disclosed regarding the potential purchase price.
Speaking to
Automobilwoche
, Buchheim said: “We do not need to make distress sales.” The restructuring is fully funded even without divestments; transactions would be an additional positive effect. Available liquidity exceeds the assumptions of the restructuring expert report from October 2025. The need for Webasto to restructure at all stems from its expansion drive after the turn of the millennium, when the supplier invested in several new fields. Webasto’s core business remains automotive roof systems.
Webasto was unable to recoup its earlier investments through steep revenue growth as planned. As a result, debts of approx. €1.5 billion euros have accumulated, pushing the automotive supplier into such a precarious position that an agreement with banks became necessary last year. Under considerable pressure, Webasto negotiated an extension of existing loans and additional borrowing.
Handelsblatt
summarises: “The owner families Baier and Mey had to temporarily relinquish control over the majority of shares. 2,000 jobs were cut.” Currently, according to Chief Restructuring Officer Johann Stohner, no further job cuts are planned. However, the downsizing course will continue in the long term. The goal is to reduce debt below one billion euros through various measures, Stohner is quoted as saying.
Among these ‘further measures’,
Automobilwoche
reports, is the search for new perspectives for the electric high-voltage heating business. Webasto is seeking new owners or partners for individual activities in this area. The division is said to generate around €50 million euros in revenue. “Here, too, a strategic partner is being sought who can integrate the technology into a larger system and scale it up,” the automotive trade journal writes. The background is the price pressure in electric vehicles. “Webasto has invested heavily in high-performance heating technology but sees a trend towards more cost-effective solutions. Further innovations would first need to be industrialised – and would again tie up capital.”

title: Walmart Hails Sustainable Supply Chain Progression
content:
Walmart Hails Sustainable Supply Chain Progression
Prioritise Us
on Google
Walmart's Sustainable Commodities Report covers the 10 years of its 20x25 initiative. Credit: Walmart
Walmart CSO Kathleen McLaughlin details how a decade of sustainable procurement and regenerative agriculture have reshaped global supply chain traceability
Enterprise supply chains are facing increasing pressure to eradicate deforestation, ensure ethical labour practices, and deploy advanced traceability across their supplier networks. Marking the conclusion of its ten-year 20x25 sourcing initiative, retail giant Walmart has released its 2026 Sustainable Commodities Report, detailing how corporate procurement can fundamentally reshape global commodity markets.
The initiative, launched in 2016, aimed to transition 20 key commodities - ranging from forests and grasslands to oceans - towards more sustainable production. Walmart is making use of these lessons to shift its supplier mandates from traditional certificate trading to rigorous traceability and jurisdictional governance.
“Healthy natural ecosystems and thriving producer communities form the backbone of retail supply chains, supporting the production of the food, apparel, and other products we deliver to customers and members,” says Kathleen McLaughlin, Chief Sustainability Officer at Walmart.
Kathleen McLaughlin, Chief Sustainability Officer at Walmart
Over the past decade, our work has focused on fostering more sustainable commodity production, helping conserve high-value landscapes and seascapes, and supporting the well-being of people involved in farming, fishing, ranching, forestry, manufacturing, and other activities across global value chains
Kathleen McLaughlin, Chief Sustainability Officer at Walmart
Kathleen McLaughlin discusses the blueprint Walmart is using to move beyond sustainability commitments and into the era of accelerated, large-scale results.
Deforestation-Free Supply Chain Verification
A major evolution in Walmart's procurement strategy is the introduction of a new deforestation- and conversion-free (DCF) verification policy. Replacing its earlier broader Forests Policy, the DCF mandate applies strict sourcing compliance to high-risk commodities such as palm oil, cocoa, coffee, timber, and South American beef. The mandate is complementary to other end-user
initiatives
to improve the sustainability of certain high-risk commodities, such as palm oil.
To maintain market access, suppliers must now undergo commercial audits that require spatial verification and third-party checks. Beyond land-use management, corporate sourcing rules increasingly demand direct human rights due diligence, tying commercial supply agreements directly to worker safety.
“While progress has varied by commodity and geography, the lessons from 20x25 continue to inform Walmart's broader approach to merchandising for people and planet and our ongoing efforts across these commodity value chains,” Kathleen adds.
Walmart has introduced a new deforestation- and conversion-free (DCF) verification policy to replace its earlier Forests Policy. Credit: Walmart
Scaling Regenerative Agriculture Partnerships
To secure upstream supply chain resilience, Walmart has aggressively scaled its investments in regenerative agriculture. Moving beyond basic soil and water stewardship, the retailer now collaborates with major packaged-goods suppliers to fund technical assistance for farmers. This localised training helps agricultural suppliers adopt vital practices such as cover cropping, nutrient management, and efficient irrigation.
Walmart has also established partnerships with PepsiCo and General Mills to provide resources to support technical assistance for farmers and help them adopt regenerative practices such as cover cropping, better soil and nutrient management, and water stewardship. PepsiCo has established several other
partnerships
to strengthen the sustainability of its sourcing.
Walmart also partnered with rice suppliers and growers in Arkansas to make irrigation more efficient and encourage more sustainable rice production.
Alongside these business efforts, Walmart Foundation investments supported adviser networks, farmer training, and local projects focused on soil health, regenerative practices, and water conservation in key agricultural regions and watersheds.
The report states that "building on this progress will require broader and deeper adoption of sustainable practices, continued improvements in traceability, verification and industry capacity, and stronger measurement of environmental and social outcomes".
The latest disclosure highlights measurable supplier performance and procurement benchmarks across the global network:
Land Stewardship Scale: Participating suppliers successfully managed 34.0 million grazing acres and 10.6 million acres of major US crops under sustainable practices.
Forestry and Fibre Standards: An impressive 95.6% of private brand pulp, paper, and timber products successfully met strict DCF verification standards.
Specialty Crop Execution: Private brand coffee achieved 99.9% sustainable procurement compliance under third-party verification frameworks.
Marine Compliance: 99.1% of US canned tuna met certified sustainable criteria or qualified for strategic Fishery Improvement Projects.
Labour Rights Monitoring: Direct suppliers accounting for 98.2% of fresh produce and floral net sales supported the Ethical Charter on Responsible Labour Practices.
Key Supply Chain Partners
: As a major multinational food and beverage corporation, PepsiCo acts as a strategic supply chain partner to Walmart. Through joint funding initiatives, PepsiCo provides vital technical assistance to agricultural suppliers, helping farmers optimize fertiliser use, improve soil health, and adopt regenerative agriculture practices across critical US row crop value chains to ensure long-term procurement stability.
General Mills
: Functioning as a leading manufacturer of branded consumer foods, General Mills collaborates with retail giants to improve agricultural resilience. By partnering with Walmart, General Mills supports local initiatives and farmer training networks, driving the adoption of cover cropping, nutrient management, and water conservation practices that secure sustainable commodity sourcing networks globally, reducing upstream supply chain risks.

title: Americold Opens Global Supply Chain Innovation Centre
content:
Americold Opens Global Supply Chain Innovation Centre
Prioritise Us
on Google
Americold opened a new Global Innovation Centre at its Atlanta headquarters in late October 2026. Credit: Americold
Americold CEO Rob Chambers launches a Global Innovation Centre to centralise automated facilities and optimise temperature-controlled supply chains
Global supply chain networks rely heavily on resilient,
temperature-controlled logistics
to safeguard food, pharmaceuticals, and sensitive commercial goods. To strengthen these critical networks, Americold Realty Trust has opened a state-of-the-art Global Innovation Centre in Atlanta, centralising the oversight of its automated logistics facilities worldwide.
Bringing together data and analytics, cybersecurity, and enterprise technology, the new facility is engineered to accelerate operational decision-making. At its core sits the Global Operations Command Centre, allowing the logistics leader to monitor and manage
automated
supply chain operations from a single hub. This eliminates the need to replicate specialised monitoring at individual regional sites - a massive benefit for globally dispersed supply chain networks that require high-reliability freight management.
Americold has responded to increasing demand for order-level fulfilment, packaging, and
last-mile delivery
Americold has been investing in technology solutions to support its ecommerce solutions. Credit: Americold.
Centralising Supply Chain Automation
Americold operates more than 220 facilities across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and South America, with an aggregate storage volume of approximately 1.4 billion refrigerated cubic feet. Americold’s 24/7 cold storage facilities rely on seamless operations, with staff using voice-guided wearable technology in sub-zero temperatures. Manual picking and scanning processes, combined with the challenge of wearing protective gloves, make voice-enabled technology a key driver of productivity and worker comfort.
The dense racking systems and high product volume pose a challenge to reliable wireless network design. Metal shelving and tightly packed items can interfere with connectivity. Americold has been investing to ensure that its network design addressed these current and future needs, delivering reliable and scalable wireless connectivity for enhanced operations.
Continuous Monitoring
: Delivers 24/7 visibility over global temperature-controlled freight, remote logistics hubs, and automated warehouse inventory
Rapid Incident Response
: Centralised problem-solving prevents minor warehouse bottlenecks from cascading into major global supply chain disruptions
Data and Analytics Integration
: Leverages digital transformation tools to optimise logistics routing, cargo execution, and facility performance
Supply Chain Resilience
: Creates built-in redundancy for automated logistics facilities, safeguarding essential consumer and industrial material flows
Capital Project ROI
: Aligns enterprise technology deployments directly with large-scale commercial operational needs to drive measurable business value
Dematic collaborated with Americold to design a WLAN infrastructure that ensured reliable coverage throughout cold store facilities in Australia and New Zealand. Credit: Dematic
New technology leadership
To lead this strategic technology rollout, Americold has promoted Anita Nanda to the role of Chief Technology and Solutions Officer. Anita was previously Senior Vice President, where she led the company's global development and automation efforts, managing the expansion of advanced cold storage infrastructure.
Before joining Americold in 2022, Anita worked as Vice President with responsibility for Project Management at Dematic. Nanda brings over two decades of experience in large-scale capital projects, automation, and intralogistics engineering. Her newly expanded role will connect enterprise technology strategy directly with operational priorities, ensuring that logistics infrastructure meets the rigorous, high-speed demands of modern supply chains.
Anita Nanda was appointed as Americold's Chief Technology and Solutions Officer in September 2026. Credit: Anita Nanda/LinkedIn
Key Logistics and Technology Partners
Americold:
As a premier global leader in temperature-controlled logistics and real estate, Americold provides essential value-added services and supply chain infrastructure. The company’s new Atlanta-based Global Innovation Centre unites automation, enterprise technology, and operational expertise to serve diverse consumer and industrial sectors, ensuring highly resilient freight transport and secure cold storage solutions for modern supply chains.
Siemens:
Operating as a global technology powerhouse, Siemens specializes in advanced industrial automation, digital infrastructure, and energy systems. As an essential ecosystem player in the logistics space, Siemens provides the foundational enterprise technology, software, and hardware solutions required to drive digital transformation, securing high-speed automated operations across complex, multi-node global supply chains and warehousing distribution networks.
Dematic:
Functioning as a leading supplier of intelligent intralogistics and materials handling solutions, Dematic designs and implements automated systems for global supply chains. Dematic's deep expertise in robotics and process automation directly supports the sophisticated, high-tech distribution centers and warehousing environments that logistics providers like Americold oversee via centralised, data-driven command centers to ensure seamless inventory flow.

title: PepsiCo: Regenerative Agriculture & Supply Chain Resilience
content:
PepsiCo: Regenerative Agriculture & Supply Chain Resilience
Prioritise Us
on Google
PepsiCo and the Earthworm Foundation are collaborating to drive more regenerative agriculture practises for supply chain resilience. Credit: PepsiCo
PepsiCo is scaling regenerative agriculture practises by partnering with Earthworm Foundation to ensure sustainable and resilient supply chain operations
PepsiCo has brought more than 250 farmers across France, Spain and Türkiye into
regenerative agriculture programmes
designed to strengthen supply chain resilience and secure long-term access to ingredients for its snack brands.
The collaboration with Earthworm Foundation addresses sourcing stability through programmes tailored to local growing conditions and farmer needs.
According to PepsiCo, the initiative supports ingredient security for brands including Lay's and Doritos while building resilience into upstream agricultural networks.
Value chain partnerships emerge
The programmes reflect a model built on multi-stakeholder engagement rather than top-down mandates. Suppliers, cooperatives, grain traders and farmers work within each regional programme to address practical barriers to adoption.
Archana Jagannathan, Chief Sustainability Officer at PepsiCo Europe, Middle East and Africa, says the approach recognises where supply chains begin. "Agriculture is at the core of our business, and farmers are at the center of our efforts to help build a more resilient and sustainable food system," she says.
"Their success is critical not only to the future of farming, but to the long-term security of the ingredients, communities and ecosystems that food production depends on.
She adds that the model requires coordination across geographies. "That's why we're committed to advancing regenerative agriculture in ways that work for farmers. Across France, Spain and Türkiye, we're partnering with farmers, suppliers, cooperatives and local experts to develop approaches that reflect local conditions and priorities.
"While each program is different, the goal is the same: to empower farmers with the knowledge, tools and support they need to strengthen resilience, improve productivity and help shape the future of agriculture."
In recent years, supply chain stability has been tested significantly. Unstable weather conditions have meant that crops are more vulnerable and yields are unpredictable. By investing in regenerative agriculture, companies like PepsiCo are investing in resilience across their supply chains, as it improves water retention, increases biodiversity and creates healthier ecosystems.
Regenerative agriculture can help farmers increase yields and reduce dependence on synthetic fertilisers, therefore
operating more sustainably
and protecting their own working conditions.
Archana Jagannathan, Chief Sustainability Officer for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at PepsiCo
France connects procurement networks
In France, the work operates through RE'COL'TE, a €1.5m (US$1.6m) initiative supporting 175 farmers in Hauts-de-France. The programme brings together PepsiCo, Nestlé, Tereos, cooperatives Agora and Unéal, grain trader Groupe Carré and ADEME France's ecological transition agency.
According to Earthworm Foundation, which leads the programme, the structure combines public funding with private capital to lower adoption barriers. The model could show how
procurement coordination reduces individual risk
across supply tiers.
RE'COL'TE builds on the Sols Vivants initiative, connecting PepsiCo with rapeseed growers already embedded in regenerative networks. That existing infrastructure allows the company to extend reach across crop rotations without building new procurement channels from zero.
Paul Pontfort, a farmer in the programme, describes the value in supply chain terms. "As farmers, we must constantly strike the right balance between long-term investments and the day-to-day economic realities.
"Programmes such as RE'COL'TE help us to reduce the risks associated with adopting new practices by providing financial and technical support. This gives us the confidence we need to take the leap and invest in the resilience of our farms for years to come."
PepsiCo aims for 2030
PepsiCo aims to see regenerative agriculture, restorative or protective practices across 10 million acres of land by 2030
The goal is to sustainably source 90% of key ingredients
Work towards deforestation- and conversion-free sourcing for high-risk commodities
Focus on building farmer, community, soil and climate resilience
Spain tailors supplier engagement
In Spain, the focus has centred on mapping obstacles within the supply base. PepsiCo assessed suppliers working in rapeseed, sunflower and corn, conducted field visits and interviewed farmers to understand financial and operational constraints.
According to the company, the insights shaped programme design around specific supplier needs rather than applying uniform requirements. The approach reflects a sourcing strategy responsive to regional differences in crop economics and infrastructure.
The programme remains shaped by direct input from farmers and suppliers rather than external consultants.
Türkiye scales implementation capacity
In Türkiye, attention is on expanding implementation capacity with sugar beet farmers. Field visits, soil assessments, technical training and ongoing support help growers adopt methods suited to local conditions.
The programme covers around 480 hectares and continues to expand as practices are tested. According to PepsiCo, the model tests how quickly new methods can be validated and scaled within a single crop supply chain.
The work reflects an approach where sourcing stability
depends on supplier capability
rather than contract terms alone.
Bastien Sachet, CEO of the Earthworm Foundation
Soil health links to sourcing risk
The partnership frames soil health as infrastructure that affects supply chain continuity. Bastien Sachet, CEO of Earthworm Foundation, says the connection between soil condition and sourcing risk has become clearer through the programmes.
"Over the years, we've come to see soil for what it truly is: one of nature's most valuable infrastructures. When soil is degraded, it doesn't only put agriculture at risk; it affects water, biodiversity, climate resilience and, ultimately, society as a whole."
He adds that regional variation requires localised sourcing strategies. "Across France, Spain and Turkey, we've learned that there is no one-size-fits-all solution. By building programs around local realities and farmers' needs, we can strengthen resilience and create lasting value for farming communities and the wider food system.
"But we cannot do it alone. Accelerating the transition to regenerative agriculture requires the entire ecosystem to move together, which is why it's so encouraging to see companies such as PepsiCo investing in and supporting this transformation."
European expansion planned
The partners plan to expand the initiative across Europe, bringing together farmers, suppliers and local
partners to scale regenerative agriculture
. According to PepsiCo, the work feeds into a target of adopting regenerative, restorative and protective practices across 10 million acres globally by 2030.
The company reported 4.7 million acres under such practices in 2025.

title: Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 2 2026 - 7:16 am PT
Toyota’s luxury brand
is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.
Lexus leans on China for next-gen EV in 2027
It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.
Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.
As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.
broke ground
on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.
The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.
The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.
Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.
Toyota’s sales
plunged nearly 20%
in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.
Lexus TZ (left) and ES (right) Source: Lexus China
In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.
Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.
The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.
Lexus TZ (Source: Lexus China)
As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.
Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.
Electrek’s Take
While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.
China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.
Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.
Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.
Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

title: Electric trucks hit 50% of China's heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls
content:
Tesla Semi
electric trucks
Fred Lambert
| Nov 2 2026 - 6:44 am PT
Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.
And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.
In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.
Electric heavy trucks passed 50% of China’s sales in September 2026.
December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.
Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.
China sold almost as many electric heavy trucks in nine months of 2026 as in all of 2025.
That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.
Why Chinese fleets are switching
It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.
CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.
Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.
CATL is already
taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy
The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.
Electric is eating LNG, too
For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.
Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.
Electric trucks overtook LNG trucks in China’s heavy-duty registrations in 2026.
So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.
Diesel demand is falling
China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.
2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.
LNG and electric trucks displaced about 680,000 barrels per day of diesel in China in 2026, according to Kpler.
Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.
There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.
Meanwhile in Europe and the US
Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.
A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.
The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent
order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE
, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.
China’s electric share of heavy-truck sales is more than 15 times Europe’s.
Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.
Electrek’s Take
This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.
Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.
And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.
The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.
Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.
The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?
Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. title: Bestselling US e-bike Lectric XP4 relaunched in limited-edition with new colors and gear
content:
Micah Toll
| Nov 2 2026 - 6:05 am PT
The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.
Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.
The new Lectric XP4 Limited Editions come in three flavors: District, (black) Jubilee (pink), and Ridge (green).
Each is priced at $1,399
and includes a 750W motor, upgraded accessories, and a distinctive matte paint job. That’s just a $100 premium over the existing XP 750, yet comes with a whole new host of accessories designed specifically for each special edition model.
So while the underlying bike remains largely unchanged from the bones of the XP 750, the new packages are designed to make the XP4 even more useful straight out of the box.
Three new Lectric XP4 editions, three different lifestyles
The District edition is aimed squarely at urban commuters, sporting a stealthy Matte Black finish and an accessory package designed for daily transportation.
That includes two waterproof pannier bags, a redesigned LevelUp rear cargo rack, a heavy-duty bike lock, and an upgraded high-output headlight. There’s also a fast charger, suspension seat post with comfort saddle, and handlebar phone mount.
It’s essentially a ready-made commuter setup, particularly for riders looking to replace some of their car trips with an e-bike.
The Jubilee edition takes a more casual approach, arriving in a distinctive Matte Thistle colorway. Designed for neighborhood cruising, weekend errands, and trips to the local farmers market, it swaps the commuter-focused panniers for a front and rear cargo package and a small roll-top bag.
It also includes the upgraded headlight, lock, fast charger, suspension seat post, comfort saddle, and phone mount.
Finally, the Ridge edition is built for riders who prefer their adventures a bit farther from the pavement.
Finished in Matte Forest green, the Ridge comes with front and rear cargo accessories for carrying outdoor gear, plus a fishing rod holder on the High-Step version. The Step-Thru model instead receives a weather-resistant roll-top bag.
Like the other two editions, the Ridge also includes the upgraded lighting, lock, charger, and comfort accessories.
“We wanted to deliver ready-made, purpose-built setups that empower our community to jump on and ride without having to configure their gear from scratch,” explained Lectric co-founder and CEO Levi Conlow.
Conlow also seems particularly proud of the new finishes, calling them the three best paint jobs Lectric has produced in its seven-year history.
Same Lectric XP4 underneath
While the new colors and accessory bundles are the main attraction, the bikes retain the same core features that helped make the XP4 such a popular choice.
That includes Lectric’s in-house developed dynamic torque sensor, which measures how hard the rider pedals to deliver a more natural-feeling electric assist experience.
The bikes also feature hydraulic disc brakes, an 8-speed Shimano Altus drivetrain, and a full-color TFT display.
As with the standard XP4, riders get the familiar folding frame design, integrated turn signals and brake lights, and 20-inch puncture-resistant mixed-terrain tires.
All three limited editions are available in both High-Step and Step-Thru frame configurations.
At $1,399
, the new models aren’t trying to reinvent the XP4 formula. Instead, they’re offering a more fully equipped version of a bike that has already proven itself with American riders.
And that’s probably a smart move. Lectric has built its reputation on delivering an impressive amount of e-bike for the money, and bundling useful accessories into a relatively affordable package plays right into that strategy.
The limited-edition models are available now, though Lectric says quantities are strictly limited.
For riders who have been considering an XP4 but wanted something a bit more distinctive than the standard colors, these new editions could be a compelling reason to finally pull the trigger.
And for those looking to score an even better deal, Lectric has also officially kicked off its
Black Friday sale.
The company is calling it its biggest sale of the year, with some of its lowest prices ever and discounts of up to $800 across its lineup.
So whether you’re eyeing one of the new limited-edition XP4 models or another e-bike in Lectric’s extensive catalog, now could be a particularly good time to buy.

title: How Europe's battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

content:
battery packs
Micah Toll
| Nov 2 2026 - 1:21 am PT
Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.
And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.
The battery passport requirement comes from the
EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation
, which established
new standards
for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.
Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.
The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.
That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.
What does this mean for e-bike riders?
Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.
Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.
With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.
The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.
Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.
It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.
What about electric bikes in the US?
There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.
Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.
That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.
And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.
For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

title: Equator Renewables Asia unveils 250 kW containerized PV system - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Singapore-based Equator Renewables Asia has developed a modular, relocatable PV system featuring up to 250 kW of solar capacity in a 40-foot shipping container. The plug-and-play solution uses n-type TOPCon bifacial modules and can be deployed by two workers in approximately two to three hours, according to the company.
Emiliano Bellini
02 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
The SolarBox system
Singapore-based renewable energy developer Equator Renewables Asia (ERA) has introduced SolarBox, a containerized solar power system designed for rapid deployment at industrial sites, remote locations and temporary installations.
The system integrates 235 kW to 250 kW of PV capacity into a standard 40-foot high-cube shipping container. Once transported to a site, the preassembled solar array unfolds to approximately 120 meters in length using linked folding PV tables mounted on a roller-wheel chassis.
According to the manufacturer, a two-person crew can deploy the system in less than three hours, with deployment taking approximately two hours under suitable conditions. The design minimizes the need for conventional foundations and allows the installation to be relocated when land-use requirements change.
Each SolarBox incorporates 368 n-type TOPCon bifacial solar modules rated at 640 W, providing approximately 235.5 kW of DC capacity in the reference configuration. The modules measure 2,382 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and come with a 25-year power warranty.
The system features two 100 kW inverters in its standard configuration, providing 200 kW of AC output. The manufacturer’s specifications also list 115 kW inverter options. The electrical architecture supports 400 V three-phase output at 50 Hz or 60 Hz, with integrated DC and AC protection, surge protection, grounding, remote monitoring and energy metering.
ERA said the system is designed to operate in grid-connected and off-grid configurations, with optional integration of battery energy storage systems and diesel generators. Its prewired architecture allows connection to a site’s electrical infrastructure through a single AC connection point, reducing the amount of electrical installation work required on site.
The company offers several system configurations, ranging from a single 250 kWp unit to multi-container installations. Four SolarBox units can be combined into a 1 MW installation, while a reference hybrid microgrid configuration combines three units, totaling 750 kW, with 964 kWh of battery storage. For utility-scale applications, ERA proposes configurations of up to 10 MW using 40 SolarBox units connected through AC combiners and medium-voltage transformers.
The container measures 12.19 meters in length, 2.44 meters in width and 2.90 meters in height, with a reported gross transport weight of approximately 24 metric tons.
ERA has recently signed a memorandum of understanding with Aster Power, the energy business of Singapore-based industrial group Aster, to assess the deployment of SolarBox at facilities on Singapore’s Bukom and Jurong islands.
Announced during Singapore International Energy Week in October 2026, the agreement will see the companies evaluate the technical and commercial feasibility of deploying relocatable PV systems in large industrial environments where land may only be available temporarily.
“Many industrial sites have land that is only available for a limited time, which makes a fixed solar installation hard to justify,” said ERA CEO Frank Phuan. “SolarBox is designed for that situation. It can be set up quickly, moved when the land is needed for something else, and redeployed elsewhere.”
ERA also provided indicative capital-expenditure-based levelized cost of electricity estimates ranging from $0.0194/kWh in Australia to $0.0292/kWh in Singapore. The calculations are based on equipment costs delivered FOB China in the third quarter of 2026 and exclude transportation, installation and other ancillary costs. They should therefore not be interpreted as full project-level LCOE estimates.
The company has not disclosed the commercial selling price of SolarBox or a timeline for potential deployment at Aster’s facilities.

Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Envision Energy’s Galaxy AI campus.
Envision Energy has claimed a major step in the race to power AI by deploying a power system that integrates solid-state transformers (SST) with battery energy storage systems (BESS).
The company announced the project as the world’s first commercial deployment of an integrated 800 V DC power system in a large-scale data center.
Installed at Envision’s Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China, the manufacturer’s integrated power system combines SSTs and BESS and equipment that adjusts DC voltage for computing hardware. Envision’s Dubhe Controller, which is supported by its Dubhe energy AI model, coordinates the transformers and batteries in real time to match power supply with computing demand and sudden load swings, according to the manufacturer.
The integrated system works by using stable SST conversion to take power from 10 kV medium voltage to an 800 V DC bus, with battery storage providing both secondary power support and minute-scale backup. The power system uses millisecond-level coordination between the SST and storage to absorb load fluctuations from the graphics processing units (GPU) that do the computational work in the data center.
Data center developers and some of the world’s largest technology companies are pursuing DC architectures at higher voltages to power new facilities with a higher density of computing power per square meter. Typical data centers operate with AC running through the facility to the edge of the computing rack, before it is converted to DC. A higher voltage, DC architecture should mean more compute power per rack.
Envision’s Galaxy campus began operations in August 2026, has a planned capacity of 3 GW and more than 80% of its power is expected to come direct from renewables, according to the manufacturer. The technology company is expected to scale the approach deployed at the Galaxy campus through its Mission Gobi initiative – a program targeting 5 GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030.
Envision is also eyeing expansion in export markets and showcased its AI Power System at The smarter E Europe 2026 in Munich in July. The manufacturer brought a model of its 2.5 MW SST to the show with specifications listing a 10/13.8 kV AC Input, 800 V DC output, and 98.5% conversion efficiency.
In a press release announcing the Galaxy AI data power system, Envision Energy Senior Vice President and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems Kevin Huang said that AI data centers need power systems that can coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand.
“Our integrated 800 V DC system is now powering live computing workloads, demonstrating an end-to-end architecture that connects renewable energy supply with computing demand. This is a critical step in turning power-compute coordination from a strategic vision into an operational reality.”
The data center announcement follows Envision unveiling a new hybrid energy system for the mining and smelting industry at All Energy Australia, combining wind, solar, battery storage, and gas turbines fueled by green hydrogen or green ammonia. Operating projects include an integrated wind and battery storage power system for a green alloy production facility.

title: Solar sector corporate funding increases 45% through three quarters of 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Total corporate funding into the solar sector, including venture capital, public market financing, and debt financing, reached $25.1 billion through three quarters of 2026, according to a report from Mercom Capital Group.
Ryan Kennedy
02 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Neoen Western Downs Green Power Hub solar farm
Corporate funding, public market financing, and debt investments in the global solar sector experienced 45% year-over-year growth through three quarters of 2026, said Mercom Capital Group.
The $25.1 billion raised across 170 deals represents substantial volume growth from the $17.3 billion secured across 127 deals in the first nine months of 2025.
“Solar corporate funding increased sharply in the first nine months of 2026, driven largely by debt financing. Public-market fundraising also improved, while both corporate M&A and solar project acquisitions increased as companies expanded their portfolios, recycled capital, and consolidated their operations,” said Raj Prabhu, CEO of Mercom Capital Group.
Driving much of this expansion, announced solar debt financing totaled $20.4 billion across 80 deals through three quarters of 2026, marking a 61% increase compared to the $12.7 billion raised over 60 deals during the same period in 2025. Public market financing similarly strengthened, totaling $2.7 billion across 32 deals, up from $1.7 billion across 12 deals in 9M 2025.
Conversely, global venture capital funding for the solar sector contracted, reaching $2.0 billion across 60 deals through three quarters of 2026, down 31% compared to the $2.9 billion raised over 55 deals in the year-ago period. Solar downstream companies accounted for $1.3 billion across 39 deals during this timeframe.
The top VC transactions through three quarters of 2026 were led by Inox Clean Energy with $343 million, followed by Nexamp at $180 million, Clean Max Enviro Energy Solutions at $165 million, Amarenco at $150 million, and Erco at $129 million.
Corporate mergers and acquisitions activity expanded year-over-year, tracking 88 solar M&A transactions through three quarters of 2026 compared to 76 transactions in 9M 2025. Large-scale solar project acquisition activity also trended upward, registering 205 transactions compared to 166 transactions in the year-ago period. In terms of capacity, a total of 34.4 GW of solar projects changed hands through three quarters of 2026, up from 29 GW in 9M 2025.
Project developers and independent power producers anchored acquisition activity as the most active buyers of solar projects in Q3 2026, picking up 6.7 GW, while investment firms secured 1.2 GW. Other buyers, including distributors and engineering and construction companies, acquired 852 MW, and utilities picked up 362 MW of projects.
Notable corporate transactions over the period included Inox Solar Americas acquiring Boviet Solar for $750 million, Drax acquiring Bluefield Solar Income Fund for $737 million, NextPower acquiring Zimmermann PV-Steel Group for $378 million, Greenbacker acquiring a 59.14% stake in Dasolar for $375 million, and strategic acquisitions by TCL Solar.
“Despite the higher activity, financing conditions remained challenging. Changes in U.S. tax policies, trade restrictions, rising equipment costs, and uncertainty over project economics complicated investment decisions. Capital remained available, but access to financing and investor appetite remained uneven across the industry,” said Prabhu.

New government provisions offer businesses interest rate subsidies of 6 to 10 percentage points on loans and leases for battery storage equipment.

The Armenian government is subsiding interest rates on loans and leasing for storage devices paired with solar systems.
Government provisions, which took effect last week, introduce interest rate subsidies for eligible loans and leasing arrangements when acquiring storage systems that will store solar energy. Under the incentive, businesses can benefit from subsidies of 6 to 10 percentage points, depending on the financing arrangement and currency, for up to seven years.
A notice
posted on Arlis, Armenia’s online legal information system, states that a loan covering batteries and their components can receive an 8% subsidy when using Armenian drams, while a lease can receive a 10% subsidy. The subsidy amount for foreign currency loans stands at 6%, and is set at 8% for foreign currency leases.
In each instance, the battery storage systems must be used exclusively for storing energy produced by solar plants or solar panels to be eligible.
In a social media post, Armenia’s Minister of Economy Gevorg Papoyan explained how the state support works.
“If you have a solar plant and want to store the energy produced, you can purchase accumulators using the new state support toolkit, subsidising the interest rate on a loan or lease,” the minister said.
Armenia’s storage market is still in its relative infancy. The country’s Energy Law was amended in May to
permit the development of energy storage systems for the first time
, subject to licensing. Systems smaller than 1 MW, or those above 1 MW designed for self-consumption, are exempt from licensing.
Meanwhile, renewable energy installations in Armenia are picking up pace. Government statistics state solar accounted for 16.3% of Armenia’s electricity generation last year. The country enjoyed a
record year
for solar deployment in 2025, taking the country past
of cumulative solar capacity.

title: The impact of dust and shading on pole-mounted PV - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A year-long comparison of five PV configurations highlights how maintenance access, shading, and structural limits influence off-grid system selection. The researchers combined field measurements with analytical models to quantify these constraints and guide configuration choices.
Lior Kahana
02 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Graphical abstract
A research team from Qatar’s
Hamad Bin Khalifa University
has investigated the techno-economic performance of different pole-mounted photovoltaic configurations with the aim of identifying the most suitable designs for off-grid applications in hot, arid environments with limited maintenance access.
These systems use solar modules attached to or integrated into poles to power off-grid equipment such as streetlights, cameras, sensors, and telecommunications devices.
“Pole-mounted solar systems have traditionally been selected based on a single metric: cost per watt. Our year-long field measurements show why engineers also need to consider maintenance access, shading, and wind loads,” corresponding author Khaled Aʼamar told
pv magazine
. “To our knowledge, this is the first framework for selecting off-grid, pole-mounted PV configurations grounded in a full year of experimental measurements.”
Aʼamar said the researchers developed indices to quantify the additional design requirements associated with different constraints, alongside a six-criterion framework to help engineers select the most suitable configuration for a given site.
“The next step is to take these findings from the test bench to the street,” he said, adding that Sunray Solutions, where he serves as chairman, is seeking partners for pilot deployments of pole-integrated systems.
The researchers monitored five PV configurations at the Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute (QEERI) outdoor test facility in Doha between August 2025 and August 2026. The configurations included U-IBC and bifacial modules mounted at a 22-degree tilt or vertically, as well as an octagonal vertical PV tube. The team recorded electrical output and environmental conditions at one-minute intervals, retaining 311 days of data after screening.
Using low-irradiance data, the researchers sized PV arrays to meet a daily load of 1 kWh, assessed installation footprints, and estimated battery storage requirements based on three reference days. They used soiling measurements and geometric factors to estimate energy losses and cleaning requirements, while analytical models were used to assess shading and wind-related structural requirements.
The team calculated penalties associated with different constraints and ranked the configurations against six criteria: installed capacity, footprint, storage, maintenance, shading resilience, and structural compactness. Sensitivity analyses examined the effects of criterion weighting, temperature, and costs.
“Geometry makes a substantial difference to the impact of dust,” Aʼamar said. “When modules are never cleaned, tilted panels need 16.04% more PV capacity to compensate, compared with just 0.70% for the vertical photovoltaic tube – a 23-fold difference.”
He added that shading posed an even greater constraint under Doha’s conditions.
“Our model predicts that all the planar configurations stop producing above 67% shading, while the tube keeps operating,” he said.
“There is no single winner, though,” Aʼamar said. “Tilted bifacial modules need the least installed capacity when the site has no constraints. But when maintenance access, shading, space, or structural limits become an issue, the tube has the lowest combined penalty, even though its baseline capacity requirement is about 2.7 times higher.”
The findings are presented in the study “
Techno-Economic Analysis of Off-Grid Pole-Mounted Photovoltaic Configurations for Accessible and Inaccessible Sites in Arid Climates
,” published in
Solar Energy

title: Japan proposes 50-metric-ton trigger for solar panel recycling plans - pv magazine Global

政策分类依据: 日本环境省与经产省提出废弃光伏组件回收法规实施细则，要求大额废弃业主提前提交处置计划，属监管落实型政策，但具体机制证据不足以细分
content:
Markets & Policy
A Japanese government study group is weighing rules that would bring almost all conventional solar panels under a new recycling law, while leaving perovskite and flexible modules out for now.
Brian Publicover
02 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
recycling
Japan’s Ministry of the Environment and Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) have proposed that owners of commercial solar installations planning to dispose of 50 metric tons (MT) or more of panels be required to file an advance disposal plan. The ministries presented the proposal to a study group drafting the implementing rules for a new recycling law.
The Act on Promoting the Recycling of Solar Cell Waste was enacted on May 29 and promulgated on June 5. It must take effect within 18 months, and the government’s working schedule targets around early December 2027.
The law itself leaves key thresholds to cabinet orders and ministerial ordinances. The study group took up panel types, weights and the large-volume threshold at its first meeting on Oct. 30. It will turn to certification and processing standards in mid-November and judgment criteria in early December.
A joint council will then review the proposals from December to March before public consultation. The ministries plan to publish the rules around spring 2027, when recyclers can also begin pre-applying for certification, ahead of the law taking effect.
Under existing law, panels must be handled as waste, but recycling is not mandatory, and the government says landfill has often been chosen. The new law sets three tiers of obligations. Everyone who disposes of panels has a general duty to promote recycling. Commercial disposers, including rooftop owners who sell their power, would receive guidance and advice under government criteria. Commercial disposers above the threshold would have to file disposal plans in advance and could face government recommendations and orders. As a result, the threshold would determine which operators face the law’s most stringent requirements.
The ministries compared thresholds of 40 MT, 50 MT and 60 MT. All three would capture a similar share of panel waste expected from 2027 to 2050: 38.7% at 40 MT, 38.3% at 50 MT and 37.9% at 60 MT. The difference is in which plants are covered. At 40 MT, 8,368 facilities would be covered, including 1,263 of 600 kW or less. At 50 MT, the figure falls to 7,398, with none of that size. At 60 MT, it is 6,784.
The ministries said 40 MT or 50 MT would capture the majority of plants of 1 MW or more. Of 6,267 module models installed in Japan, 99.3% correspond to 40 MT or more per megawatt of capacity, 94.9% to 50 MT or more and 72.2% to 60 MT or more. The ministries said 50 MT would avoid excessive regulation of smaller plants while focusing requirements on operators they consider able to recycle cost-effectively.
Industry news outlet IRU-MIRU reported that most study group members backed 50 MT, while some argued for 40 MT to widen coverage.
To prevent operators from staying under the threshold by breaking one project into several smaller disposals, the ministries proposed counting panels removed from the same plant during a single decommissioning or repowering within a set period, about one year as a guide, as one disposal. Replacements after disasters or equipment failures, and routine maintenance swaps, would not count as split disposal if documented.
The law would apply only to panels weighing at least 3.7 kg each. The cutoff is meant to exclude small products such as calculator cells while covering almost all conventional modules. The lightest module model installed since 2011 weighs 4.7 kg, and, with one small exception, the lightest earlier model weighs 3.7 kg.
Silicon modules, which the ministries said account for about 95% of global production, would be covered, along with copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) and cadmium telluride (CdTe) thin-film panels. Single-glass, double-glass and building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) panels would all be included, as the ministries said processing routes exist for these designs.
Double-glass modules made up 39.3% of Japanese shipments in 2025, based on data from 17 members of the Japan Photovoltaic Energy Association (JPEA). In a survey of 81 waste processors, 46 (56.8%) said they could accept double-glass panels and 21 (25.9%) said they could accept BIPV panels. A recent study found that
targeted recycling of glass-glass modules
lowers energy use and climate impact but reduces the value of recovered materials.
Organic cells, including both glass and film perovskite, would be excluded, along with gallium arsenide and other specialty compound cells and glass-fiber flexible panels. The ministries said recycling technologies and processing routes for these do not yet exist, and that the scope would be reviewed as technology and markets develop.
Since July 2022, solar projects of 10 kW or more under Japan’s feed-in tariff and feed-in premium schemes have had to set aside funds for decommissioning costs. The new law adds recycling and disposal-plan requirements on top of that.
The government projects end-of-life panel waste will peak at up to about 500,000 MT a year in the 2040s, well above an earlier estimate of 170,000 MT to 280,000 MT a year around 2035 to 2037.
The perovskite exclusion comes as Japan pushes the technology. The government aims to
deploy 20 GW of perovskite solar by 2040
, and in September it said it would
exclude silicon modules from new subsidies to prioritize perovskite
. In October,
Panasonic began selling glass-based perovskite panels
, a product type that falls outside the proposed scope.

title: Belgian spin-off Noak raises €5 million for perovskite-silicon solar cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Noak will use the seed funding to industrialise its perovskite-silicon tandem technology, which combines a proprietary layer stack with a 3D woven back-contact foil.
Patrick Jowett
02 Nov 2026
Research & Development
perovskites
Noak, a new spin-off from Leuven-headquartered research and development hub
Hasselt University
(UHasselt), has raised €5 million ($5.6 million) in seed funding to scale and industrialise perovskite-silicon tandem solar technology.
The investment is provided by Belgium’s Helios Foundation, Limburg-based climate investment company Nuhma and V2HFin, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Flemish Energy Holding that invests in Flemish start-ups and scale-ups.
Noak builds upon imec and UHasselt’s intellectual property portfolio on perovskite-silicon tandem technology, which is underpinned by over a decade of research within the partners’ Institute for Materials Research at the university’s campus.
It centres around a perovskite layer stack, developed through proprietary chemical compositions and scalable deposition techniques. imec and UHasselt say they have accumulated five years of outdoor operation across over ten test sites on three continents, withstanding intense sunlight, heavy rain, extreme heat and sub-zero temperatures across Asia, Europe and North America.
“This extensive real-world dataset provides a strong foundation for Noak,” a statement released by the partners says. “Building on it, the next phase will focus on demonstrating long-term stability and performance at scale, key requirements for bankability and commercial success.”
The tandem cell architecture is complemented by Noak’s proprietary 3D woven back-contact foil, which integrates the electrical connections at the rear of the cell. The partners explains this eliminates the need for front-side metallisation, in turn reducing shading losses while supporting more efficient material use and easier recycling at the end of the module’s life.
Noak’s tandem can be subdivided into smaller sub-cells connected in series and parallel, which the partners add allows for design flexibility and enabling reductions in metal usage
“The 3D foil and tile architecture make it possible to drastically reduce the use of expensive and rare metals,” they explain. “These innovations address both cost and critical raw material dependency, key concerns for future solar scalability.”
Noak CEO Geert Palmers commented the spin-off is aiming to “design a value chain through global industrial partnerships without relying on vulnerable critical dominant dependencies.
“This will enable [us] to navigate between expensive protectionism and volatile globalism.” he added.
