title: Zwitterions could be much more than defect passivators in perovskite solar cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Chinese researchers have reviewed the potential of zwitterions to improve the efficiency and stability of perovskite solar cells through defect passivation, crystallization control, and interface engineering. They found that these compounds could also enhance charge extraction, stabilize the perovskite structure, and suppress ion migration and electrode degradation.
Emiliano Bellini
02 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Researchers at
Zhengzhou University
in China have reviewed the potential applications of zwitterions in perovskite solar cells, concluding that the compounds could improve device efficiency and stability through mechanisms extending beyond conventional defect passivation.
Zwitterions
are electrically neutral molecules containing both positively and negatively charged functional groups. “This dual-charge structure gives zwitterions a broader interaction scope than conventional Lewis acid/base passivators, single ionic additives, or some polymer-based modifiers,” the scientists explained. “Depending on their molecular structure and location in the device, zwitterions can participate in defect passivation, crystallization modulation, and interfacial energy-level tuning within one integrated molecular unit.”
Previous research has primarily focused on using zwitterions to passivate ionic defects in perovskite absorbers. More recent studies have explored their incorporation into precursor solutions and application at device interfaces to reduce non-radiative recombination, suppress ion migration, and improve charge transport.
According to the researchers, the effectiveness of these mechanisms depends on the molecular structure, incorporation method, and location within the device, making zwitterions promising multifunctional additives rather than single-purpose passivation agents.
Bulk engineering
The review identified three main functions of zwitterions within the perovskite absorber: defect passivation, crystallization regulation, and phase stabilization.
The researchers explained that the oppositely charged groups can interact with defects such as undercoordinated lead ions, halide vacancies, and defects associated with organic cations, reducing charge-carrier trapping and non-radiative recombination.
Betaine-type zwitterions have been the most extensively investigated, although amino-acid-based and other functionalized compounds have also shown promising results. In tin-based perovskites, for example, the addition of L-asparagine increased cell efficiency from 10.54% to 13.31%, while formamidine sulfinic acid enabled an efficiency of 22.06% in a wide-bandgap device.
Zwitterions can also influence precursor coordination, nucleation, and crystal growth, producing more uniform films with fewer pinholes and improved crystallinity. Depending on their chemical structure and processing conditions, they can accelerate or delay crystallization and modify grain size and orientation.
The review also highlighted their ability to stabilize the photoactive black phase, particularly in cesium- and formamidinium-based perovskites. Other reported benefits include reduced ion migration, improved lattice integrity, suppressed tin oxidation, and reduced residual mechanical stress.
Interface engineering
The researchers also examined the use of zwitterions at interfaces between the perovskite absorber and the electron transport layer (ETL) or hole transport layer (HTL), where they can simultaneously passivate defects and improve energy-level alignment.
At ETL/perovskite interfaces involving tin oxide (SnO2), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and zinc oxide (ZnO), zwitterions can interact with defects on both sides of the interface. Their molecular dipoles can also modify work functions and reduce electron extraction barriers, while influencing perovskite nucleation and crystal growth.
The review identified liquid-type zwitterions as a potential solution to the poor solubility and processing limitations of conventional solid-state compounds.
At HTL/perovskite interfaces, zwitterions can facilitate hole extraction, suppress surface recombination, and improve chemical stability. They can be applied as surface modifiers or incorporated directly into transport materials such as PEDOT and nickel oxide (NiOx).
In one study, a zwitterionic additive increased the average efficiency of PEDOT devices from 10.29% to 14.29%. Another approach using L-tryptophan at the NiOx/perovskite interface achieved efficiencies of 23.79% and 20.41% for devices with bandgaps of 1.56 eV and 1.68 eV, respectively. The latter devices also maintained stable performance for more than 1,600 hours.
Electrode engineering
The review also explored zwitterionic interlayers at electrode contacts, where molecular dipoles can adjust metal work functions, improve energy-level alignment, and facilitate charge extraction.
In one study, a zwitterionic polymer interlayer increased cell efficiency from 17.31% to 19.16%, while a carboxylate-based compound improved efficiency from 15.08% to 17.10%.
Beyond contact optimization, zwitterions can limit ion migration and electrode corrosion, particularly at silver contacts. The researchers highlighted a naphthalene diimide-based zwitterion capable of capturing both silver and iodide ions, thereby suppressing interfacial degradation.
Looking forward, the academics said future research on zwitterions should develop clearer design and evaluation frameworks. “By constructing a comprehensive database encompassing molecular descriptors, processing parameters, and device performance metrics, supervised learning models can be trained to predict optimal zwitterion candidates for specific functional layers. Furthermore, generative models could be explored to propose novel zwitterionic structures beyond the existing chemical space,” they stated.
“Zwitterions may evolve from important auxiliary modifiers in current high-efficiency perovskite solar cells into a key molecular platform for advancing perovskite photovoltaics toward long-term stability, scalability, and practical application,” the scientists concluded.
Their work was presented in the paper “
Research progress of zwitterions in perovskite solar cells
,” which was recently published in
Sustainable Chemistry for Energy Materials

title: Pakistan seeks consultant for distributed solar project - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A tender is open in Pakistan searching for a consultant to verify all non-solar works that form part of a 100 MW distributed PV project in the region of Gilgit-Baltistan. The deadline for expressions of interest is November 30.
Patrick Jowett
02 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Off Grid
Residential
Pakistan’s Private Power and Infrastructure Board (PPIB), a statutory organisation under the country’s Ministry of Energy, is searching for a consultant to support the development of 100 MW of distributed solar power plants.

state the distributed PV plants will be built in the northern region of Gilgit-Baltistan. PPIB is responsible for procuring the consultancy, while the Water and Power Department of the government of Gilgit-Baltistan is the executing agency.

title: Retractable photovoltaics for wastewater treatment - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Germany’s largest retractable solar roof, with a capacity of 2.745 MW, is under construction at a wastewater treatment plant in Stuttgart. Scheduled for completion in 2027, the system will generate more than 2.2 GWh annually, covering around 9% of the plant’s electricity demand.
Sandra Enkhardt
02 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
A retractable solar roof comprising 5,280 photovoltaic modules is under construction above the aeration tanks at the main wastewater treatment plant in Stuttgart-Mühlhausen, Germany. According to local utility Stadtwerke Stuttgart, the system will have an installed capacity of 2.745 MW upon completion in the second quarter of 2027, making it Germany’s largest retractable solar roof.
The modules will cover a total area of 17,493 m2. Installation work began in June. One of the main challenges is integrating the supporting structures and framework into the existing infrastructure at a height of five meters while the wastewater treatment plant remains fully operational.
Stadtwerke Stuttgart said the system will comprise 120 retractable roof sections suspended from steel cables. Each section will be equipped with an individual motor, allowing the modules to be extended or retracted as needed. The modules can be retracted during snowfall, strong winds or hailstorms, as well as at night. The system is expected to be connected to the grid this winter.
Swiss solar technology supplier dhp Technology is implementing the project using its Helioflex retractable solar roof technology. The supporting structure comprises approximately 250 metric tons of steel. Preparatory work began in 2025, including modifications to the existing aeration tanks, before installation of the steel structure and retractable roof sections started in mid-2026.
The retractable design also allows the solar modules to be moved aside during crane operations and maintenance work, ensuring continued access to the wastewater treatment infrastructure. In addition to generating electricity, the elevated installation will provide shade for employees working around the aeration tanks during summer. Each of the 120 retractable sections will accommodate 44 solar modules, with an average rated output of approximately 520 W per module.
Once operational, the installation is expected to generate more than 2.2 GWh of electricity annually, all of which will be consumed on site. This will cover approximately 9% of the wastewater treatment plant’s total electricity demand. The electricity will help offset consumption from energy-intensive equipment, particularly the compressors used in the biological wastewater treatment process.

title: US scientists rediscover rare firefly species missing for 43 years
content: In a rare sighting from a meadow at Brandywine Creek State Park in Delaware, U.S. researchers have spotted a “lost” firefly that went missing nearly four decades ago. Scientists consider a species “lost” if it hasn’t been sighted for at least a decade.​The prolonged disappearance period of nearly 43 years for Pyractomena similis, commonly called a similar firefly, pushed conservationist group Re:wild to include it among its “Most Wanted list of lost species.”Spotted while sending mating signalsHistorically, researchers recorded these flies in several parts of the eastern and southeastern United States, including Washington, D.C., Maryland, Virginia, South Carolina, Alabama, and Mississippi. ​Scientific records show it was last seen in 1983. Two years ago, researchers began their hunt at two historical sites near Appomattox, Virginia, where the similar firefly had been observed decades earlier. However, the search was unsuccessful.​The insect was recently rediscovered by scientist Christopher “Kitt” Heckscher and his team, who began their hunt in suitable habitats in Maryland and Delaware.The search ended earlier this year in June, when Heckscher noticed a striking flash pattern, a typical signal of these insects, in a meadow with grasses, shrubs, and low vegetation that had largely been allowed to grow naturally.​He noticed eight to twelve male flies were emitting a unique light signal: ten to twenty short, amber flashes in rapid succession. They paused for a brief moment before beginning the next series. Heckscher noted these were courtship signals sent by male fireflies to attract the females during the mating season.​Recognizing the signals, Heckscher suspected they were ‘similar fireflies’ and confirmed their identity by placing them under a microscope and examining their male genitalia.Lost due ​to habitat loss, fewer lookoutsScientists believe there could be multiple reasons for a species to fade away, ranging from as simple as not enough people are looking for them or their numbers are dwindling due to habitat loss.​In the case of P. similis, both reasons could be true.​He suspected that the natural habitat of the similar firefly, which are open meadows, fields, or farmland with grasses and scattered shrubs, especially near freshwater such as streams, rivers, marshes, or wetlands, are “not terribly common” anymore. ​Most suitable habitats are being lost to development, intensive agriculture, or frequent mowing. As a consequence, the species might be in decline, he added.​A 2024 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service report found that the rate of wetland loss has risen in American states since 2009 and increased by 50 percent. As of 2019, nearly 95 percent of freshwater wetlands cover less than 6 percent of the lower 48 states, which is half the area they covered in the 1780s.​Besides habitat loss, artificial light at night is a potential threat for this species, which belongs to a family of lightning bugs. Streetlights and lighting on buildings and in gardens can make courtship signals harder to detect, reducing reproductive success, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). However, this study has not yet examined this aspect.​Further, the study reports that ‘similar firefly’ is not the only one among the firefly species in the United States and Canada to be lost. There are around 28 more from a total of 178 that remain lost, accounting for around 16 percent.​The findings were published recently in the Journal of Lost Species.

title: MIT uses flexible nanoparticle links to create stronger new materials
content: MIT and University of Delaware researchers have disproved a twenty-year rule in nanotechnology by demonstrating that nanoparticle assembly does not require rigid molecular connectors.Scientists previously believed that flexible connectors caused structures to collapse into disorder. But the team showed that super-flexible, charged polymer connectors let nanoparticles spontaneously reorganize and form customizable, open material structures. This flexible assembly method makes it easier to scale designer materials for applications in medicine, energy, and photonics.“People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into,” said Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering. “This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn’t been investigated before. It’s exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive. It’s the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail. We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well,” Macfarlane explained. Flexible ligandsNanoparticles are tiny structures designed down to the billionth of a meter, making them ideal building blocks for modern materials science. The highly customizable shapes enable applications ranging from drug delivery systems to energy storage devices.However, scaling these tiny components into larger, functional superlattices has been tough. Standard assembly techniques use rigid connector molecules called ligands. These stiff arms force nanoparticles into tightly packed, highly dense arrangements. Dense packing works for basic structures, but it severely limits the physical properties nanoparticles can form. Furthermore, custom rigid shapes for every new material are expensive, fragile, and difficult to scale.“We thought, ‘Let’s do the exact opposite: make the bonds so flexible it doesn’t matter what direction they’re initially pointing.’ The ligands can then reorganize as the particles come together, and that reorganization itself limits how many neighbors each particle can bind,” said Macfarlane.Scalable customizationThe team designed flexible polymer arms with electrically charged tips rather than pre-programming rigid connection angles through complex chemistry. The floppy chains bend and stretch to reach nearby partners as opposite charges attract.As the nanoparticles come together, the flexible connectors spontaneously reorganize to maximize bond stability. Researchers can tune a network’s structure using this self-adjusting behavior, which limits how many neighbors each particle binds to. Further, modifying the nanoparticle sizes, ligand chain lengths, or overall electrical charges allows full control over the resulting material.Researchers successfully produced previously unseen crystal lattices through natural molecular deformation. Lowering the density of nanoparticle networks opens key technological opportunities, including precise light control for photonics, open frameworks for chemical catalysis, and smart hydrogels for targeted drug delivery.This development bridges the understanding between theoretical nanoparticle control and practical application. Embracing flexibility over rigidity gives materials scientists a scalable blueprint for designing custom materials from scratch.The findings were shared in the journal Nature Materials.

title: Meta builds humanoid prototype in three months to explore home tasks
content: Meta has developed a humanoid robot prototype in partnership with Chinese robotics company Fourier to explore potential applications for home robotics. According to a report, the robot was built in just three months, with development of a second version beginning in September. Standing about 4.11 feet (1.5 meters) tall and weighing 105 pounds (48 kilograms), the humanoid reportedly uses NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor computing platform. Meta’s requirements focus on human interaction, including voice recognition, gestures, and eye contact, although the company says the collaboration is limited to internal research and experimentation.Meta enters roboticsMeta has developed a humanoid robot prototype in collaboration with Chinese robotics company Fourier, marking a step forward in its efforts to explore human-centered robotics. Internally named Max, the robot was reportedly developed in three months using customized hardware based on Fourier’s existing robotic platforms. According to The Information, Meta began developing a second version, Max 2, in September, with planned improvements to its hands, torso, and sensing capabilities.The humanoid reportedly uses NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor computing platform, which provides the processing capabilities needed to support its robotic functions. The project combines Fourier’s humanoid hardware experience with Meta’s interest in developing robots that can interact naturally with people.According to information available, Max incorporates several modifications to Fourier’s existing designs, including changes to its body proportions, head, display, and camera arrangement. The robot also features five-fingered hands designed to manipulate small objects, including bottles and toys. Chest-mounted speakers provide audio output, while its face can display expressions to support communication.Fourier’s experience with humanoid robots provided a foundation for the project. Its GR-3 humanoid, for example, is designed for close interaction with people and integrates hearing, vision, and touch capabilities. However, Max is not simply a modified GR-3. The Information describes it as a customized platform drawing on hardware and engineering experience from three generations of Fourier robots.Targets household roboticsMeta’s reported design requirements place considerable emphasis on how the robot perceives and communicates with people. These include recognizing spoken commands from a distance of approximately five meters and interpreting gestures, such as waving, from around three meters away.The company also wants the robot to maintain eye contact during interactions and communicate its operating state. This includes indicating whether it is listening, processing information, speaking, or uncertain about a task.These requirements suggest that Meta is exploring ways to make humanoid robots easier to interact with in everyday environments. However, they represent development targets rather than independently verified capabilities Max has demonstrated.The second-generation prototype, Max 2, is expected to incorporate several hardware changes. These reportedly include a redesigned torso, improved hands, and a projector. Additional sensors are also planned to help the robot navigate stairs and better understand its surroundings.The development effort extends beyond the initial prototype. According to The Information, Meta has been recruiting robotics engineers in Shanghai and Shenzhen, with positions covering prototype development and preparations for potential large-scale manufacturing.The humanoid project follows Meta’s acquisition of Assured Robot Intelligence, a company specializing in robot learning and artificial intelligence. The acquisition adds expertise in developing AI systems that allow robots to understand their environments and perform physical tasks.Meta’s broader interest in humanoid robotics also reflects its efforts to connect its consumer AI technologies with physical machines. The Information reported that Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth has discussed humanoid robots internally as a potential physical embodiment of the company’s Muse AI agent.However, Meta has clarified that its partnership with Fourier is currently limited to research and experimentation. A company spokesperson told The Information that Meta has no plans to sell the robots developed through the collaboration.According to the report, the prototypes therefore remain part of an internal development effort rather than a confirmed commercial product program. The project signals Meta’s growing interest in humanoid hardware, but questions remain about the robots’ ability to perform complex household tasks and operate safely around people.

title: New gel fuel could improve rocket and satellite propulsion
content: Concordia University researchers developed a kerosene-based gel that addresses a longstanding challenge in space propulsion: keeping fuel stable in storage and letting it flow into engines. A kerosene-based gel developed by Concordia researchers could make rocket and satellite fuels easier to store and control. The new material combines kerosene, lecithin, and calcium chloride to produce a gel that behaves more like a soft solid at rest but flows when subjected to force or heat, according to a study. Liquid fuels can slosh around tanks, complicating spacecraft control. A press release by Concordia continues that conventional gel fuels, however, can be difficult to work with. The new gel is designed to solve this problem. The research, conducted by Pranay Mudaliar and Jerin John, an associate professor of mechanical, industrial and aerospace engineering at Concordia University, examines how the gel responds to shear, temperature, and the addition of ethanol.Their findings, published in Langmuir, could help address the challenges the industry faces with conventional liquid and gel propellants, including fuel movement inside tanks and pumping fuel into engines.Its transparent appearance could also help researchers observe how fuel moves and burns.The problem of fuel Liquid propellants, because of their material, can become unstable. But fuel gels present other challenges, as they are difficult to pump and spray. So Concordia researchers developed this novel material that can act as both. When at rest, it remains solid, but when exposed to force or heat, it flows. The study explains that calcium chloride turns lecithin into long, worm-like structures called micelles. These structures form a mesh-like network that immobilizes the kerosene, producing a material with liquid and solid-like properties.The gel exhibits strong shear thinning, meaning its viscosity decreases 100 times as the shear rate increases, which is the secret sauce to making rocket and satellite fuel easier to store and deliver to engines.At rest, the gel, as a solid, could reduce problems caused by liquid fuel, such as movement and leakage, according to the university.Now, as a gel, the researchers had to figure out how to transform it into a liquid. According to the study, they used heat. At 138°F to 154°F, depending on the gel’s density, it transitioned into a liquid state, potentially offering a way to control fuel flow during propulsion operations.But adding ethanol caused the gel to liquefy almost immediately because it disrupts the micellar network that keeps the material in gel form. How long can it remain in storage?Researchers wanted to know if the material could maintain its structure in storage. According to Concordia University, samples remained stable for more than a year in sealed containers.The study reported that oscillatory testing saw an elastic linear viscoelastic regime below 1% strain. This’s associated with the gel’s ability to be stored long term. They also studied stress and strain on the material, which might cause the gel’s structure to break down. In short, this study showed how the material responds to mechanical force, temperature, and chemical changes, but its effectiveness in real propulsion systems remains to be established.Further testing is needed.

title: US' HADES completes maiden flight, promises greater reach in battlefields
content:
First flight of HADES Prototype 1
“The first
of HADES Prototype 1 transitions our vision for deep sensing from concept to reality,” said Lt. Col. (P) James Hickey, project manager for the Fixed Wing Project Office.
“This achievement reflects the dedication, technical precision, and shared mission focus of our military, civilian, and industry partners working to deliver transformational capabilities to the Army and joint force.”
Engineers, test pilots, and mission system architects synchronized aircraft structural modifications, mission system hardware integration, and preliminary baseline airworthiness verification activities to prepare the aircraft for flight.
The Army will now integrate and test HADES mission systems through a developmental flight test program. The evaluation initiative will validate multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence (SIGINT) capabilities to determine their effectiveness, integration, and operational readiness in support of upcoming operational demonstrations,
according to
a press release.
“Deep sensing is critical to maintaining decision advantage in the future fight,” Hickey said. “HADES will help commanders see farther, understand faster, and act with greater precision across the multi-domain battlefield.”
The HADES program will give the Army a modern, survivable, and responsive aerial sensing capability that supports joint force operations in contested theaters, as per the release.
One of the most important aspects of the HADES programme is its emphasis on deep sensing. Unlike conventional tactical ISR platforms that primarily support intelligence collection over relatively limited operational areas, HADES is being developed to provide enhanced sensing capabilities over greater distances and across multiple operational domains.
Its mission systems are expected to incorporate multi-domain sensing and Signals Intelligence (SIGINT) capabilities. These systems will help the Army collect and analyse information from the electromagnetic environment and other relevant intelligence sources.
In modern warfare, the ability to detect, understand and interpret an adversary’s activities before they directly affect friendly forces can provide a significant operational advantage. Deep sensing can therefore contribute to early threat identification, intelligence preparation, operational planning and improved coordination between different military components.
The capability is particularly relevant to large-scale combat operations, where commanders must maintain awareness of developments across extensive areas and multiple domains, including land, air, maritime, space and cyberspace.

title: China’s DeepSeek's new architecture can operate with less human supervision
content: Chinese AI company DeepSeek has unveiled an experimental architecture for a more autonomous AI agent designed to coordinate multiple assistants, distribute tasks and complete complex workflows with less human supervision. The proposed system, called a “super agent”, aims to address a growing limitation in AI automation: while individual agents are becoming more capable, managing several of them at once still requires considerable human attention. The proposal comes as competition intensifies between DeepSeek and US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic to develop AI systems that can take on increasingly complex software engineering tasks. Rather than simply responding to individual prompts, the next generation of coding assistants is expected to manage longer workflows, react to new information and coordinate multiple operations with limited intervention.Reducing the human bottleneck in AI automationDeepSeek argues that the growing capabilities of AI models have enabled agents to automate tasks ranging from managing calendars and drafting emails to preparing reports and writing software. However, coordinating multiple agents remains difficult because humans must still assign tasks, monitor progress and resolve conflicts between their outputs. The team estimates that a person can typically supervise only three to five active AI agent sessions at a time. That creates a practical limit on how much work organizations can delegate, even when individual agents are capable of completing tasks independently.The proposed super agent is also intended to address that constraint through a central coordinating system. It would break down larger assignments, distribute them among multiple agents working in parallel and track their progress without requiring a person to manage each session separately.The system would also be designed to respond proactively to events, rather than waiting for explicit instructions. For example, an agent could detect a software bug reported in a group chat, attempt to reproduce the problem and develop a fix. If it found a viable solution, it could submit a proposed code change for human review. Additionally, if it failed, it would remain silent rather than generate unnecessary notifications.Coding assistants become the next battlegroundDeepSeek’s latest proposal also reflects a broader shift in the AI industry, where developers are competing to build systems capable of handling entire software development workflows rather than isolated coding requests.Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex have both expanded the capabilities of AI coding assistants, allowing them to work across codebases, execute tasks and assist with more complex development processes. DeepSeek’s proposed architecture takes a different angle by focusing on how multiple agents can coordinate their work and respond to changing conditions.In experimental tests described by the company, the approach completed one task in just under 16 minutes, compared with more than 29 minutes using a conventional approach. The result suggests that parallel execution and automated coordination could reduce the time required for certain workflows.However, the benchmark alone does not establish that the system is more effective than competing coding agents. The technical article did not provide enough detail to determine how broadly the result applies, how task quality was measured or whether the approach performs consistently across different software development scenarios.

title: Which problems will quantum computers actually solve, and when?
content: Imagine designing a better battery, discovering a new medicine, or developing a material that can withstand extreme temperatures. Even the world’s most powerful supercomputers can struggle to simulate the behavior of complex molecules and materials accurately. Quantum computers could eventually help with some of these problems, potentially opening doors to discoveries that are difficult or prohibitively expensive today.But don’t expect a quantum computer to replace your laptop or suddenly solve every problem that conventional computers cannot. Its potential is much more specialized. And while companies are racing to build increasingly powerful machines, the most important applications are still taking shape. So, what could quantum computers actually solve, and how long might we have to wait?First, what makes quantum computers different?Traditional computers process information using bits, which represent either a 0 or a 1. Quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, which can exploit phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to perform certain calculations in fundamentally different ways.This does not mean they try every possible answer simultaneously. As the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) explains in its quantum computing guide, extracting useful information from a quantum calculation requires carefully designed algorithms.Their advantage comes from the ability to manipulate complex quantum states, making certain problems potentially much easier to tackle than with conventional computing.The catch? Qubits are extremely fragile. Small disturbances can introduce errors, and researchers need increasingly sophisticated error-correction systems before quantum computers can reliably perform lengthy calculations.1. Designing better medicines and chemicalsOne of the most promising applications is quantum chemistry. Molecules behave according to quantum mechanics, which makes quantum computers a potentially natural tool for simulating them.Even powerful classical computers struggle to accurately model certain complex chemical interactions, particularly in systems involving strongly correlated electrons. Quantum computers could eventually simulate these interactions more directly, helping researchers understand how molecules behave and react.That could have implications for drug discovery, chemical manufacturing, and the development of more efficient catalysts. For example, researchers could investigate molecular structures and reaction pathways to identify promising compounds or chemical processes.A particularly interesting possibility is developing better catalysts for producing ammonia, a key ingredient in fertilizer manufacturing. More efficient chemical reactions could also help reduce the energy required for industrial production.A 2025 research perspective published in the Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation, involving researchers from several national laboratories and universities, identified potential applications in photochemistry and materials design using early fault-tolerant systems with approximately 25 to 100 logical qubits.When? Early, scientifically meaningful demonstrations could emerge as fault-tolerant systems become available over the next few years. Broader applications in pharmaceutical development and industrial chemistry will likely take longer, potentially extending into the 2030s.2. Discovering better batteries and materialsWhat if researchers could simulate a material’s properties before spending years developing and testing it in a laboratory? Quantum computers could help investigate the behavior of electrons in complex materials, potentially improving the search for better battery components, superconductors, solar cells, and industrial materials.This is closely related to the chemistry problem, but the implications extend into energy and manufacturing. Better simulations could help researchers understand why certain materials conduct electricity, store energy, or exhibit unusual magnetic properties.The US Department of Energy’s Quantum Genesis initiative specifically identifies chemistry, materials science, plasma physics, and high-energy physics as potential application areas. Research applications could begin gaining traction in the late 2020s, with more substantial materials-discovery applications potentially emerging during the 2030s. These are estimates, not guaranteed delivery dates.3. Breaking today’s encryptionNot every potential quantum application is something to look forward to. Many widely used encryption systems rely on mathematical problems that are extremely difficult for conventional computers to solve. One example is the factorization of very large numbers, which underpins the security of RSA encryption.In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor developed a quantum algorithm that could theoretically solve this problem efficiently. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running this algorithm could threaten RSA and other public-key cryptographic systems.That does not mean today’s quantum computers can crack bank accounts or unlock encrypted internet traffic. They are nowhere near the required capabilities.However, the threat is serious enough that governments and technology companies are already preparing alternatives. NIST has published post-quantum cryptography standards designed to withstand attacks from both conventional and future quantum computers.The US Government Accountability Office reported in October 2026 that experts believe a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could emerge as soon as the 2030s, although estimates vary. The threat is a 2030s concern, not an established capability today. The transition to quantum-resistant encryption is already underway because sensitive information collected now could remain valuable for decades.4. Tackling complicated optimization problemsQuantum computers could also help with problems involving enormous numbers of possible combinations. Consider organizing airline schedules, optimizing industrial supply chains, managing electricity grids, or coordinating complex manufacturing operations. Finding the best solution among countless possibilities can become computationally expensive.Quantum algorithms may eventually help explore certain optimization problems more efficiently, particularly when combined with conventional computers. However, this is one area where expectations need to be tempered. There is no established evidence that quantum computers will routinely outperform the best classical methods across everyday business optimization problems.When? Experimental applications are already being explored, but commercially meaningful advantages remain uncertain. Some optimization problems may benefit during the late 2020s or 2030s, while others may never offer a worthwhile quantum advantage.So, when does the quantum era actually begin?There is no single arrival date. IBM’s current quantum roadmap targets a large-scale fault-tolerant system for 2029, while the US Department of Energy’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to demonstrate scientifically relevant fault-tolerant systems by 2028.These are ambitious development targets, not guarantees that commercially useful breakthroughs will follow immediately. The likely future is not quantum computers replacing conventional machines. Instead, they will work alongside classical supercomputers and AI systems, handling specialized calculations that are particularly difficult for traditional hardware.The first big breakthroughs may not come as a flashy new consumer gadget. Instead, they could show up as a better battery, a more efficient industrial chemical process, or a new understanding of how a complex molecule behaves.

title: Why China’s mystery warship has 3 hulls and may carry 16 missiles
content: China is testing a warship that could hide its hull underwater before surfacing to raise concealed missile launchers. Its unusual three-hull design could help keep the vessel stable as the launch tubes rise into firing position.Built in Guangzhou and now undergoing trials at Huludao on the Bohai Sea, the vessel may carry 16–18 missiles and operate without a permanent crew, according to imagery-based analysis. China has not disclosed its specifications, but the emerging picture suggests a missile carrier that combines submerged transit with surface-launched firepower.Why does it have three hulls?A trimaran consists of a central hull flanked by two smaller hulls. On this vessel, the side hulls, also called outriggers, sit toward the stern rather than extending along most of its length.The arrangement could help stabilize the vessel when its suspected missile launchers are raised. Elevating heavy launch tubes would shift weight upward, making stability an important consideration during firing.Early satellite analysis estimated its length at approximately 65 meters. Much of the vessel was then hidden beneath tarpaulins at the Huangpu shipyard, leaving its forward compartments difficult to examine.Later photographs revealed depth markings on the bow and sail, supporting assessments that the craft could operate fully or almost fully submerged. Those markings, however, do not establish how deep it can dive.A prominent snorkel provides another clue. Diesel engines need atmospheric air, and a snorkel allows them to operate while the hull remains underwater. The mast must still reach above the surface, limiting how deeply the vessel could travel while running those engines.How would its missiles launch?The central hull contains two large compartments believed to house missile tubes. Unlike fixed vertical launch cells on conventional warships, these tubes appear to be stored horizontally and raised before firing.In his latest assessment, naval analyst H. I. Sutton identifies at least eight apparent tubes. A total of 16–18 is considered more likely if both compartments contain matching arrangements.The proposed firing sequence would require the vessel to surface, open the compartment doors, and elevate its launchers. That interpretation comes from imagery analysis; the reporting does not establish a demonstrated missile launch.The weapons themselves remain unidentified. Sutton suggests anti-ship or land-attack missiles, with the YJ-20 among the possible candidates. There is no public confirmation that this particular missile has been integrated.The operating concept has a Cold War precedent. Soviet Juliett-class diesel-electric submarines carried four cruise missiles and had to surface to launch them. China’s vessel could apply a similar approach with a larger weapons load.Why might it operate without a crew?Ship-design specialist Rachel Pawling estimates that the vessel would displace approximately 900 tonnes when fully submerged. Her assessment suggests the weapons compartments occupy so much space that little remains for crew accommodation.That supports the possibility of uncrewed operation, although it does not confirm it. An open bridge on top of the sail could accommodate a pilot during harbor movements.Its potential role also helps explain the design. An arsenal ship primarily carries weapons, while other platforms can supply information needed to locate and engage targets. The Chinese vessel could therefore function as a missile carrier within a wider network.Such an arrangement would make targeting data and communications important dependencies. Submerging could offer concealment, but surfacing to prepare and launch missiles would create a period of greater exposure.For now, its speed, endurance, diving depth, control arrangements, and operational status remain undisclosed. Available evidence points to an unusual experimental missile platform, but its eventual capabilities remain unresolved.

title: China backs sodium-ion battery expansion with tax exemption through 2028

政策分类依据: 中国财政部等出台税收政策，对钠离子电池消费税豁免至2028年，属对清洁能源电池的税收支持工具
content: China is giving sodium-ion batteries a temporary tax advantage over conventional lithium-ion technology as manufacturers look to bring the alternative chemistry into commercial electric vehicles. One of the country’s leading sodium-ion battery developers, Hina Battery, is planning a 10 GWh production base in Wuhan and has partnered with a vehicle manufacturer to develop electric sanitation trucks.The expansion comes as China introduces a consumption tax on specified lithium-ion batteries while exempting qualifying sodium-ion batteries through 2028. The policy could improve the economics of sodium-ion production, although falling lithium prices have narrowed the cost gap between the two chemistries.The technology is also attracting attention for its performance in extreme cold. FAW Jiefang reported that one of its electric heavy trucks equipped with a sodium-ion battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity during testing at minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit.Creating a tax advantage for sodium-ion batteriesChina’s Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs and State Taxation Administration issued Announcement No. 20 (2026) on July 16, revising consumption tax rules for several battery categories.From September 1, 2026, specified lithium-ion batteries became subject to a 2% consumption tax. The rate is scheduled to rise to 4% on September 1, 2027. Qualifying sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries and fuel cells are exempt from the tax through December 31, 2028, provided they meet applicable national standards. The exemption gives sodium-ion manufacturers a temporary fiscal advantage, but it does not automatically make their products cheaper to produce. Battery-grade lithium carbonate averaged approximately $13,500, per metric ton on October 28. Meanwhile, square lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells for electric vehicles averaged about 5.7 US cents, per watt-hour on October 22.Sodium is more widely distributed geographically than lithium, potentially offering manufacturers a more diversified raw-material supply. However, the downstream sodium-ion supply chain remains concentrated in China, particularly in cell manufacturing, cathode materials and hard-carbon production.Hina targets commercial vehicle production in WuhanHina Battery signed an agreement with Wuhan’s Jiangxia District on October 14 to establish a sodium-ion battery production base with planned annual capacity of 10 GWh, with the first phase expected to provide 3 GWh of capacity.Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, with initial production targeted before the end of that year. The project was announced during the fourth National Sodium Battery Symposium, showcasing China’s effort to move sodium-ion technology beyond laboratory development and into larger-scale manufacturing.Hina has also signed a separate agreement with Chengli Special Automobile Group to develop sodium-ion-powered sanitation vehicles. The planned lineup includes refuse collection trucks, hook-lift vehicles, dust-suppression trucks and food-waste collection vehicles.Sodium-ion batteries have several potential advantages over lithium-ion alternatives, including access to more widely available raw materials and the possibility of better performance in low temperatures. Their main limitation remains lower energy density, which can translate into heavier or larger battery packs for the same amount of stored energy.

title: The secret to finding aliens may be hidden in firefly's flashing pattern
content: For decades, the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) has largely operated on the assumption that if aliens are trying to contact us, they will probably use signals that resemble our own technology. This has meant looking for unusual radio transmissions and, more recently, optical laser signals. However, what if an alien civilization communicates in a way that is nothing like human technology? A new study suggests we may be overlooking an entirely different approach to finding extraterrestrial signals, one inspired by the flashing patterns of fireflies. Rather than trying to understand what an alien message says, scientists propose looking for a signal that stands out from its natural surroundings.“The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) has historically been a search for aliens like us, shaped by human-centric ideas of intelligence, communication, and technology. However, humans are not the only instance of an intelligent, communicating species on Earth, and thus not the only guide to how we might think about ETI,” the study authors note.What fireflies can teach us about alien communicationThe problem with conventional SETI strategies is that they tend to search for signals that humans recognize as potentially intelligent. Yet intelligence and communication do not necessarily have to follow human patterns. On Earth, animals such as dolphins, crows and fireflies communicate in ways that are very different from ours.Fireflies offer a particularly interesting example. During mating season, these insects use sequences of flashes to attract potential partners. Their signals vary in timing, duration, color and repetition rate, helping them distinguish themselves from other fireflies flashing nearby. Producing these flashes also costs energy and can attract predators, giving the insects reasons to make their signals both distinctive and economical.Inspired by this behavior, researchers developed a simplified mathematical model to explore how an extraterrestrial civilization might make its transmissions recognizable against the natural signals already present in space.They drew on earlier research examining how firefly mating signals could evolve to become more distinguishable from competing signals in a crowded environment while conserving energy. They applied the same underlying idea to astronomy where an artificial signal might not need to be complicated if its structure makes it noticeably different from the natural activity around it.“Our model demonstrates that alien signals need not be inherently complicated nor must we decipher their meaning to identify them; rather, signals might be distinguishable as products of engineering or evolutionary design,” the study authors added.Making an alien signal stand out from pulsarsFor their model, the researchers turned to pulsars, rapidly rotating, highly magnetized neutron stars that emit regular beams of radiation. As these beams sweep across Earth, they appear as remarkably consistent pulses. Their regularity makes them interesting candidates for comparison because a deliberately transmitted alien signal could potentially resemble a pulsar’s emissions.The researchers used data from 3,724 pulsars in the Australia Telescope National Facility database to generate simulated radio-pulse patterns. They converted the pulsar profiles into simple binary sequences, assigning a value of 1 when the measured radio brightness exceeded a selected threshold and 0 when it fell below it.For their main experiment, they selected 158 pulsars located within five kiloparsecs, or approximately 16,000 light-years, of Earth. These formed the natural astronomical background against which hypothetical alien transmissions would have to stand out. The selected pulsars had mean flux densities above 1 millijansky (mJy) at 1,400 megahertz, the frequency used in the main test. This frequency is close to the famous 1,420-MHz hydrogen emission line. Radiation at this wavelength, around 21 centimeters, can penetrate interstellar dust clouds, making it useful for astronomical observations and a potential choice for extraterrestrial broadcasting.The model then generated repeating radio-pulse patterns designed to be as different as possible from the surrounding pulsar signals while minimizing energy consumption. It focused on two properties: the period between repeating pulses and the fraction of each period during which the signal remained switched on, known as its absolute duty cycle. The researchers also accounted for differences in the timing, or phase, of incoming pulsar signals. The optimization produced two signal structures: one that prioritized maximum distinctiveness without considering energy costs, and another that balanced distinctiveness with the energy required to transmit. The latter treated the fraction of time a signal remained switched on as a measure of its energy cost. The resulting approach suggests that an artificial signal could be recognizable without being particularly complex or carrying a message that humans could decipher.Finding intelligence before understanding itThe study offers a different way to think about the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Instead of assuming that alien civilizations must communicate through elaborate messages, scientists could first look for signals whose patterns appear deliberately different from their natural surroundings.However, this remains a conceptual demonstration, not a system that has discovered an extraterrestrial transmission. Converting continuous pulsar profiles into simple on/off sequences also discards finer details that could contain useful information. Moreover, an unusual signal is not necessarily artificial, so the approach would need to distinguish engineered patterns from naturally occurring ones in real astronomical observations, an ongoing challenge for radio telescopes searching for extraterrestrial technology.“This would complement, not replace, existing SETI methods,” the researchers note. Their broader message is that scientists may need to look beyond familiar forms of technology and consider the fundamental properties that make a signal recognizable as artificial. After all, an alien civilization might not need to send us a complicated message to announce its presence. It might simply need to stand out.The study is published in the journal Scientific Reports.

title: Scientists Discover a New Type of Depression That Common Antidepressants May Miss
content:
Researchers have identified a possible subtype of depression linked to disruptions in the body’s internal clock. Credit: Shutterstock
For some people with hard-to-treat depression, the body’s internal clock may help explain why standard antidepressants fall short.
University of Sydney
researchers have identified a proposed subtype called “circadian depression,” marked by disrupted sleep and daily rhythms. It accounted for nearly a quarter of participants in a study of more than 10,000 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.
The findings, published in the
British Journal of Psychiatry
, suggest that recognizing this pattern could help clinicians identify people who may benefit from treatments targeting the body clock earlier in their care.
“Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression,” said first author Dr. Emiliana Tonini, from the university’s
Brain and Mind Centre
A Depression Pattern Hidden in Sleep
Using clinical and genetic information from the nationwide
Australian Genetics of Depression Study
, the researchers classified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Its features included seasonal episodes, sleeping longer when depressed, waking up exhausted, and a tendency to stay up late.
These symptoms point toward the circadian system, the body’s internal 24-hour timekeeping network that regulates sleep and wakefulness. The researchers identified genetic characteristics of the subtype that could help explain why treatments aimed at other brain pathways are less effective.
Participants with circadian depression were more likely to have developed depression earlier in life and experienced more severe symptoms (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). They also had greater genetic susceptibility to inflammatory and cardiovascular conditions and major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.
“Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them,” Tonini said.
Why Standard Antidepressants May Fall Short
SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are commonly offered as initial treatments for depression. People with the circadian subtype reported less benefit and more side effects from these medications.
The researchers suggest that this group may respond better to behavioral and medical therapies targeting the brain circuits involved in circadian rhythms. Options include light therapy, melatonin, and antidepressants that act on melatonin pathways.
Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse, from the Brain and Mind Centre, said, “Because circadian depression is linked to people’s internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.
“For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.”
Recognizing Circadian Depression Earlier
For young people, identifying this pattern early could help avoid unsuccessful initial treatments and additional side effects, according to Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist.
“We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.
“Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition.”

title: Human Bodies Are Producing Two Billion Tons of CO2 a Year
content:
Scientists have uncovered a largely overlooked component of the global carbon cycle, revealing how population changes are reshaping the amount of CO
humans produce. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased dramatically over three decades.
The carbon dioxide produced by human bodies as they convert food into energy increased by 74% over three decades, according to a University of Bath-led study. By 2015, the global total had reached an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) annually, highlighting a substantial component of the Earth’s carbon cycle that scientists had not previously quantified on this scale.
Unlike emissions from burning fossil fuels, the CO
humans exhale largely comes from carbon recently absorbed from the atmosphere by plants and transferred through food. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas releases carbon that has been stored underground for millions of years, adding it to the active carbon cycle.
Population Growth Drove Most of the Increase
To estimate global emissions from metabolism, the researchers analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO
production in people ranging from infants to older adults. They combined these findings with worldwide population and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic activity changed over time.
Professor Javier Gonzalez, who led the research at the University of Bath’s Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism, explained:
“We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven’t had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.
Improving Our Understanding of the Carbon Cycle
“What we’ve found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.”
Human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment, particularly in densely populated cities. Accounting for that activity could help researchers develop more accurate carbon budgets and better assess the effects of strategies designed to reduce emissions.
Why Human Breathing Is Not Driving Climate Change
The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest people should exercise less, change their diets, or attempt to reduce the carbon dioxide they breathe out. The purpose is to improve scientific measurements of carbon movement, not identify respiration as a contributor to fossil fuel emissions.
Gonzalez stressed the distinction: “The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We’re not saying that breathing is driving climate change.
“What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO
people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs.”

title: Scientists Discover That a Giant Bird Thought Extinct for Thousands of Years Never Actually Disappeared
content:
The common crane (pictured above) is the same species as a prehistoric giant crane once thought to be extinct, according to new ancient DNA research. Credit: Shutterstock
Ancient DNA analysis has challenged a 150-year-old belief about a giant bird thought to have disappeared after the last Ice Age.
For more than 150 years, scientists believed that enormous crane bones found in European caves belonged to a giant bird species that disappeared after the last Ice Age. Now, ancient DNA has overturned that identification, revealing that the supposedly extinct bird was actually a larger version of a species still living in Europe today.
Researchers at Bournemouth University (BU) found that the fossils attributed to
Grus primigenia
belonged to the common crane. Their findings also raise questions about whether other prehistoric birds classified as extinct species were simply larger forms of birds that survive today.
Ancient DNA Solves a 150-Year-Old Mystery
The mystery began in the 19th century when French biologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards examined unusually large crane bones discovered in caves in southern France. Believing they represented a distinct species, he named the bird
Grus primigenia
. The remains dated to the end of the last Ice Age and were long considered evidence of an extinct giant crane.
To investigate the bird’s identity, a team led by Dr. John Stewart, Professor of Evolutionary Paleoecology at BU, analyzed ancient DNA from 18 crane bones recovered across England, Wales, France, Germany, and the Balearic Islands. Working with the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden, the researchers used genetic evidence to determine which species the bones belonged to.
“Previous studies had merely used the size and shape of the bones to attempt to understand these large birds. The use of DNA analysis has given us a more accurate picture of what they represent,” Stewart explained.
Why Scientists Mistook the Cranes for an Extinct Species
The genetic findings indicate that the oversized fossils belonged to common cranes rather than a separate extinct species. Stewart believes differences in body size between male and female cranes may have contributed to the original misidentification.
“We suspected that these large cranes were not extinct and instead represented larger, modern European common cranes. We believe that the reason for the mistaken identity was that cranes have large males and smaller females, and we think this contributed to previous speculation that there were two different species: the living, common crane we see today and the extinct, larger species,” Stewart said.
What Caused Ancient Cranes to Shrink?
Although the DNA evidence clarifies the birds’ identity, it leaves another question unanswered: Why were some prehistoric common cranes considerably larger than those living today?
“The challenge going forward is to investigate the reason for the cranes decrease in size. Wetland drainage and human land use changes are what we suspect, but more work is needed to resolve that,” Stewart said.
The researchers plan to investigate whether changes in wetland habitats and human land use contributed to the reduction in crane body size. These remain possible explanations rather than established causes.
Could Other Supposedly Extinct Birds Still Exist?
The findings suggest that some prehistoric bird species identified primarily through fossil measurements may need to be reconsidered. Differences in bone size do not necessarily indicate separate species, and ancient DNA could help determine whether other supposedly extinct birds were actually larger or smaller populations of surviving species.
“While it is true that many species of birds are vulnerable to human actions today, it may be that we have overestimated the number of extinctions in the past,” Stewart said.
“Some of these may instead represent size changes to living species,” he concluded.

title: Scientists Finally Identify Mysterious Creature Nearly 90 Years After It Was First Found
content:
Colobothrix deckeri. Mesibov, 2026. Credit: Image by Ben Parslow, SAMA.
A mysterious millipede first collected nearly 90 years ago has resurfaced in South Australia.
A millipede first collected nearly 90 years ago in South Australia has finally been identified as a new species, challenging assumptions about where its moisture-loving relatives can survive. Named
Colobothrix deckeri
, the species belongs to the family Dalodesmidae, which typically inhabits damp environments. Yet its original collection site receives just 400 to 500 millimeters (15.7 to 19.7 inches) of annual rainfall, making it the first member of its family recorded from such a dry region of Australia.
The new species also possesses an unusual microscopic feature. Mature males in Dalodesmidae and certain other millipede families have tiny, ball-shaped structures on their legs called sphaerotrichomes, normally topped by a long, pointed bristle known as a seta. In
C. deckeri
, that bristle is reduced to a short, blunt rod. This distinctive anatomy inspired the new genus name
Colobothrix
, meaning “stunted hair.”
A Museum Specimen Overlooked for Decades
The discovery began with a specimen collected in 1936 on South Australia’s lower Yorke Peninsula. It remained unidentified in the South Australian Museum (SAMA) until 2015, when German researcher Peter Decker encountered it while examining borrowed museum specimens for his doctoral research on a different millipede family, Paradoxosomatidae.
Recognizing that the animal belonged to Dalodesmidae, Decker sent photographs of its microscopic features to Australian millipede specialist Robert Mesibov. The specimen provided the first evidence that this family occurred in dry South Australia. Mesibov searched the original collection area in 2016 and 2017, but neither expedition located another specimen. He later named the species in Decker’s honor, publishing the description in the peer-reviewed, open-access journal
A cluster of sphaerotrichomes on a leg of C. deckeri. Scanning electron micrograph image by Robert Mesibov. Credit: Robert Mesibov
An Unexpected Connection to Kangaroo Island
Unknown to the researchers at the time, additional specimens had already been collected about 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the original location. In 2010, arachnologists Michael Rix and Danilo Harms were surveying spiders and leaf-litter invertebrates on Kangaroo Island when they discovered a remarkable
new assassin spider species
in the island’s relatively wet northwestern region. Their collections also included several unidentified millipedes, which were deposited in the Western Australian Museum (WAM).
The island’s devastating 2020 bushfires later destroyed the original collection site, raising fears that the rare assassin spider might be approaching extinction. During a follow-up survey in 2021, arachnologist Jessica Marsh found the spider at additional locations several kilometers (a few miles) away. Her collections of other invertebrates also contained specimens of the unidentified millipede.
A Rediscovery Nearly 90 Years in the Making
In early 2026, Mesibov discovered the Western Australian Museum’s millipede record online and contacted curator Mark Harvey. Close-up photographs supplied by Harvey confirmed that the Kangaroo Island specimens belonged to the same species collected on the Yorke Peninsula in 1936.
Mesibov subsequently visited Kangaroo Island and successfully located living specimens near the earlier collection sites. “Third time lucky!” said Mesibov. “I found the new millipede alive and well this year at relatively wet sites not far from its 2010 and 2021 localities.”
He collected several specimens for the formal species description and future genetic research. The specimens collected in 1936, 2021, and 2026 are now housed at the South Australian Museum.
Could the Millipede Be Hiding Beneath the Limestone?
Although
C. deckeri
has been confirmed on Kangaroo Island, researchers still do not know whether it survives at its original Yorke Peninsula location. That mainland site receives considerably less rainfall than the species’ known habitats in northwestern Kangaroo Island.
Mesibov suspects that the peninsula’s underlying limestone could provide a possible explanation for how the millipede survives in such a dry environment.
“The 1936 locality is underlain by limestone,” said Mesibov, “and the rock is broken where it is exposed at the ground surface. I wonder if the species survives in small voids in this bedrock, as a relict from wetter periods in South Australia’s past. That might explain why I couldn’t find it in 2016 and 2017, and how it could persist in such a dry climate.”

title: Scientists Create a Tiny Electronic Device That Can Learn Like the Human Brain
content:
Innovative components based on an oxide interface, developed by researchers at the ctd.qmat Cluster of Excellence in Würzburg, electronically replicate key functions of neural networks and open up new prospects for energy-efficient hardware. Credit: Image: Jochen Thamm, think-design
A breakthrough in brain-inspired electronics could lead to devices that process information and learn without relying on conventional computing architectures.
A single nanoscale electronic component can perform three different jobs, switching electrical current, storing information through resistance, and remembering past electrical activity through changes in capacitance. Researchers in Germany have demonstrated this versatility using unusual oxide materials, opening a possible path toward computer hardware that processes information and adapts more like the human brain.
Today’s artificial intelligence systems can consume enormous amounts of electricity, particularly during the training of large models. One reason researchers are exploring alternative hardware is that conventional computers typically separate memory from computation, requiring information to move between them. The brain operates differently. Its neurons communicate through synapses, connections that can change in response to repeated or intense signals. This ability to adapt, known as neuroplasticity, helps the brain learn from experience.
An Unusual Material Interface That Can Learn
A research team at the University of Würzburg, working within the Würzburg and Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, has developed electronic components that reproduce several important behaviors of neurons and synapses. Their approach uses complex oxides, materials whose electrical properties can be adjusted to support different functions within the same system.
The devices rely on two materials: lanthanum aluminate (LaAlO₃, or LAO for short) and strontium titanate (SrTiO₃, or STO for short). Both are electrical insulators individually, but when brought together, they form an extremely thin conductive layer at their interface. This layer, called a quasi-two-dimensional electron gas, allows electrons to move through a region confined to the boundary between the materials.
Three Electronic Functions in One Tiny Device
Using this material platform, the Würzburg researchers created components that can act as a transistor, a memristor, or a memcapacitor. A transistor controls current flow, while a memristor stores information through changes in electrical resistance. A memcapacitor behaves differently: its ability to store electrical charge depends on its previous electrical state.
The researchers demonstrated that a single nanoscale component can provide any of these three functions depending on how it is connected electrically. This versatility could simplify the design of artificial neural networks built directly into electronic hardware.
“What makes our platform so exciting is that we can realize very different functions using the same material system. This brings us closer to hardware that not only computes but can also learn directly within the component and temporarily store information,” says Soumen Pradhan, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Technical Physics in Würzburg.
Toward More Energy-Efficient Brain-Inspired Computing
“Brain-inspired computing” seeks to reproduce some of the brain’s information processing and learning mechanisms in electronic circuits. Rather than continually transferring data between separate processing and memory units, these systems aim to combine computation, information storage, and adaptation within individual components.
“Complex oxides are an especially exciting field for us because they combine many electronic properties in a single material platform. That is precisely what makes them so interesting for a new generation of energy-efficient and adaptable computer hardware,” says Ralph Claessen, spokesperson at JMU Würzburg for the Würzburg–Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat and a co-author of the study.
Future Applications in Wearable Health Technology
One potential application is health monitoring. Wearable devices incorporating this type of adaptive electronics might eventually analyze physiological signals directly, without requiring separate computing hardware for every processing task.
Such “self-learning” sensors could potentially track heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen saturation, or blood glucose while adapting their responses to incoming data. Processing signals locally could also reduce the energy required to transfer information to external systems.
For now, these possibilities remain long-term goals. The research demonstrates the underlying electronic functions rather than a complete artificial intelligence system or medical sensor. Further development will be needed to establish whether the technology can deliver practical improvements in energy consumption, reliability, and performance.
Reference: “Oxide interface-based polymorphic electronic devices for neuromorphic computing” by Soumen Pradhan, Kirill Miller, Fabian Hartmann, Merit Spring, Judith Gabel, Berengar Leikert, Silke Kuhn, Martin Kamp, Victor Lopez-Richard, Michael Sing, Ralph Claessen and Sven Höfling, 9 April 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-71642-2
