title: This Unusual Spider’s Genome Is Roughly 50% Larger Than a Human’s
content:
This trapdoor spider, named after comedian Stephen Colbert, has an outsized genome. Credit: Jason Bond / UC Davis
Scientists have sequenced the unusually large genome of a trapdoor spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert, uncovering surprising features of its DNA.
A spider no bigger than a quarter has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome. Known as
Aptostichus stephencolberti
, this elusive trapdoor spider lives beneath California’s coastal dunes and carries 4.6 billion DNA base pairs. Researchers at the
University of California, Davis
, have now sequenced its genome, uncovering features that could help explain how spider DNA has evolved.
“At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it’s not the largest genome among the spiders, but it’s significant,” said Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology. The research, published in the
Journal of Heredity
, marks the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a species in this spider family.
Why This Small Spider Has So Much DNA
The spider’s enormous genome is not packed with an unusually large number of genes. Instead, approximately 77% consists of repetitive DNA sequences, stretches of genetic material copied many times throughout the genome. Its DNA is organized into 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human body cells.
Another feature involves telomeres, protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional telomere repeat sequences found in many other animals, a difference that may help explain why their chromosomes evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.
“It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life,” Bond said.
A Secretive Predator Beneath California’s Beaches
A. stephencolberti
lives in coastal sand dunes between the San Francisco Bay Area and Monterey, often sharing beaches with people who never realize the spiders are there. Females spend their entire lives inside underground burrows lined with silk and concealed beneath hinged, camouflaged doors. They detect vibrations from approaching prey and rapidly emerge to capture unsuspecting insects and other small animals.
Although these spiders use venom to subdue their prey, they are not dangerous to humans. According to Bond, among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.
Rising Seas Threaten an Already Fragmented Habitat
The genome sequencing is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative developing genetic resources to support wildlife conservation. Because trapdoor spiders rarely travel far from their burrows, populations can become genetically isolated when their habitats are separated. Examining their DNA could help scientists identify distinct populations that may need protection.
“We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us,” Bond said. “We’re hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.”
The spider’s limited coastal range makes it particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels threaten the dunes where it lives, while invasive species place additional pressure on its habitat. “They’re going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they’re also very sensitive to invasive species,” Bond said.
How Stephen Colbert Got a Spider Named After Him
The species has an unusual connection to comedian Stephen Colbert. In 2008, after learning that Bond had named another trapdoor spider after musician Neil Young, Colbert demanded similar recognition. He made his case during the “Who’s Not Honoring Me Now?” segment of his former Comedy Central program, “The Colbert Report.”
Bond granted the request, naming the species
Aptostichus stephencolberti
(the “t” in Colbert is silent). The spider’s oversized genome now provides an unexpected scientific distinction for an animal named after a comedian known for playing an exaggerated, self-important television pundit.
Spider Venom Could Hold Untapped Compounds
Beyond conservation and evolutionary research, spider genomes may help scientists investigate venom compounds with potential medical or agricultural applications. Some molecules found in spider venoms are being studied for their possible use in pain relief, while others could offer new approaches to controlling agricultural pests.
The full range of these substances remains largely unexplored, and the newly sequenced genome could provide a foundation for further investigations.
“We don’t really know what’s out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms,” Bond said.
Reference: “Reference genome of the Californian trapdoor spider Aptostichus stephencolberti Bond 2008 (Araneae: Mygalomorphae: Euctenizidae)” by Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe, Oanh Nguyen, Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann, Merly Escalona, Robert D Cooper, H Bradley Shaffer, Erin Toffelmier and Jason E Bond, 8 September 2026,
Journal of Heredity

title: Einstein’s Equations Reveal an Unusual New Way Space-Time Can Transfer Energy
content:
A gravitational field is the region around an object where its gravity influences other objects. According to Einstein’s theory of general relativity, gravity arises from the curvature of space-time caused by mass and energy. Credit: Shutterstock
A new interpretation of Einstein’s equations reveals previously hidden rules governing how space-time evolves.
Einstein’s equations suggest that gravity may be capable of a process resembling the one behind powerful solar explosions. In a new theoretical study, physicists show how gravitational field structures can change their connections and transfer energy into matter. They call this process “gravitational reconnection.”
Luca Comisso of Columbia University and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile describe the discovery in
Physical Review D
. Their work reveals a mathematical connection between gravity and the behavior of plasmas, electrically charged gases found in stars and throughout space.
The Physics Behind Explosive Solar Flares
In plasmas, magnetic field lines can become stretched and twisted until they rearrange through a process called “magnetic reconnection.” This releases stored magnetic energy and drives powerful events such as solar flares.
“Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration,” Comisso said. “When they break and reconnect, they release energy.” He added, “It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events.”
How Gravitational Fields Can Reconnect
Gravity operates differently because Einstein’s theory describes space-time as a four-dimensional structure rather than three-dimensional space.
“Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field ‘sheets’ rather than field lines,” explained Comisso. “Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a ‘sheet.’”
These sheets are mathematical structures, not physical surfaces. The researchers found that when the conditions preserving their connections break down, the sheets can reconnect, allowing energy to transfer from the gravitational field into matter.
Hidden Rules in Einstein’s Equations
The researchers uncovered this behavior by expressing Einstein’s equations using different mathematical variables, revealing similarities with equations that describe plasmas. Their study builds on
earlier research
with Maricarmen A. Winkler that identified previously unrecognized constraints on how space-time can evolve.
“Einstein’s equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent,” said Asenjo. “By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves.”
“Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them,” Comisso said. “You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior.”
What This Could Mean for Black Hole Collisions
One potential application involves merging black holes, where extreme gravity severely distorts space-time. Scientists rely on powerful computer simulations to predict the gravitational waves produced by these collisions, which detectors such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) are designed to measure.
The newly identified constraints could help researchers determine how gravitational fields must behave without calculating every detail of their evolution.
“It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time,” Comisso said. “Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints.”
Gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical discovery. Researchers must now investigate whether it occurs in astrophysical environments, how much energy it could transfer, and whether it might produce detectable signatures in gravitational waves.
Reference: “Reconnection of gravitational fields” by Luca Comisso and Felipe A. Asenjo, 28 October 2026,
Physical Review D
DOI: 10.1103/lmqy-pf9k
The research was supported by the National Science Foundation and NASA.

title: Scientists Discover a Common Treatment for Chronic Tendon Pain May Not Actually Work
content:
Achilles tendinopathy is a common condition that causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the Achilles tendon, which connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. Credit: Shutterstock
A major clinical trial is challenging the effectiveness of commonly used injections for chronic Achilles tendon pain.
A widely used injection treatment for chronic Achilles tendon pain may offer little lasting relief, according to a clinical trial published in
. Researchers found that high-volume injections, including those containing corticosteroids, did not significantly improve pain or physical function compared with a sham procedure after one year. The findings challenge the routine use of injections for a condition that can persist for years and interfere with everyday movement.
Achilles tendinopathy causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the tendon that connects the calf muscles to the heel. Approximately 6% of people experience the condition during their lifetime, and although exercise-based rehabilitation is the recommended treatment, up to 44% of patients do not recover. Many consequently explore other options, including injections intended to reduce pain and improve tendon function.
Testing Popular Injections Against a Placebo
To investigate whether these treatments provide meaningful benefits, researchers conducted a randomized clinical trial involving 192 adults with midportion Achilles tendinopathy in Melbourne, Australia, between December 2019 and July 2022. Participants were 49 years old on average, and their symptoms had persisted for a median of two years.
The researchers divided participants into three groups receiving either a sham injection (64), a high-volume injection without corticosteroid (63), or a high-volume injection containing corticosteroid (65). The active injections delivered saline and local anesthetic around the affected tendon, with corticosteroid added in one group. Everyone also received the same exercise program, education, and guidance on modifying physical activity.
The primary measure was pain and disability after 52 weeks, assessed using the Victoria Institute of Sport Assessment-Achilles scale (0-100, where 100 is no pain or disability). Participants began the trial with an average score of 48.7, indicating substantial symptoms and functional limitations.
Steroid Injections Provided Only Temporary Relief
At the one-year follow-up, researchers obtained results from 181 participants (94%). Neither high-volume injection treatment produced a clear improvement in pain or disability compared with the sham procedure. The two active injection approaches also showed no meaningful difference in their overall outcomes.
Injections without corticosteroid failed to outperform the placebo at any assessment point. Adding corticosteroid produced small improvements after six weeks, but these benefits were short-lived. By 26 weeks, participants who received corticosteroid had worse outcomes than those given high volume injections without the drug.
An economic analysis found that corticosteroid-containing injections were less costly and generated more quality-adjusted life-years than sham treatment. However, the overall clinical results did not justify their routine use. No serious adverse events related to the trial treatments were reported.
What the Findings Mean for Achilles Tendon Treatment
The researchers acknowledged several limitations. Many participants were recruited through social media, which could affect how well the findings apply to other patient populations. Clinicians administering the injections also knew which treatment they were providing, and some observed differences may have resulted from chance.
Despite these uncertainties, the authors concluded that the evidence “should prompt clinicians to reconsider the rationale for using these injections in people with Achilles tendinopathy.”
In a linked editorial, John Orchard of the University of Sydney cautioned that corticosteroids are neither universally beneficial nor inherently inappropriate. Their use should depend on the patient’s circumstances, particularly when immediate symptom relief takes priority over longer-term outcomes (where short-term needs predominate over longer-term needs). He emphasized that patients should never be told corticosteroid injections will fix or cure tendinopathy.
“All clinicians recommending or performing corticosteroid injections for tendinopathy need to understand this trade-off and make every effort to explain the broader overview to the patient as part of the informed consent process,” he concluded.
Reference: “Efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid compared with sham for midportion Achilles tendinopathy (Inject trial): randomised controlled trial” by Peter Malliaras, David Connell, Anders Ploug Boesen, Rebecca S Kearney, Hylton B Menz, Dylan Morrissey, Shannon E Munteanu, Karin Gravare Silbernagel, Martin Underwood, Andrew Forbes and Terry P Haines, 28 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1136/bmj-2026-100807

title: Depression Symptoms Improved in Just 48 Hours After a Single Psychedelic Dose
content:
Psilocybin is a naturally occurring psychedelic compound found in certain species of mushrooms, commonly known as magic mushrooms. In the body, it is converted into psilocin, which acts on serotonin receptors in the brain, altering perception, mood, and thought processes. Credit: Shutterstock
A single dose of psilocybin produced rapid antidepressant effects in a small Swedish clinical trial, with improvements lasting for weeks.
A single dose of psilocybin, the psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms, produced rapid improvements in depression symptoms in a small Swedish clinical trial. After six weeks, 53% of participants who received psilocybin were in remission, compared with just 6% of those given a placebo.
Some participants reported improvements within two days, and the antidepressant effects persisted for more than three months in self-reported assessments. The findings come from Sweden’s first randomized, double-blind trial of psilocybin for depression, conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and published in
JAMA Network Open
Hampus Yngwe Credit: Photo: Stefan Zimmerman
Testing Psilocybin for Common Depression
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are among the most widely prescribed treatments for depression, but they can take several weeks to work, cause unwanted side effects, and provide insufficient relief for some patients. Previous research has suggested that psilocybin may act more quickly, although much of that work has focused on treatment-resistant depression or depression associated with cancer.
The new phase 2 trial investigated whether psilocybin could also help people with more common forms of recurrent depression. Researchers enrolled 35 adults between the ages of 20 and 65 who had moderate to severe symptoms. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 25 milligrams of psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin used as an active placebo because it produces noticeable physical sensations.
Both groups received psychotherapeutic support across five sessions before, during, and after treatment. During the dosing session, participants wore eye masks, listened to music through headphones, and were encouraged to direct their attention inward.
Depression Symptoms Improved Within Days
Researchers measured depression severity using the MADRS (Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale), with assessments conducted by clinicians who did not know which treatment each participant had received.
Eight days after treatment, depression scores had fallen by an average of 9.7 points in the psilocybin group, compared with 2.4 points in the placebo group. The 7.3-point difference was statistically significant and considered clinically meaningful. The advantage remained evident at assessments conducted 15 and 42 days after treatment, while participants’ own ratings indicated improvement as early as the second day.
“Our results suggest that psilocybin can provide rapid, clinically meaningful improvement in depression and may serve as an alternative to standard treatment when fast symptom reduction is important,” says lead author Hampus Yngwe, consultant psychiatrist and PhD student at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet.
Long-Term Effectiveness Remains Uncertain
Although the initial results favored psilocybin, the difference between the groups was no longer statistically confirmed after one year. At that point, 53% of participants in the psilocybin group remained in remission, but many people who had received the placebo had also recovered.
Johan Lundberg Credit: Photo: Stefan Zimmerman
“However, the long-term effects are uncertain. Repeated treatments may be needed to prevent relapse. This needs to be investigated in larger studies.”
The findings suggest that a single supervised dose may provide relatively rapid symptom relief for some patients, but the small trial cannot establish how consistently those benefits will last or whether additional doses would improve long-term outcomes.
Side Effects and the Challenge of Blinding
Psilocybin was generally well tolerated, with most reported side effects being mild or moderate and temporary. However, two participants who received the psychedelic experienced severe, persistent anxiety that required medical attention.
“It is important to emphasize that the treatment is not risk-free and that some patients may need extra support,” says Johan Lundberg, professor at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience and the Centre for Psychiatry Research, Karolinska Institutet, who led the study.
Another limitation involved the difficulty of keeping participants unaware of their assigned treatment. Psychedelics produce distinctive psychological effects, and almost everyone in the trial correctly guessed whether they had received psilocybin or the placebo. Such awareness can influence expectations and make it harder to determine how much improvement comes from the drug itself.
“We want to understand how factors such as treatment expectations and lack of blinding affect the results, as previous studies may have exaggerated the treatment effects,” says Hampus Yngwe.
Investigating How Psilocybin Changes the Brain
Researchers are now turning to biological measurements collected during the trial to investigate how psilocybin might influence depression. Their next analyses will examine PET brain scans alongside blood and cerebrospinal fluid samples obtained before and after treatment.
One area of interest is synaptic density, which reflects the number of connections through which nerve cells communicate. Depression has been associated with disrupted communication between brain regions, while preclinical studies suggest that psychedelics may promote the growth of synaptic connections. Whether comparable changes occur in people receiving psilocybin remains an open question.
“Research suggests that the interaction between parts of the brain is impaired in depression and that this may be linked to changes in the connections between nerve cells, known as synapses. In preclinical studies, psychedelics have been shown to stimulate synaptic growth. We therefore want to investigate whether psilocybin alters synaptic density in the brain,” concludes Hampus Yngwe.
Reference: “Short-Term and Late-Term Effects of Psilocybin on Symptoms in Major Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Hampus Yngwe, Pontus Plavén-Sigray, Carl Johan Ekman, Eva Henje, Anders Berglund, Mikael Tiger, Maria Beckman and Johan Lundberg, ,
JAMA Network Open
DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.12589

title: Scientists Say This Medication Could Be the Next “Wonder Drug”
content:
Sotagliflozin, marketed under the brand name Inpefa, is an FDA-approved medication that blocks two proteins, SGLT1 and SGLT2, involved in glucose transport. Credit: Stock
A diabetes medication may protect against heart attacks and strokes through an unexpected biological mechanism.
Two medications used in people with type 2 diabetes produced dramatically different results when scientists tested their ability to prevent dangerous blood clots. In mice with injured blood vessels, sotagliflozin reduced clot formation by approximately 60%, compared with just 5% to 10% for the widely prescribed drug empagliflozin.
Researchers at Michigan Medicine also found that sotagliflozin suppresses excessive platelet activity, a process that can block blood flow to the heart or brain. Published in the
Journal of Clinical Investigation
, the findings suggest a possible explanation for the drug’s ability to reduce heart attack and stroke risk beyond its effects on blood sugar.
Why Sotagliflozin Works Differently
Sotagliflozin, marketed as Inpefa, belongs to a group of medications called sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) inhibitors. These drugs interfere with proteins that transport glucose through the body. Common treatments such as empagliflozin (Jardiance) and dapagliflozin (Farxiga) primarily block SGLT2, a protein that helps the kidneys reabsorb glucose. Sotagliflozin acts on both SGLT2 and SGLT1, which is also present in other tissues.
Although SGLT2 inhibitors have established cardiovascular benefits, clinical trials have shown that sotagliflozin can also reduce ischemic events, including heart attacks and strokes. These occur when blood clots or other blockages restrict circulation. The researchers investigated whether the drug’s broader action on glucose transport proteins might help explain this protection.
“A drug that can both decrease the risk for diabetes along with the risk for having a heart attack or stroke could be a turning point in our ability safely treat this growing population in the US and abroad,” said Michael A. Holinstat, Ph.D., M.S., co-senior author and professor of pharmacology, internal medicine, and surgery at the University of Michigan Medical School.
A Powerful Effect on Blood Platelets
Scientists compared sotagliflozin and empagliflozin using blood samples from healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes. Sotagliflozin significantly reduced platelet activation and made platelets less likely to clump together. Empagliflozin produced little or no comparable effect.
Platelets normally help stop bleeding by gathering at damaged blood vessels. However, excessive activation can produce clots inside arteries, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke. Sotagliflozin’s ability to suppress this activity may contribute to its cardiovascular benefits.
“These experiments showed that sotagliflozin has a unique effect, and blocking SGLT2 alone is not enough to inhibit platelet aggregation,” said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., co-senior author and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
“Sotagliflozin may offer additional protection against blood clots, potentially lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.”
Blocking SGLT1 Explains Only Part of the Effect
The researchers next investigated whether inhibiting SGLT1 alone could account for sotagliflozin’s effects. When they genetically removed SGLT1 from mouse platelets, blood clot formation decreased by approximately 40%. However, neither this genetic approach nor treatment with mizagliflozin, a drug that selectively blocks SGLT1, fully reproduced sotagliflozin’s results.
This suggests that other biological mechanisms contribute to the drug’s ability to prevent clot formation. One possibility involves SGLT1 in endothelial cells, which form the inner lining of blood vessels and interact with circulating platelets. Researchers have not yet established whether these cells contribute to sotagliflozin’s anti-clotting effects.
“Sotagliflozin appears to be in the sweet spot because compounds that have higher levels of SGLT1-selective inhibitors can cause gastrointestinal issues,” said Bertram Pitt, M.D., co-author and professor emeritus of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
“We think this could be a wonder drug with potential to offer benefit for many conditions.”
Could the Benefits Extend Beyond Diabetes?
Sotagliflozin is FDA-approved to reduce certain cardiovascular risks in adults with heart failure and in adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and additional cardiovascular risk factors. The researchers hope to investigate whether its effects on clotting could benefit patients with other conditions, including chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm associated with increased stroke risk.
The laboratory and animal findings provide evidence that sotagliflozin affects clotting through mechanisms beyond conventional SGLT2 inhibition. However, further clinical research is needed to determine how much this platelet effect contributes to preventing cardiovascular events in humans and whether it can do so without increasing bleeding complications.
“The search for medications that reduce the risk of life-threatening blood clots without increasing the risk of bleeding has continued for decades,” Holinstat said.
“Sotagliflozin has now been demonstrated to serve both functions and may represent the next advancement in prevention of blood clots, heart failure and stroke in patients with and without diabetes.”

title: A Breakthrough in Magnetism Could Make Computer Chips Use Dramatically Less Energy
content:
Researchers have overcome a longstanding obstacle that has prevented promising materials from being used in ultra-low-power computer chips.
A promising class of materials could help dramatically reduce the electricity needed for computing, but a persistent problem has kept them out of computer chips. When these materials are made thin enough for modern electronics, the electrical and magnetic properties that make them valuable can disappear.
Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces ultrathin films of bismuth ferrite that retain their essential properties and develop an additional form of magnetism with potential advantages for future computing devices. The findings were published in
Nature Materials
Why Promising Materials Stop Working at Small Scales
Bismuth ferrite belongs to a class of materials called multiferroics, which have interconnected electrical and magnetic properties. Within their crystalline structures, positive and negative charges are displaced in opposite directions, creating electrical polarization. Applying a small voltage can reverse that polarization, allowing information to be stored as binary data (ones and zeros). Because the electrical and magnetic states are linked, the stored information could also be read magnetically, potentially enabling memory and logic devices that consume far less power.
The obstacle is a phenomenon known as the “dead layer” effect. When multiferroic films become extremely thin, their atomic structures and chemical environments can change enough to disrupt their functionality. At the same time, internal electric fields can destabilize their polarization. Together, these effects can eliminate the ferroelectric and magnetic behavior needed for electronic applications.
A New Method Eliminates the Dead Layer
The Brown team addressed both problems by carefully engineering the layers surrounding the bismuth ferrite. First, they grew the material on dysprosium scandate, a rare earth-based crystalline substrate with a smaller lattice spacing than bismuth ferrite. The mismatch places the film under compressive strain, helping preserve the atomic arrangement required for its electrical and magnetic properties.
The researchers also incorporated a metallic layer that screens unwanted electric fields, preventing them from destabilizing the film’s polarization. With both effects controlled, bismuth ferrite remained functional even at thicknesses of only a few angstroms. An angstrom measures approximately four billionths of an inch.
“We’ve established that we can get rid of the dead layer,” said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. “We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want — down to a few angstroms — and it’s still ferroelectric, and it’s still magnetic.”
An Unexpected Magnetic Property Could Improve Future Chips
Beyond preserving the material’s original properties, the engineered structure enhanced its magnetic behavior. The researchers demonstrated that the thin film exhibits altermagnetism, a magnetic state with characteristics that could overcome some limitations of conventional magnetic materials.
“Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out,” Caretta said. “The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds — they can be fast, densely integrated, and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout.”
These characteristics could eventually support faster, more densely packed electronic components while reducing energy consumption. Although the researchers have demonstrated the material’s properties rather than a finished computing device, the technique addresses a major barrier to incorporating multiferroics into practical chips, particularly as artificial intelligence increases demand for computing power.
“We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials,” Caretta said. “The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that’s useful — and sometimes even better than what nature gives us.”

title: A Mysterious Explosion in Space Just Did Something Scientists Didn’t Expect
content:
Artist’s impression of GRB 260310A. A massive star collapses and launches a jet made by a narrow, ultra-fast core (white beam) wrapped in a broader and slower outflow. The jet points away from Earth. We first saw light from the jet’s outer wings and only later from its energetic core. The inset shows the image acquired by the Large Binocular Telescope, displaying the bright optical afterglow (marked) next to its host galaxy. Credit: Fortuna/Yang/ERC BHianca
An unexpected resurgence of X-rays weeks after a stellar explosion has challenged existing models.
An explosion that initially appeared unremarkable in gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. Its visible light became brighter than its host galaxy, and its X-ray emission unexpectedly intensified again weeks later.
An international research team believes the extraordinary behavior can be explained by the direction of the explosion’s powerful jet. Rather than pointing directly toward Earth, the jet was viewed from an angle that initially concealed its most energetic region. The findings, published in
The Astrophysical Journal Letters
, suggest that some exceptionally powerful stellar explosions may be difficult to recognize from their initial gamma-ray flashes alone.
A Modest Gamma-Ray Burst With an Extraordinary Afterglow
NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected the event, designated GRB 260310A, on March 10, 2026. Its initial burst of gamma rays lasted approximately 53 seconds and appeared to release relatively little energy. Over the following hours, however, its visible afterglow steadily grew brighter before eventually fading.
The contrast became even more pronounced at other wavelengths. Compared with samples of previously observed gamma-ray bursts, the event’s X-ray and optical afterglows ranked among the brightest 1%, while its radio emission placed it among the brightest 5%. Approximately three weeks after the explosion, the X-ray afterglow brightened again, remaining unusually luminous for more than a week and detectable for months.
“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” says co-author Roberto Ricci, who led the radio observations. “We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”
A Massive Star’s Death Viewed From an Unusual Angle
Gamma-ray bursts are among the most energetic explosions in the universe. Many occur when massive stars collapse and launch narrow jets of matter traveling at nearly the speed of light. As these jets collide with surrounding gas, they generate afterglows that can be detected in X-rays, visible light, and radio waves.
Astronomers typically observe the brightest gamma-ray flashes when a jet points almost directly at Earth. GRB 260310A appears to have been different. Its relatively weak initial emission, followed by an exceptionally bright afterglow, is consistent with a jet viewed from outside its most intensely beamed region.
“Much like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on. Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” explains Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar and lead author of the study.
How a Hidden Jet Can Become Brighter Over Time
The researchers propose that the explosion produced a jet with a narrow, highly energetic core surrounded by a wider, slower outflow. From Earth’s viewing angle, the broader outer regions would dominate the early afterglow, while much of the core’s radiation would initially be directed elsewhere.
As the jet slowed, its emission became visible across a wider range of angles. Radiation from the energetic core could then reach Earth, potentially explaining the delayed increase in X-ray brightness. This structured jet model offers a possible explanation for the unusual observations, although the precise configuration remains uncertain.
“We looked at it from a side angle. As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”
The delayed X-ray brightening was particularly difficult to explain. “That was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalls Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring. “This prompted us to explore a more complex jet’s shape.”
An Explosion With Enormous Hidden Energy
To investigate the event, the international team, led by the ERC-funded BHianca group at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, combined observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESA’s XMM-Newton, the Einstein Probe mission, the Large Binocular Telescope, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. Additional observations from Calar Alto Observatory detected the signature of a supernova, confirming that the gamma-ray burst accompanied the death of a massive star.
The team’s models indicate that the jet’s central region may have carried vastly more energy than the initial gamma-ray measurements suggested. “What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” notes Yang. “Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”
The Search for Powerful Explosions Hidden From Earth
The findings also point toward a population of stellar explosions that conventional gamma-ray observations may overlook. As powerful new sky surveys, including those conducted by the Vera Rubin Observatory, expand their coverage, astronomers expect to identify more afterglows from jets that are not directed toward Earth. Such detections could help establish how frequently collapsing massive stars produce relativistic jets and how those jets escape through the stars’ outer layers.
“Gamma rays are not the most efficient route to spot these hidden jets: we find them once in a blue moon,” concludes Muskan Yadav, a graduate student who contributed to the study. “Upcoming surveys will pick up hundreds of them. Identifying them among millions of variable sources won’t be easy, but it’s a challenge I’m excited to take on.”
Reference: “An Extremely Bright Slow-rising Afterglow from an Off-axis Jet in GRB 260310A” by Yu-Han Yang, Roberto Ricci, Eleonora Troja, Muskan Yadav, Yi-Han Iris Yin, Rubén Sánchez-Ramírez, Brendan O’Connor, Niccolò Passaleva, Alberto J. title: “Nearly Everybody Had Given Up” – Scientists Finally Solve a 60-Year Chemistry Mystery
content:
Chemistry
Structure, bonding and electronic aspects of a newly-prepared oxoborane. Credit: Lukas Lubczyk, Christian Markl, Dr. Thomas Kupfer, Dr. Rian Dewhurst / University of Wuerzburg)
After more than six decades of failed attempts, chemists have achieved a breakthrough involving a class of molecules long considered too unstable to isolate.
Chemists have succeeded in isolating a group of molecules that researchers have struggled to capture for more than 60 years. Known as oxoboranes, these compounds contain an unusual triple bond between boron and oxygen, a combination long considered too unstable to isolate in a lasting form.
Researchers led by Professor Holger Braunschweig at the University of Würzburg have now developed a method that produces three surprisingly stable oxoboranes. Published in
Nature Chemistry
, the work was supported by computational research from Professor Ashwini K. Phukan’s team at Tezpur University in India.
An Unexpected Reaction Produces Elusive Molecules
The breakthrough began when Würzburg doctoral students Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl independently reacted a compound called a diboracumulene with different ketones, chemicals commonly used in organic synthesis. Instead of the anticipated products, they obtained unusual orange or yellow solids. The reactions had unexpectedly produced oxoboranes as their main products.
“The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something,” says Lukas Lubczyk.
Solving a 60-Year Challenge in Chemistry
Boron has a strong tendency to avoid forming triple bonds, making these molecules particularly difficult to synthesize. Braunschweig has spent more than 15 years investigating this type of chemical bonding. His team created the first molecule containing a boron-boron triple bond in 2012, followed by the first neutral molecule with a boron-carbon triple bond in 2025. Organic oxoboranes represented the remaining challenge involving triple bonds between boron and other elements in the first row of the periodic table’s p-block.
Chemists have pursued oxoboranes since at least the early 1960s. Although previous experiments detected or trapped them under extreme conditions, inferred their presence from chemical reactions, or produced related derivatives, researchers had been unable to isolate stable examples.
“Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them,” says Holger Braunschweig.
The successful preparation of three oxoboranes suggests that the new approach could provide access to additional members of this difficult-to-synthesize molecular family. The researchers are now investigating whether the method can be extended to produce other elusive compounds involving elements across the periodic table.
Reference: “Synthesis and isolation of stable oxoboranes” by Lukas Lubczyk, Christian Markl, Mudit Jain, Sourav Kar, Thomas Kupfer, Rian D. Dewhurst, Ashwini K. Phukan and Holger Braunschweig, 27 October 2026,
Nature Chemistry
DOI: 10.1038/s41557-026-02272-w
The work was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

title: Flexell Space and Satoro plan two in-orbit demonstrations of space solar cells
content:
Flexell Space and Satoro plan two in-orbit demonstrations of space solar cells
Flexell Space
and Singapore-based Satoro have agreed to pursue two in-orbit demonstrations of Flexell’s solar cells, one planned for 2027 and the other for 2028, each aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Under the plan, Satoro will build the CubeSat satellites, while Flexell will provide the solar cells and test modules. The companies say they will coordinate the satellite-platform and payload requirements. The demonstrations are intended to compare ground-test results with operating data collected in orbit, assessing the cells’ power output and how their performance changes over time.
Flexell is developing solar cells based on both CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide) and perovskites, including perovskite/CIGS tandem designs for space. The reported plan does not assign either technology to a specific mission.

title: 中电联发布《2026年三季度全国电力供需形势分析预测报告》-索比光伏网
content:
10月29日，中国电力企业联合会对外发布《2026年三季度全国电力供需形势分析预测报告》(以下简称《报告》)。《报告》指出，今年前三季度全国电力消费呈现总量稳增、结构调优、动能焕新、韧性增强的特征，全国电力系统安全稳定运行，电力供应结构持续绿色低碳转型，电力供需总体平衡。
《报告》显示，前三季度，全国全社会用电量8.07万亿千瓦时，同比增长3.9%。全国新增发电装机容量2.5亿千瓦，其中风电和太阳能发电合计新增装机1.7亿千瓦，占新增发电装机总容量的67.8%。
截至9月底，全国全口径发电装机容量达41.3亿千瓦，同比增长11.2%，其中非化石能源发电装机容量25.9亿千瓦，同比增长14.4%，占总装机容量比重为62.6%;太阳能发电装机规模历史性超过煤电成为国内第一大电源，风光发电装机合计已超20亿千瓦，新能源发电成为我国主体电源，发电装机延续绿色低碳发展趋势。
前三季度，全国规上口径发电量7.49万亿千瓦时，同比增长2.2%，非化石能源发电量增量占全社会用电量增量的比重为87.2%。
《报告》预测，四季度全国电力消费增速较三季度明显回升，全年全社会用电量10.8万亿千瓦时左右，同比增长4%-4.5%。迎峰度冬期间，预计全国电力供需形势总体平衡，若出现大面积寒潮天气、一次能源供应紧张等极端情况，局地高峰时段可能出现电力供需偏紧。
预计2026年全年新增发电装机有望超过3.5亿千瓦，到2026年底，全国发电装机容量将达到43亿千瓦左右，其中非化石能源发电装机约27亿千瓦，占总装机的63%左右;风电和太阳能发电装机规模达到总发电装机的一半;煤电装机占总装机的比重将降至31%左右。

title: 河北：大力推进港口“风光储充”一体化建设，加快绿色港口创建-索比光伏网
政策分类路径: 政策 > 战略规划型政策 > 产业方向
政策分类依据: 《绿动渤海》行动方案确定绿色港航、海上风电光伏等重点发展方向与路径
content:
10月29日，从省政府新闻办召开的《“绿动渤海”行动方案（2026—2030年）河北篇》政策解读新闻发布会获悉，河北围绕加快航运绿色低碳转型、推进港口低碳智能建设、赋能临港绿色产业升级、强化全域污染协同防治、健全要素支撑保障机制”五大板块，提出20项具体任务，着力打造绿色港航示范区，赋能经济强省、美丽河北建设。
加快航运绿色低碳转型
优化运输结构体系
方案从船舶、燃料、运输组织、航线网络四个维度系统推进：
01推动船舶绿色低碳转型
加快老旧营运船舶报废更新，引导新建改造船舶应用新能源清洁能源，聚焦沿海短途货船、港作拖轮、旅游游艇推广电池动力等清洁动力，支持秦皇岛山船重工等企业强化绿色船舶研发制造。
02推进船舶绿色燃料应用
研究推进港口绿色燃料加注基础设施建设，支持曹妃甸LNG码头加注改造等绿色燃料加注产业发展，有序落地绿色燃料加注示范项目。
03优化交通运输组织模式
纵深推进“公转铁”“公转水”，深入实施多式联运，建立绿色船舶库，实行绿色船舶“一船一策”、绿色航线“一线一策”、绿色走廊“一廊一策”，推广船舶“四直”绿通和“八优”快线模式，提升港口作业效率、减少船舶待港时间。
04打造绿色示范航线网络
推动唐山港至山东博兴港海河联运等绿色航线建设，探索构建国际绿色航运走廊，全面提升航运绿色化、集约化水平。
推进港口低碳智能建设
夯实绿色发展根基
01深化港口清洁能源使用
全面推进岸电设施提档升级，组建渤海“岸电使用绿色联盟”，有序推动港口作业装备新能源替代，大力推进港口“风光储充”一体化项目建设。
02加快绿色低碳港口创建
支持建设“近零碳港区”“零碳码头”“零碳运输线路试点”，聚焦黄骅港煤炭港区打造近零碳港区，到2030年专业化散货码头全部建成星级绿色港口。
03提升港口智慧绿色运营水平
依托数字化智能化技术升级运营管控体系，强化能耗排放实时监测，推进港区绿化美化和生态缓冲带建设，实现港口生产与生态保护协同发展。
赋能临港绿色产业升级
培育低碳发展动能
01有序推进海上风电光伏项目建设
加快秦皇岛、唐山、沧州海上清洁能源项目建设，推进海上风电与海洋石油、海洋牧场、海水制氢、海洋算力融合发展，结合唐秦负荷中心需求实施“海上风电+绿电直连”实施项目。
02加快推动油田绿色发展
鼓励绿电就近接入油田生产系统，推动秦皇岛—曹妃甸油田群岸电扩容，支持秦皇岛27-3油田建成“低碳零碳作业区”。
03壮大海洋绿色新兴产业
大力发展新能源船舶、高端海工装备等绿色制造产业，谋划实施秦皇岛无人船制造、智能港口设备制造等项目，有序布局海水制氢等前沿产业，培育临港经济新的绿色增长极。
强化全域污染协同防治
提升海洋生态环境
01从严管控船舶污染排放
综合运用卫星遥感、无人机巡查等科技手段构建立体化监管体系，严格船舶排放控制区监管，常态化开展燃油硫含量和尾气处理装置检查。
02系统提升港口污染治理水平
严格落实环保设施“三同时”制度，完善船舶污染物接收转运处置闭环管控，打造煤炭码头“无废港口”示范港，到2030年煤炭本质抑尘技术全面应用，干散货码头绿色化水平国际领先。
03提升海上污染应急能力
充分发挥环渤海区域海上污染应急协同机制作用，加强溢油应急队伍建设，常态化开展应急演练。
04深化海洋生态环境风险防范
动态排查涉海环境风险隐患，编制海湾生态环境风险“一湾一图”，巩固提升秦皇岛湾等美丽海湾建设成效，与天津市协同加强入海排污口监管，促进津冀区域海洋环境规范管理水平共同提升。
健全要素支撑保障机制
夯实绿色发展根基
方案从法规、金融、体系、人才、数智、履约六个方面强化保障：
01完善法规标准政策体系
修订完善《河北省防治船舶污染海洋环境管理办法》等法规，推动水运领域绿色低碳标准制修订。
02发挥蓝色金融支撑作用
创新蓝色信贷产品，探索海域使用权、海洋碳汇等非传统抵押品信贷模式，推广EOD模式，鼓励研发清洁能源船舶专项保险。
03推动降碳减污动态监测和科学评价体系建设
探索建立港航和海洋产业碳排放统计核算评价体系。
04加强人才队伍建设
深化校企合作产教融合，布局双燃料船舶船员培养见习点。
05提升数智化管控能力
加快智慧航道、智慧交管建设，在秦皇岛、沧州开展低能见度通航技术研究应用，建设海上搜救智能化辅助决策系统。
06强化国际海事履约与涉外航运治理
严格落实国际防止船舶污染公约等国际公约，提升河北港口国际化服务能力和对外开放水平。

title: 宁夏新能源完成三次转型 风光资源变身新型生产要素-索比光伏网
content:
31日，记者从国网宁夏电力有限公司获悉，前三季度宁夏回族自治区新能源装机达到6079万千瓦，占总装机比重64.94%，稳居区内第一大电源。区内售电量811亿千瓦时，同比增长5.05%;外送电量815亿千瓦时，同比增长7.01%。塞上风光资源正实现三次转身，从发电资源变为外销商品，最终成长为可调度、可交易的新型生产要素。
高比例新能源并网，最大难题是风光出力的波动性。宁夏以储能+调峰火电+坚强电网协同托举，破解“靠天吃饭”困境。截至9月底，宁夏储能装机1125万千瓦，规模位居全国第四。当地对电网侧储能实行清单化管控，明确下半年33个储能项目、1004万千瓦并网计划，工期逾期将予以清退。中卫电厂机组作为全国首个“沙戈荒”大基地配套调峰电源，灵活调节出力，为新能源腾出消纳空间。
市场化机制进一步盘活储能收益。随着宁夏电力现货市场V2.0连续结算试运行，独立储能可自主报价参与交易，“低充高放”收益更加稳定。储能配套电网工程同步提速，前三季度新开工55项电网工程、投运61项基建工程，骨干网架承载力持续增强。储能的规模化应用，直接将宁夏新能源利用率稳定维持在96%以上。
绿电就地消纳通道持续拓宽。宁东煤化工园区、硅基、铝锰基工业企业纷纷签订绿电协议，清洁电力走进厂房车间。依托源网荷储一体化建设，工业柔性负荷主动参与电网平衡，供需联动更加紧密。
算力产业成为绿电就地转化的核心载体。前三季度，宁夏算力用电量达20.31亿千瓦时，同比大增85.92%，其中绿电占比56%。中卫依托“算电协同”模式，把大漠风光直接转化为AI算力。当地出台八项举措保障算力用电，搭建多层次电力市场，推行小时级绿电交易，引导非实时算力任务在光伏大发时段集中运行。目前中卫已投运17家数据中心，绿电占比最高突破80%，为“东数西算”提供可复制经验。
如今，宁夏形成“就地转化+跨区外送”双轮并行格局，戈壁风光不再只是并网发电的资源，已然成为支撑产业升级、服务全国双碳转型的新型生产要素。

title: 2026“光能杯”光伏评选持续进行中｜缩量之年，谁在逆风换挡？-索比光伏网
content:
2026年的光伏，
关键词不是“更大”，而是“换挡”。
上半年新增并网71.77GW，累计装机突破1271GW，但增速明显回落；组件出口同比下降，价格在历史低位震荡。与此同时，BC、THBC、钙钛矿的技术迭代没有减速。行业不再奖励“谁做得更大”，而是在筛选“谁换挡更快、谁在低价环境里守住了质量与口碑”。
一年一度的“光能杯”光伏评选，要做的就是把这个分化年份里逆风换挡的企业找出来，让它们被行业看见、被市场记住。
一年一度的“年终奥斯卡”
2012年，索比光伏网发起“光能杯”，迄今已连续举办十四年，被业内称为光伏行业的“年终奥斯卡”。上一届评选共有300余家光伏企业参与报名，颁奖盛典在苏州举行。
2026年，光能杯官方对行业阶段的判断很明确：光储产业告别规模竞速，迈向价值化、场景化、市场化高质量转型。这意味着今年的评选，比的不是谁的增长曲线最陡，而是谁在调整期展现了穿越周期的能力——技术切换的执行力、产品在低价环境中的品质底线、供应链上的履约责任、细分场景里的真实落地。
为什么今年的“光能杯”
值得你认真填一张申报表
因为在这个年份，“被看见”本身正在变成一种稀缺资源。
一面是，行业信息噪声前所未有地大。价格每天在变，产能每天在出清，企业的真实进展很容易被淹没在“内卷”叙事里。另一面是，客户、渠道、资本在当下做判断时，比任何时候都更需要一个超出企业自我陈述的第三方参照。

title: Cadeler's Wind Mover to install 72 wind turbine generators at Inch Cape
content:
Cadeler's Wind Mover to install 72 wind turbine generators at Inch Cape TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Cadeler's Wind Mover to install 72 wind turbine generators at Inch Cape
Vestas Wind Systems A/S is set to begin the installation and commissioning
of 72 wind turbine generators (WTGs) at the 1.1GW Inch
Cape offshore wind farm,
with Cadeler's construction jack-up vessel Wind Mover leading the installation
campaign.
Turbine components will be loaded at the Port of Dundee before being transported
to the project site offshore. Ahead of the first load-out operations, Wind
Mover is expected to arrive at Inch Cape on or around 30 October.
Commissioning activities will be carried out from the service operations
vessel Acta Hercules. Technicians will access the turbines using a walk-to-work
system during the commissioning phase.
Additionally, the campaign will be supported by the crew transfer vessels
NOS Exceller and NOS Empowerer. Installation and commissioning of all 72
turbines are expected to continue through to September 2027.

title: LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution sign Taean Wind Farm agreement
content:
LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution sign Taean Wind Farm agreement TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution sign Taean Wind Farm agreement
LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution have signed a Capacity Reservation
Agreement (CRA) with Taean Wind Power Co. to supply and install submarine
cables for the 504 MW Taean
offshore wind farm.
The agreement secures production facilities and construction vessel availability
needed to support cable manufacturing and installation. The announcement
follows the selection of the companies as preferred bidders in 2024.
The Taean offshore wind farm is located off Taean-gun in Chungcheongnam-do
and is being developed by Korea Western Power, Vena Energy and Copenhagen
Infrastructure Partners.
“Due to the unique offshore construction environment, it is crucial to
closely link cable production and installation to enhance on-site responsiveness
and accountability,” an LS Cable & System official said.
Adding, “We will proceed with the main contract without any setbacks to
expand our penetration of the domestic offshore wind market.”
The offshore wind farm is currently expected to be completed by 2030.

title: Nordlicht I has Installed all 68 foundations
content:
One of Germany’s largest offshore wind farm has reached a major milestone,
with all 68 foundations installed in the German North Sea ahead of schedule.
Once completed, the Nordlicht
I offshore wind farm
will have an installed capacity of 980 MW. The project forms part of the
Nordlicht cluster, which consists of two offshore wind farms with a combined
capacity of 1.6 GW.
“Nordlicht is far more than just an offshore wind project. It is a significant
investment in Germany’s energy future and an important contribution to
the transition of Europe’s electricity supply to renewable energies,”
said David Flood, head of offshore at Vattenfall.
The milestone follows an installation update in September that confirmed
all monopiles had been installed. Since then, transition pieces have also
been successfully fitted.
The foundations were manufactured by EEW Special Pipe Constructions and
CS WIND Offshore, while DEME was responsible for transporting and installing
both the monopiles and transition pieces.
The company highlighted several environmental measures implemented during
the installation phase, including the use of turbine towers made from reduced
emissions steel, continuous environmental monitoring, and bird and marine
mammal observation programs.

title: All 52 turbines installed at 760 MW Ecowende offshore wind farm
content:
The final turbine has been installed at the 760 MW Ecowende
offshore wind farm,
marking the project's final construction phase, with all 52 turbines installed
over the past five months.
The installation was completed through a joint effort between Van Oord
and Vestas. Van Oord was responsible for the transportation and installation
of the turbines and other wind farm components, while Vestas supplied the
V236-15.0 turbines.
Ecowende, a joint venture between Shell, Eneco and Chubu, is located 53
kilometres off the Dutch coast and is expected to meet around 3% of the
Netherlands' electricity demand.
“Ecowende is designed to gain knowledge on how to build and operate a
wind park in harmony with nature. We will share that knowledge, so that
researchers, governments and wind park developers can build on it,” said
Ecowende CEO Tjalling de Bruin.
According to the company, the project aims to be the most ecologically
focused offshore wind farm developed to date. The wind farm will test
measures designed to protect birds and bats while supporting underwater
biodiversity.

title: New T5 Terminal opens in Gdańsk to support Poland’s offshore wind expansion
content:
New T5 Terminal opens in Gdańsk to support Poland’s offshore wind expansion TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
New T5 Terminal opens in Gdańsk to support Poland’s offshore wind expansion
The Polish Development Fund (PFR) has completed construction of the T5
Terminal at the Port Gdansk.
The milestone follows a gross investment of PLN 1.2 billion.
The new terminal is expected to strengthen Poland’s energy security while
increasing opportunities for suppliers and contractors to participate in
the country’s energy transition.
“Energy security is the foundation of a strong Poland. That's why we are
investing in new energy sources, modern infrastructure, and the development
of domestic industry,” said Andrzej Domañski, Poland’s minister of finance
and economy.
Following the completion of construction, the terminal will support the
2 offshore wind project.
A lease agreement for the facility has already been signed back in 2024
with Elektrownia Wiatrowa Baltica 2.
“This is a breakthrough moment for the development of the domestic offshore
sector and proof that a complete ecosystem for implementing this type of
investment is being created in Poland,” said Dariusz Lubera, CEO of PGE
Polska Grupa Energetyczna.
The terminal was developed by Istrana, with an 85% stake currently held
general contractor.

content:
N-Sea Group has announced the completion of the 2026 Vattenfall seabed
survey campaign. The project aimed to gather valuable data to support the
monitoring and management of offshore assets.
N-Sea supported the campaign by providing seabed monitoring services, deploying
a range of vessels and nearshore assets, as well as offshore and nearshore
teams, to complete the work.
The campaign covered several major offshore wind farms, including Hollandse
Kust Zuid,
Vesterhav
North and South,
and Kriegers
in Denmark. In total, the survey encompassed 253 wind turbine locations,
inter-array cable corridors, export cable routes, and offshore substations.
According to the company, high-resolution survey data was successfully
collected with no recorded incidents.

title: It’s Contract Renewal Season, But Some Customers Aren’t Biting
content: My colleagues and I have been hearing a lot of stories about big enterprise customers renegotiating their annual contracts with model developers. Traditionally, software sellers use this time as an opportunity to convince customers to increase their annual commit by, for instance, reminding them how they exceeded their usage limits this year or highlighting new features they’ve released. In the past, model developers have had success using that playbook. This year has been a different story, though, some customers tell me. For instance, one executive at a major financial services firm said their company was hesitant to increase their spending commitment with Anthropic , OpenAI or any other model provider for a couple reasons. First, this executive said, the rapid pace of model releases means enterprises want flexibility to quickly switch to whatever the best new model is, something that can change week to week. Switching the models that power a company’s application is much easier now than it used to be. We previously reported that AI coding startup Replit took just mere hours to make the code changes to switch their product from primarily using Anthropic’s models to OpenAI’s. The second reason is that these model providers keep releasing cheaper, “good-enough” AI, such as OpenAI’s Terra and Luna versions or Anthropic’s Haiku , the exec said. When the model providers do so, companies move as many workloads to these cheaper models as they can, which can sometimes quickly cut their bills to a fraction of what they used to be, the exec said. (Over time, though, their overall spending could increase because they might use more AI.) In doing so, the model providers are essentially cannibalizing their more expensive models with cheaper ones. We’re not trying to argue that revenue growth at Anthropic and OpenAI will fall off a cliff. The potential market is enormous, and both are growing pretty well right now. It’s also not lost on us that Anthropic says that in the third quarter, its net retention rate was 900%, meaning existing customers spent many more times what they were spending a year earlier. And Anthropic’s inference margins were crazy good in the first half of the year. Still, anecdotes like the one involving the major financial services firm raise the perennial question of whether models will eventually be commoditized. Such a scenario would crush trillions of dollars in market caps, and we aren’t ready to buy into the idea. A more realistic framework to hold is that the rapid improvement in models, and their capabilities frequently leapfrogging each other, has caused some decision paralysis among some enterprise customers. That could explain why, instead, they are turning to model routers like OpenRouter —where they can access nearly any model from a single application programming interface—or platforms that offer multiple models, such as Snowflake . That puts the model providers in an awkward position. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it wants more enterprise customers to sign non-cancelable, multiyear contracts with minimum spending commitments, just as some of those customers are trying to avoid getting locked in. Meanwhile, both Anthropic and OpenAI have committed to spending hundreds of billions of dollars on computing over the next decade. If big customers keep their options open, the model providers could end up being the only ones locked into long-term commitments. You can expect that subject to come up during Anthropic's first quarterly earnings call early next year. title: Inside Apple’s Slog to Create Its First Robot
content: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots, but judging by Apple’s plodding progress on the first one it hopes to sell—a device with a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp—he could face an uphill battle. Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it. The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get off a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it. Much of the hardware needed for the robot has been finished for around two years, but the software team has found it difficult to keep pace, people who have worked on the project said. The hardware team responsible for J595 has pushed to hurry up and release the product. Meanwhile, the software team has advocated for delaying its release, and for the past year, it has attempted to strip back some proposed features and focus the product on a few capabilities related to FaceTime and automating home tasks, like switching on a light. Apple hopes to sell the robot for around $1,000. It could cost even more—depending on the market prices for the robot’s components. Several former employees said they expect Apple may call the device HomeView Ultra, borrowing the name from HomeView, the stationary tabletop device that Apple unveiled last month. Right now, Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though. (The hardware team behind the robot had initially planned to release it this year.) Apple’s struggles to get the robot ready highlight the challenges the company faces as Ternus’ reign begins. While Apple is a finely tuned machine at cranking out new, incremental updates to iPhones and Macs every year, it is less adept at developing entirely new products, and the company has a long-standing tendency to move at a placid pace. For instance, it took around eight years for Apple to complete work on its Vision Pro headset, which it released two years ago to muted fanfare. (If the J595 robot does come out next year, it will have taken roughly the same amount of time.) Apple has appeared particularly sluggish in the AI era. Its overhaul of Siri took years to complete, and even with new AI features rolled out earlier this year, the assistant is still seen as a laggard behind what AI agents like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots can do. As a gesture to Ternus, Tim Cook, his predecessor, delayed the release of some new products so that their debuts coincided with Ternus’s start in September. Since then, Apple has unveiled HomeView, the foldable iPhone Duo and a touchscreen MacBook. But those products have received a mixed reaction from consumers. The $2,899 MacBook is seen as expensive. The Duo has genuine buzz around it but has also attracted complaints about cracked screens. And HomeView has been critiqued as just a giant repurposed Apple Watch, one that relies heavily on a still disappointing Siri. Ternus arrives in the top job at a moment when many other fierce competitors are working on AI-powered devices and robots. A year ago, OpenAI acquired a hardware startup co-founded by Jony Ive, the former Apple design chief. Since then, Ive has been devoted to creating a line of AI devices for OpenAI, which has hired more than 400 ex-Apple engineers to work on those devices. Next year, OpenAI hopes to release a doughnut-shaped smart speaker that will have moving parts and a camera that allows it to gather information about its user and environment. New Apple CEO John Ternus unveils the new $2,800 touchscreen MacBook Pro in October. (Getty Images) Meta has been rolling out a slew of its own devices, including AI glasses and virtual reality headsets. Compared with Apple, Meta has been able in some cases to move rapidly from concept to product: It has said it took less than a year to develop Charm, a pocket-sized AI device that it plans to ship in December. Tesla is working on a humanoid robot, Optimus, that CEO Elon Musk has said will help with household tasks. And then there are a slew of startups trying to compete with the established tech giants, including robotics startup 1X, which had hoped to have its humanoid robot in homes this year. 1X’s robot, Neo, caught a moment of virality when it was first unveiled last year in videos showing it washing dishes and folding clothes. In addition to the J595 robot, Apple’s robotics team, which is led by Kevin Lynch, a longtime company executive, has explored other types of robots, such as one that follows a user around the home on wheels and another that flies inside the home. There is also an Apple project focused on robots that can complete specific everyday tasks, such as folding clothes. Robots devoted only to a few specific chores are, theoretically, much easier to develop than humanoid robots made to do many different things. Ternus has been particularly enthusiastic about discussions around robots that focused on household tasks, people familiar with the meetings said. As one former engineer who worked on the J595 robot put it, Apple “is tearing itself apart at the seams trying to get on this AI bandwagon.” An ‘iPad on a Stick’ The creation of the J595 robot has unfolded over nearly a decade, with responsibilities for the robot falling to a slew of Apple executives, some of whom were working on multiple projects at once and never had an opportunity to focus solely on the device. (Bloomberg has previously reported some details about the robot.) Early prototypes of the robot were done in 2018. A year later, Cook received a demo of a prototype and gave the green light to continue working on it. The prototypes were bigger than the one currently being envisioned, and the initial designs drew jokes from some Apple engineers, who remarked that it looked like “an iPad on a stick.” The robot’s hardware was developed by a team led by Matthew Costello, who’d previously worked on Beats, the headphones brand acquired by Apple in 2014. Software development fell to employees within Apple’s Special Projects Group, which was then primarily working on Project Titan, Apple’s autonomous car initiative. For a time, Brian Lynch, a veteran Apple engineer whose time stretched back to the iPod, was working on both the car’s interior and the J595 robot: He envisioned the robot being able to sit not only inside people’s homes but on the front console of the Apple car too. Apple may call its new robot the HomeView Ultra, making it expansion from its stationary tabletop device, HomeView, that it unveiled in September. (Getty Images) In 2021, leadership of the Special Projects Group shifted from Doug Field, who departed for Ford, to Kevin Lynch, who got credit for saving the Apple Watch by developing its health-tracking features. But most of Lynch’s attention was on the car, and much of the robotics effort fell to Chris Saari, who had led efforts to develop the Apple Watch’s software. Even at these early stages, the people working on the J595 robot knew it had to be more than a fancy way to make FaceTime calls if Apple wanted to justify a high price tag on it. After the ChatGPT’s launch in 2022 ignited the AI boom, they began to develop AI features to make it more sophisticated. Employees working on the robot began pushing for a wide range of proactive agentic AI capabilities, envisioning a device that could accomplish a variety of tasks. There was even an agentic AI research arm opened up inside the robotics group, led by Vladlen Koltun, who joined Apple in 2021 after leading AI at Intel. But Apple’s in-house AI technology was meager compared with what competitors were creating. As a result, the robotics team was given permission to use any available AI models, including open-source models and licensed models from Google. They hoped to eventually integrate the J595 robot with Siri, but during the robot’s early development, the Siri team was kept separate from the robotics squad and was overwhelmed in its own work in trying to improve Siri itself. Apple’s Kevin Lynch, who is created with saving the Apple Watch, had advocated for developing the new robot slowly and to release an early version with limited features. (Getty Images) When Apple shuttered its work on its autonomous car in 2024, Lynch moved all of his focus to robots that would be used within a home, redeploying many of the people who’d been working on the car with him to work on robots. Some of the Apple employees who had been working on robots before Lynch shifted his attention were disappointed with his leadership and felt he rarely talked to or consulted with them, three people involved in the project said. Lynch tried to pull back on some expectations for what a debut version of the J595 robot would be able to do. He wanted to slowly add features to it after it launched—a similar approach to what had been done with the Apple Watch. While the initial Apple Watch came out in 2015, Apple later added the sensors for tracking someone’s health and fitness that made the wearable more popular. Ternus Takes Command Prior to becoming CEO, Ternus, then the company’s hardware chief, was skeptical of many new products, like the failed autonomous car project and the Vision Pro headset. But he has been more enthusiastic about Apple’s potential robots, three people familiar with the company’s robot projects said. Last year, oversight of Lynch and the Special Projects Group was taken away from Senior Vice President John Giannandrea and put under Ternus. (Giannandrea, who’d been responsible for Apple’s AI efforts, left Apple earlier this year.) In April, Apple announced it would promote Ternus to CEO later in the year. But even as he was preparing to take the job, Ternus made an effort to be at every demonstration and product planning meeting for J595 and Apple’s other robots, people involved in those projects said. Much of the development of the J595 robot has fallen to a team that reported to John Giannandrea until last year. Giannandrea departed Apple earlier this year. (Getty Images) Across the company, Ternus has been advocating for Apple to run faster with leaner teams, people familiar with his strategy said. And the team working on the robots remains relatively small. Apple has very few employees with deep backgrounds devoted to robotics; one person estimated the company has only 10 or so “true roboticists.” Under Lynch, the team working on software is around 300—with around 30 of them focused on research, said people familiar with the team. The employees dedicated to the J595 robot have already been talking about a second-generation version of the robot that would have some of the proposed features they’ve discarded. Meanwhile, many of the engineers who initially worked on the robot have since departed, including hardware leader Brian Lynch, who joined fitness device maker Oura, and robotics research head Jian Zhang, who joined Meta. While many J595 employees want the robot to come out as soon as possible, some employees worry it could face the same lack of enthusiasm that has greeted HomeView. But they fear the longer Apple waits to release the robot, the higher expectations will be for it as AI capabilities grow more sophisticated across the industry.

title: Apple, Uber and Elections Headline Week
content: Can Apple, Uber and Palantir turn this stock market around? It sure needs it. Worries about excessive AI spending tanked Google’s stock last week and sent the Nasdaq Composite to its worst month since March 2025. While the major indexes are still in the green for the year, a few more days like Friday’s could change that. Fortunately, we have a handful of earnings that might temper the gloom. Palantir Technologies, which reports Monday, has told investors to expect an 83% jump in the third quarter from the year-ago period. That’s a slowdown from the second quarter’s blistering 93% growth . But at least investors will get a reprieve from enormous capital expenditures. Palantir only spent $22 million in capex in the first half. As for Apple, it’s already warned investors that supply constraints for advanced chip manufacturing would contribute to slower revenue growth, to a range of  9% to 11% in the September quarter from a year ago, slower than its 16% growth in the June quarter. Apple has also forecast iPhone revenue growth in the mid-teens versus 22% in the June quarter. An improvement on that outlook could buoy the mood. On the other hand, a sharper slowdown in growth from either companies could give investors another reason to sell tech stocks. Here’s what else is going on… Ternus’ Turn When the iPhone maker reports results late Monday, it will be the first time new CEO John Ternus will lead the conference call. Ternus, Apple’s former senior vice president of hardware engineering, got off to a fast start after he took the torch from Tim Cook, Apple’s long-running CEO, who is now executive chair. In just the last two months, Apple announced three notable new products—an iPhone with a folding screen , a MacBook with a touchscreen and the HomeView, a tabletlike smart home device . The first two products, which followed designs popular with competitors like smartphone maker Samsung and laptop maker Lenovo, were a sign of a new Apple adventurousness under Ternus (though the products were almost certainly greenlit some time ago under his predecessor). But brand-new products have a habit of glitching at the start, even for a company with superlative manufacturing processes (anyone remember Antennagate or Bendgate?). In recent weeks, media reports have highlighted cracks in the Duo’s wide folding screen and other operational issues. Apple’s announcement last week that the new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen would cost at least $2,899 —a whopping $900 more than the version without a touchscreen—will likely hold some buyers back. As for the HomeView, I’ll be curious if enough households think a $299 standing tablet is really that necessary—or if they can get by with how most people use FaceTime, change songs and watch videos while they putter in the kitchen: by propping the phone against the mayonnaise jar (additional cost: zero). • Uber reports quarterly results Wednesday. Uber has already been in the news recently, thanks to Instacart’s agreement to sell to DoorDash for $17 billion in cash and stock. As Valida reported last week , Instacart leaders had shopped the company to Uber. But those talks fizzled, in part because Uber had just recently announced another big acquisition, a $15 billion deal for Europe-based Delivery Hero, and was also worried that an acquisition would hit antitrust hurdles. Uber has forecast that gross bookings—the value of dollars spent on its various apps—will rise in a range from $58.25 billion to $60.25 billion, with the median up 19% from the same period last year. • Tuesday midterm elections. Tech heads to the polls in a variety of ways Tuesday. As Shane reported this morning , in 21 of the 36 states electing a governor on Tuesday, at least one major-party nominee backs a data center moratorium. And that’s not all. An expected return to a Democratic majority in Congress could increase headaches for large tech companies like Meta Platforms, Nvidia and Amazon if Democrats decide to hold oversight hearings into their executives’ work with the Trump administration, as this Politico article details . Even a blue sweep wouldn’t overcome Trump’s veto power, meaning any potential AI legislative pushes next term will likely still need his support. We’ll also be watching the outcome of California’s Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire’s tax. Several well-known tech CEOs have lambasted the proposition—or protested by moving their zip code out of state—but probably more notably, the measure has lost ground after a number of large groups like the state teachers’ union have also criticized it. Abe has more here . In Other News The Federal Bureau of Investigation said Saturday that North Korea was r esponsible for the $6.3 billion theft from crypto exchange Binance, the largest crypto hack in history. S&P Global Ratings lowered its credit rating outlook on Meta from stable to negative, citing limits on the company’s ability to monetize its AI investments. OpenAI lowered the target for its fundraising to $20 billion from $30 billion, at a $1.25 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reported. Amazon disclosed a new loan facility up to $80 billion to purchase technology infrastructure assets. Cyera, a five-year-old cybersecurity startup focused on protecting corporate data against AI-powered attacks, has discussed nearly doubling its valuation to $20 billion. Today on The Information’s TITV The Information’s crypto reporter Yueqi Yang and Predicate co-founder and CEO Nikhil Raghuveera discuss the $6.3 billion Binance hack .
