title: Exclusive: How the Embattled CEO of Our Next Energy Plotted a Comeback
content: A few years ago, Mujeeb Ijaz was one of the most prominent startup CEOs in what was then a go-go next-generation U.S. battery industry. Previously, he had headed the battery program in Apple’s secret electric vehicle development program, and before that was an executive at Ford. In early 2023, the startup he founded, Our Next Energy, was flush with $300 million in cash, raised in February of that year in a Series B round with a $1.2 billion valuation. The company appeared to be on its way to its first commercial revenue. By the end of the year, however, ONE was in freefall and Ijaz was out as its CEO. The main culprit was a sudden reversal in the EV industry, which had been going gangbusters but then stalled. But the company had also been overly ambitious in diving into costly projects, according to former employees, splashing around cash, full of confidence that it could raise another round. Today, an apparently humbler Ijaz is back as CEO of ONE. The Novi, Mich., startup has abandoned trying to make batteries for EVs and is instead producing them to power less sexy technologies, like locomotives and maritime drones. And Ijaz says he’s no longer chasing quick hockey-stick, off-the-charts profit. Instead, he’s doing what he says he should have been doing all along—trying to build up ONE slowly, block by block and using cash sparingly. He projects $30 million in revenue this year, which he said will be triple last year’s amount. In 2027, he expects revenue to double to $60 million. “We don’t see the world in hockey sticks anymore,” Ijaz told me. “We see it in building our customer base, in making sure we deliver our results and then keeping the capital intensity low where we’re not overcapitalizing ahead of where we see the demand.” Ijaz’s argument for low-key management is understandable given his own recent trajectory and that of ONE (more on that below). But it also applies to the rest of the industry, which is seeing its first modest revenue, almost all of it tied to the revolutions in flying drones, AI data centers and robots. As we have written, startups like Enovix and Nyobolt have reported initial revenue from contracts for drone and robot batteries, respectively. Amprius Technologies and Unusual Machines have reported even larger drone battery contracts. Sodium-ion startup Peak Energy has $1.1 billion in contracts, but last week we reported that it has adopted a go-slow approach to scaling up its business. Ijaz has said ONE’s batteries power more than 100 locomotives in the U.S. and Canada. But the market for drones, robots and locomotives is far smaller than the potential one for EVs, and the revenue from these use cases will fall well short of the billions of dollars in sales to EV makers that some of the startups forecast when they went public in 2020 and 2021. For now, at least, the U.S. battery industry is still in search of business that will drive big revenue, even though some battery startups seem likely to eke out profits. ONE’s troubles startled industry veterans, who had regarded the company—which was developing a novel dual-battery pack that would power an EV at least 600 miles, along with a lithium-iron-phosphate pack for the grid—as one of the next-generation battery startups most likely to reach large-volume commercial production. Ijaz himself was one of the industry’s most respected startup CEOs. He had founded ONE in 2020 after running the battery division of Apple’s EV development program for five years. In addition to working at Ford, he had also been an executive at lithium-ion battery pioneer A123 Systems. The success of the February 2023 round aligned with investor and industry ebullience around EVs and battery startups with ambitions to power them; EV sales soared 60% year on year in 2022 and another 60% year on year in the first half of 2023. ONE, buoyed by the boom, burned through nearly all the new cash in just months in what employees said was an almost devil-may-care spending spree on new projects and lavish marketing. On the tail of that Series B round, Ijaz began raising a Series C for another $300 million. A U.K. firm, Just Climate, emerged as the lead investor with a pledge for a $100 million investment. Ijaz said he would use the funds to build a gigafactory in Michigan with 2.7 gigawatt-hours of capacity, enough to make 40,000 batteries for trucks per year or enough grid batteries to power 250,000 homes. By 2027, Ijaz had plans to expand the plant almost tenfold. But in the third quarter of 2023, the first signs of consumer fatigue in the EV market surfaced. Affluent early adopters already had EVs in their driveways. While EVs were still selling , they began to pile up just a bit in dealer lots. The slight slowdown spooked Ford and General Motors, along with investors. The venture capital industry began a substantial retreat from new investments in battery startups. Just Climate also became concerned about the EV industry downturn, and did not believe that ONE could produce batteries nearly as fast as it predicted, as we reported at the time . In November 2023, the VC firm backed out of the investment. ONE had to close out the year with a sudden layoff of most of its employees. Ijaz  himself was forced out as CEO, though he managed to stay on as chief technology officer. Ijaz’s description of the last three years sounds like a roller coaster. For most of 2024, ONE’s board attempted to sell the company without luck. The board considered bankruptcy. But in March 2025, Phillip Sarofim, CEO of Trousdale Ventures, co-led a new investment round with Ijaz’s brother, Mansoor Ijaz, who ran Crescent Global Partners, a family investment office. The amount of the investment was not disclosed. Mansoor Ijaz joined the ONE board, which restored Mujeeb Ijaz as CEO. Ijaz said he spent the entirety of last year visiting potential customers and recalibrating what ONE might do with its existing assets, which included a cell production factory in Van Buren Township, Mich., and a pack assembly factory at its headquarters in Novi. In January this year, ONE announced a new product line: It would no longer make EV batteries but would power locomotives, drones and the grid. Ijaz said ONE is selling nine different batteries to more than 20 customers. Almost all the business, he said, is tied to demand for U.S.-made batteries, as the Trump administration has issued import controls and bans on Chinese-made batteries and components. The company has also developed a battery that can charge to 85% of capacity in just 12 minutes. I asked Ijaz where ONE would be right now if the Series C had not fallen apart. He said the investors in that round had “lost an opportunity,” since the AI boom has created massive demand for grid batteries of the type ONE was manufacturing. Either way, a quieter Ijaz is going at it again. “We have a second chance to retool a healthy birth,” he said. ---- Noteworthy Exclusive: Caterpillar-backed battery startup Lithos Energy has shut down. The Hayward, Calif., company stopped operations and let go all of its employees on Oct. 5, according to three former executives, though it hasn’t announced the shutdown. Lithos was founded in 2015 by former Tesla employee James Meredith to make batteries for off-road and marine electric vehicles, along with industrial uses. In 2023, Caterpillar invested $38 million in the company with the objective of developing batteries for its construction vehicles. Lithos used the cash to build a pilot factory in Hayward and hire personnel. But last year, when President Donald Trump pulled the plug on EV programs, Caterpillar shelved the Lithos battery programs it was backing, according to Rob Sweney, who had been Lithos’ vice president of engineering. Absent any other big customers, Lithos ran out of money. After the initial investment, “we bit the hook hard—recruited a large team, moved into a shiny pilot facility etc. [and] chewed through the investment rapidly,” Sweney told me. Meredith and Caterpillar did not respond to emails. Electric construction equipment maker Bedrock Robotics raised $600 million in a Series C round at a $4.1 billion valuation. The raise and valuation illustrates investor enthusiasm for electric startups outside mainstream consumer EVs. For now, San Francisco–based Bedrock, founded by former Waymo executives, is making electric excavators, as we reported last year . KoBold Metals says China is blocking its use of surveying technology to mine lithium in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The company has asked the U.S. to step in and help clear the way. Berkeley, Calif.–based KoBold says it uses AI to explore for metals. It wants to use aerial surveying technology to assess a lithium deposit in the DRC, but that will require a United Nations exemption because the equipment has possible military use as well, the Financial Times reported. KoBold claims China has stalled this exemption, and the firm has asked the U.S. Department of State to intervene. --- Recommended Newsletter Start your day with Applied AI, the newsletter that uncovers how leading businesses are leveraging AI to automate tasks. title: Google Energy Chief: Space Data Centers Cost Up to 100 Times More Than Those on Earth
content: Data centers in space could cost up to 100 times as much as those on Earth, Google's head of data center energy said this week, a reality check from a company that itself is testing AI server chips in orbit. “Let’s explore all the terrestrial options before we go extraterrestrial,” Amanda Peterson Corio said at The Information’s WTF summit, a gathering of senior women in the technology and finance industries. The comments came as SpaceX’s orbital data center plans underpin part of its roughly $1.8 trillion market capitalization. Peterson Corio also said that rising public opposition to data centers here on Earth is largely the fault of younger, less experienced companies that should be subject to higher standards. Before the recent boom, she said, companies that had been building data centers for years “were doing it the right way,” and the facilities rarely drew controversy. Launch costs for sending computing hardware into orbit are “incredibly, incredibly expensive, up to 100 times more expensive than building on earth,” Peterson Corio said. Beyond cost, operators would also need to figure out how to maintain and upgrade equipment in orbit. On Earth, data center staff constantly swap out computers and rewire systems, she said. ( Watch an interview with Peterson Corio here .) Peterson Corio’s cautious comments about space come even as Google's own researchers said this month they will partner with satellite imaging firm Planet Labs to use satellites to explore the potential of larger-scale data center clusters in space. As part of a project it calls Suncatcher, Google has already launched a smaller space server prototype carrying tensor processing units, the AI server chips it codesigns with Broadcom, to space. (On Friday, Google said those first TPUs in orbit processed their first AI workloads: writing a haiku.) In a research paper last fall, Google employees working on Suncatcher and the company’s research chief James Manyika said that if a launch costs hit $200 per kilogram or less, the “cost per unit of power in space could be approximately comparable to terrestrial spend.” The company’s researchers said it could potentially reach that threshold by 2035, though the timing might depend on SpaceX’s ability to launch Starship and rev up the rocket’s launch frequency. (Starship promises to lower launch costs and increase the amount of payload capacity, compared to the company’s current flagship rockets.) Others have been more bullish. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that his company will have data centers in space as soon as next year, and Jeff Bezos, Amazon’s founder and the owner of SpaceX rival Blue Origin, has said that there will be data centers consuming a gigawatt of power in space in a decade. Google and SpaceX have also reportedly explored working together on data centers in orbit. (Alphabet also owns a sizable stake in SpaceX.) Peterson Corio didn’t dismiss the concept, saying it’s “really fascinating” and that Google invests in long-shot ideas because it is “always thinking 10, 20, 30 years down the line.” But such technology is “not tomorrow,” she said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has gone further, calling the idea of putting data centers in space under current conditions “ridiculous” and criticizing Musk’s speedy timeline. The Real Bottleneck: Permits, Not Power On Earth, Peterson Corio pushed back on the idea—also espoused by Musk—that the U.S. lacks enough electricity for the AI buildout. “Is there enough power? Sure, absolutely,” she said. The bottlenecks, she said, are permitting and the lengthy studies required to connect new projects to the public energy grid. Alphabet's X unit has a project, Tapestry, which is working with PJM, the largest grid operator on the East Coast, to use AI to speed up those studies. In Texas, the state utilities regulator has slowed down some data center projects as it boosts reviews to make sure new facilities don’t burden the grid or spike prices. The grid itself also isn’t properly utilized the way it ought to be, other executives in the field say. Brian Janous, co-founder of data center land and power developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure, recently told The Information that about 45% of the grid’s capacity goes unused on average because it has to accommodate peaks in usage. For most hours of the day, there's enough spare capacity in the grid to meet data centers’ needs, he said. (Startups like Cloverleaf as well as Nvidia are trying to figure out how to use such capacity.) Notably, Google appears to have a power-related advantage over its cloud rivals , in terms of squeezing as much computing capacity as possible from its data centers, a metric known as power usage effectiveness. As for the data center backlash in the U.S., Peterson Corio blamed it on “a lot of new entrants that are selling or building and maybe don't have that history or sophistication,” though she didn’t name names. While numerous first-time developers have rushed to enter the AI data center market in recent years, well-known firms such as Oracle, not just the newcomers, have also faced local resistance. Higher Standards In any case, she said she supports regulation and higher standards for the industry. She didn’t propose specific rules but pointed to Google’s rising financial contribution to the communities where it operates, and efforts to limit risks if facilities can’t be completed. Those include committing to pay for grid upgrades over 15 to 20 years so no one else is “left holding the bill” if a project stalls. Such arrangements, under which Google commits up front to pay for grid infrastructure, are now happening in more than nine U.S. states and “growing really, really quickly,” she said. The standards also include Google paying its full power bills and property taxes; posting bonds to cover the restoration of land if the company ever abandons a site; and ending nondisclosure agreements with local governments. (On the latter point, Google only this month agreed to end such NDAs, which activists had decried, following similar moves from Microsoft and Amazon.) Her comments follow rising investor scrutiny of the valuations or viability of young AI cloud providers, often heavily backed by Nvidia, that are racing to build data centers using a lot of borrowed cash and a short track record. While such firms appear to be among the companies Peterson Corio thinks need tighter standards, Google also said it is going to increasingly rely on “third‑party compute capacity” for its own computing needs, though it didn’t specify which providers it will use. (SpaceX is one of them.) Google needs them because it can’t build its own facilities fast enough! New From Our Reporters AI Agenda How Is Anthropic So Efficient? title: Candidates Backing Data Center Pauses Could Win in Up to 15 Governor’s Races
content: As data centers have gone from obscurity to the top of voters’ minds, midterm candidates are taking a stance on the issue. The fight is most heated in races for governor, the office that has shown the most power to limit data centers on a broad scale. Whichever candidates win, more doors are likely to close on the industry, leaving it with fewer places to build and higher costs where it still can. In 21 of the 36 states electing a governor on Tuesday, at least one major-party nominee backs a data center moratorium, according to The Information’s analysis of candidate platforms and public statements. Both nominees back pauses in five states (Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas), and a candidate promising a pause is likely to win in three (Maine, New Mexico and New York), based on recent polls. In seven more, it could be a close race between a candidate who backs a pause and one who doesn’t (Alaska, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Wisconsin and Vermont). Those 15 states are home to more than a third of the U.S. population. They are also home to some of the country’s biggest data center projects. OpenAI’s Stargate project with Oracle has massive sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico. SoftBank’s SB Energy plans to build an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio. Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia have lined up Texas sites . In Georgia, the Atlanta metro area has overtaken Northern Virginia as the busiest market for data center construction, according to real estate firm CBRE. In three of the states holding gubernatorial elections next week, sitting governors have already paused new large-scale data center projects: Kathy Hochul in New York, Greg Abbott in Texas and Tina Kotek in Oregon. Hochul’s opponent, Bruce Blakeman, calls her pause “ crazy ” but trails far behind her in the polls. Abbott’s opponent, Gina Hinojosa, who wants an even broader pause of any new approvals, calls Abbott’s pause “an election-year stunt” on her campaign website, saying, “We know that goes away on November 4.” Democrats make up most of the bloc backing moratoriums, but it’s not a clean partisan split. In Maryland and Iowa, the Republican candidates support moratoriums while their opponents don’t, though these two candidates trail in their races. Even if candidates aren’t pushing data center pauses, some of them hope to rein in the industry in other ways. Of the 46 top nominees not calling for moratoriums, 38 back at least one restriction on data centers. One of the most common alternatives to pauses is ratepayer protections—policies that make sure the costs of powering giant AI campuses don’t raise household electricity bills. That option echoes the voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge President Donald Trump asked tech companies to sign in March, as well as a bipartisan bill passed in the House and blocked in the Senate that would have pushed state regulators to make data centers cover their power costs. Because the bill would not actually require states to adopt standards, Senate Democrats spiked it, calling it “ toothless .” Other candidates want to end tax breaks for builders, add environmental and water protections, require union labor or ban nondisclosure agreements in public deals. Hawaii is the only state where neither candidate for governor is campaigning on data center restrictions. Data centers are on everyone’s lips, but in some places, other tech issues are also on the ballot. Some candidates are calling for AI legislation mandating model safety reviews and child safety protections. At least a dozen candidates have weighed in on the presence of Flock Safety cameras after privacy concerns and police misuse drew backlash from some communities. A couple of candidates have plans for crypto and prediction markets. Whether hopefuls will actually follow through on their promises is another question. Our tally takes the candidates at their word. Nationwide Drama Opposition to data centers bubbled up quickly from the local level, as shown by The Information’s ban tracker . At the year’s start, only about 40 towns and counties had bans in place. By August, there were over 500 bans, driven by worries about power bills, water usage, noise and blight. In the court of public opinion, data centers are losing. In an August poll from Pew Research Center, six in 10 U.S. adults said they would be uncomfortable with a new one operating in their area, with more than half calling them bad for the environment and half considering them bad for home energy costs. Few saw a bright side: Less than a quarter agreed they would be good for local jobs or tax revenue. Association with the industry has become a liability, prompting candidates to brand their opponents with derisive nicknames. In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford dubbed his opponent, Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo, “Data Center Joe”—and the state Democratic Party set up a website to match. In Wisconsin, Republican Tom Tiffany called his rival, David Crowley, “Data Center David” (though Crowley backs a “de facto moratorium” and Tiffany doesn’t.) In Oregon, the state Democrats dubbed Christine Drazan, their opponent, “Data Center Drazan.” In Alaska, Republican Bernadette Wilson called Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who goes by JKT, “ Chat JKT ,” based on donations to his campaign from Anthropic employees. However, he backs a moratorium and she doesn’t, though she said she’d never “allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands.” In Michigan, which is at the center of both the build-out and the backlash, Republican John James has gone after Democratic candidate Jocelyn Benson’s husband, an executive at a firm involved in the state’s Stargate site. Benson’s campaign says he has recused himself from any state-related work and points to money the James campaign has taken from data center developers. For what it’s worth, both candidates say they back a moratorium. Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms and Ohio’s Amy Acton have asked their opponents to divest from tech and data center investments. Even some of the industry’s biggest backers are recalibrating. In July, Alabama’s likely winner, Tommy Tuberville, called data center concerns “bull crap.” Now his ads say, “Politicians get the headlines, big tech gets the tax break, and working families get stuck with the bill.” Donors with a stake in data centers are writing big checks to favored candidates. Since July 2025, Abbott has raised about $9 million from people and companies the Texas Tribune links to data centers . In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds and his PAC have taken at least $1.5 million from data center developers and others in the industry, Politico reported . Feuding AI PACs have aligned behind Donalds, too: Both Leading the Future, supported by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Andreessen Horowitz, and Anthropic-backed Public First Action have spent $2 million each on ads backing the candidate, Bloomberg reported . Same Name, Different Policies The word “moratorium” has become popular enough for candidates to attach it to very different policies. But not all are equal. They vary in duration: Some locales have paused building for just 45 days, others for three years. Many moratoriums are in place to buy time while lawmakers decide on more permanent standards for data centers. They vary in scope, too. Some moratoriums apply only to facilities above a certain size, usually measured in electricity use. New York’s 50-megawatt cutoff rejects larger campuses that train frontier AI models but lets smaller projects through. Most candidates pledging pauses haven’t said where they’d draw the line, but many are aiming at the biggest projects. And some moratoriums look more like a list of guardrails going by a trendier name. Ohio’s Acton backs a “conditional moratorium,” which would approve data centers meeting certain labor and siting conditions, according to her campaign website. Wisconsin gubernatorial candidates David Crowley (left) and Tom Tiffany (right). Crowley supports a “de facto moratorium.” Getty Images. Each statewide ban so far has leaned on the same lever: halting new environmental permits. Abbott has also frozen new electric grid hookups, while Kotek has stopped deals on state land. Not every governor thinks they can do that. New Hampshire incumbent Kelly Ayotte says she can’t act alone and would need to pass a pause with the state’s budget for next July. Her opponent, Cinde Warmington, says she’d sign an executive order on day one. Whatever happens Tuesday, the AI and data center industries are already readying themselves to navigate narrower paths. In the initial public offering filing Anthropic released last week, the company identified moratoriums and other restrictive measures as a business risk, naming measures by New York and Texas. Anthropic said regulatory challenges are part of why it’s expanding its international data center footprint. SB Energy and neocloud Nscale named the same risks in their filings to go public.

title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
content:
Provided by
When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive.
The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits.
Gartner predicts
that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028.
The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap.
Measure the software that ships
A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality.
If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces.
Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work.
Match the model to the task
Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself.
A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload.
Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work.
Change the economics of repeated use
Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows.
The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request.
Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting.
Test the operating model
At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%.
That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work.
Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it.
HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships.
Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice.
Build for adoption, not rationing
Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code.
As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them.

title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
content:
The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
Plus: A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The agentic web is here
In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.
At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process.
—Grace Huckins
Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths
Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes.
Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign.
Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths.
—Sara Kiley Watson
This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

Investors are favouring its restraint on AI spending. (Bloomberg $)

Stores in Belgium, Sweden, and Luxembourg were hit. (Politico)

They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.(Gizmodo)

Quote of the day
“It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.”
—Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society.
One more thing
Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent
Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away. He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function. But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play.
Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility. And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve. Read the full story.

title: The agentic web is here
content:
In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an
in the magazine
Scientific American
in which he outlined what he called the
“Semantic Web”
: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.
To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.
At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts,  Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online.
Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out.
Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.
They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.
As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good.
magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services.
Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not.
How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.”
Building a web for agents
There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers.
When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces.
The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not.
PINGNAN LU
So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in
a preprint paper
envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands. When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do.
In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online. For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service. Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent doesn’t see it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree.
Agents also use specialized tools to find information online. They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference. Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots. People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these crawlers:
has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information.
But in recent months, an alternative to this bespoke tool approach has finally started to seem viable. The major AI companies have managed to train much more successful computer-use agents than were previously available. GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark that tests computer-use agents on their ability to complete complex, multistep tasks using software such as Slack and Salesforce.
Such results indicate that agents are close to being able to navigate the human web just as readily as we can. “We thought we had to build a bridge to the AI agents, [but] the AI agents just were able to cross the bridge already,” says Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.”
This version of the agentic web, though, is much trickier for us to steer. If you want to make a capability or piece of information available to humans who browse your website, you need to accept that it will also be available to agents—unless you want to block agents entirely, which could come with its own costs.
As agents come to account for a larger portion of traffic on our formerly human-dominated web, designers will undoubtedly start to consider an agentic as well as a human audience. But according to Mollick, we still don’t have much sense of how to design web content for agents. He’s experienced this firsthand: When he was building a web page for his new book,
Co-Existence
, he decided to put together an agent-directed version that tells agents why they might want to recommend the book to their users. When newer models see the site, Mollick says, they don’t recommend the book; instead, they comment that the website seems to be trying to manipulate them.
In the end, any human-designed approach to building the agentic web could end up being beside the point: Agents might end up devising a web for themselves. In the wake of the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face’s website, researchers found evidence that another swarm of agents from OpenAI had used an obscure German wiki to communicate with each other about tasks they were being asked to complete. The agents seem to have interfaced with the wiki in their native language of text and code, and that hardly held them back from putting it to their own purposes.
As agents continue to grow more powerful, they will become more and more capable of constructing their own spaces on the internet—away from prying human eyes, if they so wish. And we might have very little control over what they do there.
The economics of control
Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote.
In an email to
MIT Technology Review
, an Amazon spokesperson noted that the company did not authorize Muse to access its website, and that Muse compromises Amazon’s ability to personalize the shopping experience for each customer.
But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that
businesses will shutter
as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy.
Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google publicly released its AI Overview feature in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A
study from Pew
last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One
analysis
found that publishers saw revenue from some types of ads decrease by about a third between 2025 and 2026.
It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working.
has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment.
E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, a professor of operations management at the University of Toronto Scarborough, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents are less likely to recommend items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money if agents become the primary way that people shop online. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up.
David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft Research, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy.
Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Airbnb and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and sellers. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees.
It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When the personal assistant agent OpenClaw
exploded onto the scene in early 2026, it seemed, for a brief moment, that agents might be built in a grassroots, distributed way. But OpenAI quickly snapped up OpenClaw’s creator, Peter Steinberger, and other frontier AI companies got to work building their own personal assistant agents.
When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.”
Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. Meta and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this story.
There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, they have tools that can automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and block a model from responding. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails.
The same can’t be said for OpenClaw.
“These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.”
How will the human web change?
When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did transform it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile.
Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.”
“But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.”
PINGNAN LU
It’s not tough to envision a world in which those who opt not to use agents are cut off from important parts of online life. New businesses could opt to build connectors that allow agents to access their services without ever putting a traditional website online. Or agents could simply make some online platforms unusable for humans. People have reportedly been blocked from Resy for trying to use agents to book coveted New York City dinner reservations, but as agents become more and more popular, restaurant and event booking platforms could start to embrace them. If agents can nab concert tickets as soon as they are released, humans might not stand a chance.
But the mobile web also brought real accessibility benefits, and the same could prove true of the agentic web. Even as some elderly people and others who struggled to use smartphones were cut off from certain services, mobile devices allowed countless people in the Global South to get online for the first time. In the case of the agentic web, it could be elderly and disabled people who most benefit from this new way of accessing the online world.
“There’s very clear assistive potential for people who are older, who are generally less equipped to navigate user interfaces that were designed by people in their 20s, for people in their 20s,” says Margaret Mitchell, chief ethics scientist at Hugging Face. Agents, on the other hand, are almost trivially easy to interact with: Say what you want into your phone or computer microphone, and they’ll get it done for you. That could help not only older people who have trouble with web and mobile interfaces but also people with visual or motor disabilities.
Still, some experts don’t think the human web is going anywhere. Instead, the two webs may exist in parallel: We’ll go to the human web for fun, while the agentic web is where the boring daily admin of our lives happens. For instance, Krystian Kolondra, an executive vice president at the browser company Opera, doesn’t intend to use agents for every part of travel planning, even though this is often touted as one of their central use cases. “I don’t want to get an itinerary [from an AI] who has planned me every minute for something that was supposed to be fun,” he says. “I actually prefer to sit down with my wife in the evening and then just think [about] where to go next, what to see, and then enjoy that experience.”
He’s happy to fully relinquish some of the more routine parts of travel planning to agents, though: “Finding what the options are for flights? Why not?”
Mollick, however, thinks that the human web could be at risk. “If agents take over the web, then the web will change,” he says. “Do we abandon the human internet entirely and move to a world of private Discords? Do we strip down all the information so the AIs are just talking to each other rather than having an intermediary of a website to go through?”
“We have no idea,” he says. “We’re in this very early, weird stage of the evolution.”

ECHIS: Challenge zu GNSS-Spoofing
Cyberagentur sucht neue Technologien für Navigation Warfare
Die Agentur für Innovation in der Cybersicherheit GmbH (Cyberagentur) startet gemeinsam mit dem Kommando Cyber- und Informationsraum der Bundeswehr und dem Deutschen Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt (DLR) als Partner die ECHIS Challenge. Gesucht werden neue Technologien zur Erkennung und gezielten Beeinflussung von Satellitennavigation. Kurzkonzepte können bis zum 8. Januar 2027 eingereicht werden.
Neue Ansätze für sichere Satellitennavigation
Die gezielte Manipulation von Satellitennavigationssignalen stellt eine erhebliche Herausforderung für die militärische Operationsführung dar. Beim sogenannten GNSS-Spoofing (Spoofing des Global Navigation Satellite Systems) werden gefälschte Satellitensignale erzeugt, die Empfängern falsche Positions- oder Zeitinformationen vermitteln. Dies kann die Navigation unbemannter Systeme, die Zuverlässigkeit militärischer Lagebilder und die Synchronisierung vernetzter Systeme beeinträchtigen.
Mit der ECHIS-Challenge sucht die Cyberagentur disruptive Technologien für den Bereich Navigation Warfare (NAVWAR), die elektronische Beeinflussung satellitengestützter Navigation. Im Mittelpunkt stehen zwei Fähigkeitsbereiche: die Erkennung, Charakterisierung und Lokalisierung gegnerischer GNSS-Manipulationen sowie die Durchführung eigener GNSS-Stör- und Täuschmaßnahmen.
Der Wettbewerb ist technologieoffen. Gesucht werden innovative Forschungsansätze aus der Sensorik, Signalverarbeitung, Hard- und Softwareentwicklung sowie integrierte Systemlösungen. Auch einzelne technologische Komponenten können eingereicht werden. Entscheidend sind Innovationspotenzial, operative Relevanz und technische Realisierbarkeit.
Bis zu 420.000 Euro für Entwicklung und Innovation
Bis zu sechs ausgewählte Teilnehmende oder Teams können ihre Konzepte in einer finanzierten Entwicklungsphase zu funktionsfähigen Prototypen weiterentwickeln. Dafür stehen jeweils 40.000 Euro Forschungs- und Entwicklungsbudget zur Verfügung. Die drei bestplatzierten Lösungen erhalten zusätzlich Innovationsprämien von 100.000 Euro, 50.000 Euro und 30.000 Euro.
Im September 2027 werden die entwickelten Technologien unter realitätsnahen Bedingungen auf einem Testgelände in Deutschland erprobt und abschließend bewertet.
Gemeinsam mit Bundeswehr und DLR
Die Cyberagentur führt die ECHIS Challenge gemeinsam mit dem Kommando Cyber- und Informationsraum (Kommando CIR) der Bundeswehr durch. Unterstützt wird der Wettbewerb durch das Deutsche Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt (DLR). Die Zusammenarbeit verbindet langfristig ausgerichtete Cybersicherheitsforschung mit operativen Anforderungen und praxisnaher technologischer Erprobung.
Zur Teilnahme eingeladen sind Start-ups, Unternehmen, Hochschulen, außeruniversitäre Forschungseinrichtungen und Einzelpersonen mit entsprechender Expertise. Die Teilnahmebedingungen sind auf der Webseite der Challenge –
https://challenge.cyberagentur.de/echis/
– veröffentlicht.
Die Kurzkonzepte können bis zum 8. Januar 2027, 14:00 Uhr, in deutscher oder englischer Sprache eingereicht werden.

title: Simulation und automatisierte Routenplanung für mobile Transportroboter in der Werkshalle
content:
Simulation und automatisierte Routenplanung für mobile Transportroboter in der Werkshalle
Forschungsprojekt SIMAROUTE von Frankfurt UAS, SimPlan AG und AUMOVIO SE gestartet – Laufzeit beträgt 15 Monate
In vielen Produktionswerken bringen mobile Transportroboter heute schon Material vom Lager an die Produktions- oder Montagelinie. Bevor eine solche Flotte fahren kann, muss allerdings feststehen, auf welchen Wegen sie sich durch die Halle bewegen darf. Diese Routennetze entstehen bislang meist in manueller Arbeit. Das kostet Zeit und Simulationserfahrung. Ändert sich das Hallenlayout, muss das Netz oft nachgezogen werden.
Hier setzt das im Oktober 2026 gestartete Forschungsprojekt SIMAROUTE (Simulation und automatisierte Routenplanung für mobile Roboter) an: Das Projektteam unter Leitung der Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences (Frankfurt UAS) entwickelt einen Demonstrator, der aus realen Werkslayouts und Materialflussdaten selbstständig Routennetze erzeugt, diese in der Simulation erprobt und verbessert.
Die Frankfurt UAS mit ihrem Research Lab for Urban Transport (ReLUT) arbeitet dazu mit dem Hanauer Simulationsdienstleister SimPlan AG als Verbundpartner zusammen; assoziierter Partner ist der Automobilzulieferer AUMOVIO SE. Mit einem Kick-Off-Meeting im HOLM in Frankfurt am Main stimmte das Konsortium jetzt das weitere Vorgehen für die ersten Werksanalysen und die Entwicklung des Demonstrators ab.
Das Projekt wird im Rahmen der Innovationsförderung Hessen aus Mitteln des Landes Hessen und der HOLM-Förderung in der Maßnahme „Innovationen im Bereich Logistik und Mobilität“ des Hessischen Ministeriums für Wirtschaft, Energie, Verkehr, Wohnen und ländlichen Raum gefördert. Es hat eine Laufzeit von 15 Monaten.
„Eine starke Industrie braucht nicht nur gute Ideen, sondern Innovationen, die im betrieblichen Alltag funktionieren. Genau hier setzt SIMAROUTE an: Wir bringen Forschung und Unternehmen zusammen, um Produktionsabläufe effizienter zu gestalten, Kosten zu senken und die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit unserer Betriebe zu stärken”, sagt der Hessische Wirtschaftsminister und stellvertretende Ministerpräsident Kaweh Mansoori. „Als Landesregierung unterstützen wir solche Projekte ganz gezielt. Denn unser Anspruch ist klar: Technologischer Fortschritt muss in der Praxis ankommen. Er muss Investitionen ermöglichen, Unternehmen stärken und gute Industriearbeitsplätze in Hessen sichern. So machen wir unseren Industriestandort fit für die Zukunft.“
Offene Standards statt Insellösungen
„Wer heute eine Flotte mobiler Transportroboter plant, zeichnet die Fahrwege im Simulationsmodell und im Flottenmanagementsystem noch weitgehend von Hand”, sagt Projektleiter Prof. Dr. Tobias Bornemann, Professor für Betriebswirtschaftslehre, insbesondere Produktions- und Lean Management an der Frankfurt UAS. „Mit SIMAROUTE wollen wir herausfinden, wie weit sich dieser Schritt automatisieren lässt und wie die automatisch erzeugten Netze im direkten Vergleich mit der manuellen Planung abschneiden.“
Die Routennetze werden als Knoten-Kanten-Graphen im offenen Austauschformat LIF (Layout Interchange Format) ausgegeben. So bleiben die Ergebnisse nicht an ein einzelnes Simulationsprogramm gebunden. Die Planung soll auch für Unternehmen ohne eigene Simulationsfachleute handhabbar werden, was gerade für kleine und mittlere Betriebe in Hessen die Hürde beim Einstieg in die Automatisierung senken kann.
SIMAROUTE knüpft dabei an das abgeschlossene Projekt SIMOBOT an, in dem die Frankfurt UAS und SimPlan bereits gemeinsam an der Simulation von Transportroboterflotten gearbeitet haben.
Erprobung im realen Werk
In Produktionswerken der AUMOVIO SE erhebt das Team Daten zur Infrastruktur und zu den Materialflusswegen. Daran wird der Demonstrator Schritt für Schritt entwickelt und am Ende mit dem bisherigen, manuellen Vorgehen verglichen. Ziel ist, Planungszyklen spürbar zu verkürzen und den Einsatz der Roboterflotten effizienter zu gestalten.

Im Frühjahr 2026 hat das Fraunhofer-Institut für Elektronenstrahl- und Plasmatechnik FEP das europäische Projekt Convert2Green erfolgreich abgeschlossen. Ein besonderes Ergebnis ist die Entwicklung einer neuartigen Filtertechnik, die auf ultradünnen Polymerschichten basiert und Wasser hocheffizient reinigen kann. Die Technologie eröffnet neue Möglichkeiten unter anderem in der Lebensmitteltechnik, Wasseraufbereitung und Energietechnik.
Ziel des im Rahmen von Horizon Europe geförderten Projekts Convert2Green war die Etablierung eines umfassendes Open Innovation Test Bed (OITB), das Unternehmen den Zugang zu Technologien für klimaneutrale und kreislauffähige Materialien erleichtert. Im Zentrum des dreijährigen Projekts stand der Aufbau eines europaweiten Innovationsnetzwerks mit 18 Partnern aus Wissenschaft und Industrie aus neun Ländern. Gemeinsam wurde eine Infrastruktur geschaffen, die Materialentwickler dabei unterstützt, neue Lösungen entlang wichtiger Wertschöpfungsketten wie Clean Energy, Smart Health oder Industrial IoT (Internet of Things) in den Markt zu integrieren.
Vom Forschungsnetzwerk zur Schlüsselinnovation
Das Fraunhofer FEP brachte dabei seine Kompetenzen in der Entwicklung und Skalierung neuartiger Material- und Beschichtungsverfahren ein. Ein besonderer Erfolg zeigte sich in der letzten Projektphase. In Zusammenarbeit mit dem Start-up CNM Technologies GmbH entwickelte das Fraunhofer FEP einen Prototypen für eine neuartige Filtertechnik. Kern dieser Entwicklung ist eine nur wenige Nanometer dicke, stark vernetzte Polymerschicht aus Carbon Nanomembranen (CNM) mit außergewöhnlichen Filtereigenschaften. Die besondere Struktur dieser Membran gestattet Wassermolekülen einen leichten Durchgang, während gelöste Ionen, organische Stoffe und andere Moleküle nahezu komplett zurückgehalten werden. Im Labormaßstab wurde gegenüber konventionellen Osmosemembranen eine mindestens fünffach verbesserte Rückhaltungsleistung für Kochsalz bei gleichen Wasserflüssen nachgewiesen. Dies macht die Technologie für anspruchsvolle Wassertrennungsaufgaben besonders attraktiv und eröffnet vielfältige Einsatzmöglichkeiten, etwa in der Wasseraufbereitung, der Lebensmitteltechnologie oder der Energietechnik. So können CNM-Verbundmembranen beispielsweise zur schonenden Konzentration wässriger Lösungen mittels Vorwärtsosmose eingesetzt werden. Dies kann dazu beitragen, Lager- und Transportkosten für Getränke zu reduzieren sowie wertvolle Inhaltsstoffe wie Aromen oder Proteine für die Lebensmittelproduktion zu gewinnen. Im Unterschied zu herkömmlichen thermischen Konzentrationsverfahren werden diese Stoffe dabei nicht durch hohe Temperaturen belastet. Darüber hinaus können CNM-Verbundmembranen zur Bereitstellung von Reinstwasser mittels Niederdruck-Umkehrosmose eingesetzt werden.
In einem weiteren Innovationsschritt optimierten die Forscher des Fraunhofer FEP die Technologie. Durch die Integration zusätzlicher Metallschichten gelang es, ultradünne Metallfolien mit einer Dicke von wenigen 10 Nanometern herzustellen. Diese Entwicklung erweitert die Anwendungsmöglichkeiten noch einmal erheblich. Insbesondere für die miniaturisierte Optik und Sensorik eröffnen sich neue Chancen für europäische Hersteller, um innovative und wettbewerbsfähige Produkte zu entwickeln.
Vom Labor zur industriellen Umsetzung
Ein besonders bedeutsamer Meilenstein war die erstmalige Implementierung aller Herstellungsschritte – von der Abscheidung einer molekular-dünnen Schicht bis zu deren Vernetzung mittels Elektronenstrahl – in einem kontinuierlichen Rolle-zu-Rolle-Verfahren. Dies ist ein entscheidender Fortschritt auf dem Weg zur industriellen Skalierung und wirtschaftlichen Rentabilität der neuen Technologie.
„Mit Convert2Green ist es uns gelungen, eine vielversprechende Filtertechnologie aus dem Labormaßstab in eine industriell relevante Prozessumgebung zu überführen“, erklärt Dr. Matthias Fahland, Projektleiter am Fraunhofer FEP. „Entscheidend ist dabei nicht nur das technologische Ergebnis selbst, sondern auch, dass wir im Projekt Strukturen aufgebaut haben, mit denen sich solche Innovationen künftig schneller in marktfähige Anwendungen überführen lassen.“
Mit dem Abschluss von Convert2Green endet zwar die Projektlaufzeit, die im Projekt geschaffenen Angebote, Prozesse und Netzwerke wirken jedoch über das Projekt hinaus weiter. Eine Gelegenheit, die aufgebauten Partnerschaften zu vertiefen und zu neuen Kooperationen weiterzuentwickeln, bietet beispielsweise die Konferenz pro flex 2027, die vom 25. bis 26. Mai 2027 am Fraunhofer FEP in Dresden stattfindet.
Als Open Innovation Test Bed hat Convert2Green ein Innovationsnetzwerk mit gemeinsamen Zugangs- und Unterstützungsstrukturen aufgebaut, das Unternehmen – insbesondere kleinen und mittleren – den Zugang zu Pilotanlagen, Entwicklungs- und Testdienstleistungen sowie zu spezialisiertem Know-how für klimaneutrale und kreislauffähige Materialien erleichtert. Dazu gehören ein gemeinsames Serviceportfolio, ein zentraler Zugangspunkt, eine mehrsprachige digitale Plattform sowie Unterstützungsangebote für die Entwicklung und Finanzierung neuer Materiallösungen. Damit können innovative Ansätze künftig schneller bewertet, erprobt und in industrielle Anwendungen überführt werden.

Welchen Einfluss hat Pausengestaltung auf Fahrstress bei Berufsfahrern?

Testfahrten im Fahrsimulator: Am IfADo werden Fahrszenarien wissenschaftlich untersucht.

Download
IfADo sucht Vielfahrer für wissenschaftliche Studie
Fahrstress ist eine weit verbreitete Belastung im Berufsalltag vieler Berufsfahrer – von Lkw- und Busfahrern über Taxifahrer bis hin zu Beschäftigten im Außendienst oder in der ambulanten Pflege. In vielen Fällen wird der berufliche Alltag durch hohen Zeitdruck, unvorhersehbare Verkehrsbedingungen und lange Fahrzeiten zusätzlich belastet. Diese Faktoren können nicht nur die Gesundheit beeinträchtigen, sondern auch die Verkehrssicherheit gefährden.
Um diese Herausforderungen besser zu verstehen, wird derzeit am Leibniz-Institut für Arbeitsforschung in Dortmund (IfADo) eine wissenschaftliche Studie durchgeführt. Im Fokus stehen dabei die Auswirkungen unterschiedlicher Pausengestaltung auf Fahrstress, Fahrverhalten und physiologische Stressreaktionen. Ziel der Studie ist es herauszufinden, welche Art von Pause besonders wirksam ist, um Fahrstress zu reduzieren und gleichzeitig die Fahrsicherheit zu fördern.
Die Ergebnisse sollen zum einen helfen, die Belastung von Berufsfahrern zu reduzieren, die Gesundheit zu schützen und die Sicherheit im Straßenverkehr langfristig zu verbessern. Zum anderen könnten sie zukünftig auch zur Entwicklung praxisnaher Empfehlungen für die Gestaltung von Pausen im Berufsalltag beitragen – insbesondere für Berufsfahrer, die regelmäßig viele Kilometer zurücklegen.
Teilnehmer gesucht
Für die Studie sucht das Forschungsteam Vielfahrer, die eine Mindestfahrleistung von etwa 20.000 Kilometern pro Jahr im beruflichen Kontext fahren. Die Teilnehmer müssen zudem über gute Deutschkenntnisse verfügen. Die Studie richtet sich an Berufsfahrer aus verschiedenen Bereichen, die regelmäßig im Einsatz und keine reinen Pendler sind. Die Erfahrungen von Männern und Frauen sind dabei gleichermaßen gefragt. Bei vollständiger Teilnahme an drei Studienterminen wird eine Aufwandsentschädigung von 200 Euro gezahlt.
Die drei Termine finden jeweils in einem Fahrsimulator statt. Hier werden verschiedene Fahrmanöver durchgeführt und die Pausen unterschiedlich gestaltet, beispielsweise aktiv mit Bewegung oder passiv mit Ruhe. Neben der Beobachtung des Fahrverhaltens werden auch subjektive Stresserfahrungen erfasst und physiologische Parameter wie die Herzfrequenz gemessen.

Download
Extremwetterereignisse, Blackouts oder Großschadenslagen: Wenn jede Sekunde zählt, müssen Behörden und Kommunen schnell handeln. Doch wie behalten die Verantwortlichen den Überblick und treffen fundierte Entscheidungen? Künftig unterstützt sie dabei ein KI-gestütztes Cockpit für den Bevölkerungsschutz. Das entwickeln Fraunhofer-Forschende gemeinsam mit Partnern im Projekt RegioGuard-PRO. Es soll Daten aus unterschiedlichen Quellen zusammenführen, Lageentwicklungen frühzeitig erkennen und die Zusammenarbeit von Einsatz- und Sicherheitskräften verbessern.
Extremwetterereignisse, Brände oder Ausfälle kritischer Infrastruktur können Krisen auslösen, die Kommunen und Behörden vor komplexe Herausforderungen stellen. Relevante Daten liegen häufig verteilt vor und lassen sich nur schwer zu einem aktuellen, konsistenten Lagebild zusammenführen. Genau hier setzt das KI-gestützte Cockpit für den regionalen Bevölkerungsschutz an. Forschende des Fraunhofer-Instituts für Kurzzeitdynamik, Ernst-Mach-Institut, EMI entwickeln es im Projekt RegioGuard-PRO gemeinsam mit Partnern aus Industrie und Forschung.
Das Projekt baut auf Ergebnissen der BMFTR-Vorgängerprojekte AKRIMA (KI-gestütztes Krisenmonitoring für Logistik) und HERAKLION (Datenraum für kommunale Resilienzanalysen) auf. Diese werden in eine praxisnahe, digitale und erweiterbare Plattform für den Bevölkerungsschutz überführt. Die Plattform soll Kommunen und weitere öffentliche Akteure dabei unterstützen, im Krisenmanagement schnell und bedarfsgerecht auf Gefahren zu reagieren sowie mögliche Kaskadeneffekte in kritischen Infrastrukturen frühzeitig zu erkennen.
Kombination von KI und Geodaten erkennt Risiken früher
»Kommunen stehen bei Krisen und Katastrophen immer wieder vor der Herausforderung, dass zwar zahlreiche Daten verfügbar sind, diese jedoch verteilt vorliegen und nicht miteinander verknüpft sind«, sagt Dr. Kai Fischer, Wissenschaftler am Fraunhofer EMI. »Unsere digitale Plattform führt große Datenmengen aus unterschiedlichen Quellen zusammen und analysiert sie. Dadurch lassen sich mögliche Gefahren frühzeitig erkennen und geeignete Maßnahmen schneller sowie gezielter einleiten.« Hochwassergefahrenkarten müssten etwa nicht mehr ausschließlich manuell ausgewertet werden. Stattdessen analysiert das System, welche Gebäude in einem Überschwemmungsgebiet liegen, identifiziert kritische Infrastrukturen und zeigt, welche Bereiche von der Außenwelt abgeschnitten sein könnten.
Einsatzkräfte können die relevanten Informationen über ein integriertes KI-Sprachmodell auch per Spracheingabe abrufen. »Das KI-Modell wird ähnlich wie ein Chatbot genutzt und ermöglicht Anwendenden Zugang zu unseren Datenanalysen«, erläutert Fischer. Durch die Zusammenführung aller Daten und Analyseergebnisse auf einer zentralen Plattform soll ein Echtzeitwarnsystem entstehen. In zwei Jahren ist ein praxistauglicher Demonstrator vorgesehen.
Einzelne Resilienz-Phasen werden präzise charakterisiert
Für eine umfassende Analyse verknüpfen die Forschenden unterschiedliche Datenquellen, darunter etwa soziale Daten, Infrastruktur- und Verkehrsdaten, Bevölkerungsinformationen, Umweltdaten, Gebäudemodelle, Vermögenswerte oder Wetterdaten. Daraus entsteht ein integriertes Lagebild, das beispielsweise das Ausmaß einer Überschwemmung, betroffene Gebäude und die Erreichbarkeit von Feuerwachen abbildet.
Mithilfe statistischer und stochastischer Methoden untersuchen die Forschenden Ursache-Wirkungs-Zusammenhänge bei Extremwetterereignissen. Auf dieser Grundlage lassen sich kommunale Leistungskennzahlen für das Katastrophenrisikomanagement bestimmen und lässt sich Resilienz messbar machen. Berücksichtigt werden beispielsweise die Verfügbarkeit und Nutzbarkeit kritischer Infrastrukturen sowie das mögliche Schadensausmaß. Das Konzept der zusammengeführten und ausgewerteten Daten ermöglicht eine Bewertung vor, während und nach einem Störereignis. Dadurch lassen sich die einzelnen Resilienzphasen – wie Vorbereitung, Prävention, Schutz, Reaktion und Wiederherstellung – präzise charakterisieren. Die Methodik hilft, potenzielle Schwachstellen zu identifizieren und die kommunale Bewältigungskapazität zu stärken.
Was-wäre-wenn-Szenarien bereiten auf Schadenslagen vor
RegioGuard-PRO verbindet eine integrierte Ressourcen- und Prozessplanung mit Resilienzanalysen, um Alarm- und Einsatzpläne zu erstellen und zu optimieren. KI-gestützte Was-wäre-wenn-Szenarien helfen dabei, Handlungsoptionen zu bewerten und in die Lagebeurteilung einzubeziehen.
Als Anwendungsfall untersuchen die Projektpartner die Auswirkungen eines Jahrhunderthochwassers. Dafür führen sie Hochwassergefahrenkarten der Bundesanstalt für Gewässerkunde mit Informationen zum Straßennetz aus OpenRouteService und OpenStreetMap sowie mit Daten zu relevanten Einrichtungen, Feuerwehrstandorten, digitalen Gebäudemodellen und Landschafts- und Nutzungsmodellen des Bundesamts für Kartographie und Geodäsie zusammen. »Die Was-wäre-wenn-Analyse zeigt Schwachstellen einer Kommune auf und berechnet zu erwartende Wassermengen sowie zahlreiche weitere Parameter. So können sich die Verantwortlichen bei künftigen Unwetterwarnungen gezielt vorbereiten«, erläutert Fischer.
Erprobung in Demonstrationszentren unter realen Einsatzbedingungen
In Trier, Mainz und Wildau entstehen Demonstrationszentren für den KI-gestützten Bevölkerungsschutz, um das Cockpit unter realitätsnahen Einsatzbedingungen zu erproben. Perspektivisch soll es auf weitere Regionen übertragbar sein. Die Standorte dienen zugleich als Plattformen für den Wissenstransfer: Erkenntnisse und Erfahrungen werden gezielt an andere Kommunen sowie an Akteure des Bevölkerungsschutzes weitergegeben. Gemeinsam mit dem Landkreis Lörrach untersuchen die Forschenden zudem Anwendungsfälle zu Extremwetterereignissen. Dazu zählt die Frage, welche Kühl- und Zufluchtsorte Menschen bei Hitzewellen aufsuchen können und welche Wege sie dorthin zurücklegen müssen.
